The blast of God's anger is, in Hebrew, the word for the great wind that brought the house down on Job's children (1:19). Whether he means it or not, Eliphaz has described how the wicked die, and it is how Job's children died.

verseByVerse.quote: The roar of the lion, the voice of the fierce lion, the teeth of the young lions are broken. The strong lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The roar of the lion, the voice of the fierce lion, the teeth of the young lions are broken. The strong lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered.

Five different Hebrew words for lion in two verses, a showpiece of the poet's art. The picture: the most powerful beast grows old, its teeth break, it starves, and its cubs are scattered. The mighty cannot keep their strength or their children when God is against them. Eliphaz does not say "you". He does not need to. The strong man of the east has lost his wealth, and his children are gone.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A word came to him in the night, a whisper, a spirit gliding past his face, a form he could not make out (vv. 12-16). Its message: Can mortal man be in the right before God? Even angels are charged with error; how much more men in houses of clay, crushed like the moth, who die without wisdom (vv. 17-21).
verseByVerse.theology: The question is the right one, and the gospel answers it. But this voice asks it only to leave a man with no hope, and the book gives us no reason to trust where it came from.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now a word was brought to me stealthily; my ear received the whisper of it. Amid thoughts from visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on men, dread came upon me, and trembling, which made all my bones shake. A spirit glided past my face; the hair of my flesh stood up. It stood still, but I could not discern its appearance. A form was before my eyes; there was silence, then I heard a voice:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a word was brought to me stealthily; my ear received the whisper of it. Amid thoughts from visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on men, dread came upon me, and trembling, which made all my bones shake.

Eliphaz now claims something more than experience: a revelation. A word came to him secretly, a whisper, in the night. A spirit glided past my face; the hair of my flesh stood up. It stood still, but I could not discern its appearance. A form was before my eyes; there was silence, then I heard a voice.

It is written to make the reader's skin crawl, and it does. But look at what is missing. There is no thus says the LORD. The spirit has no face. It comes by stealth. Some readers take it as a true revelation that Eliphaz misapplies; others as a voice that did not come from God at all, since its message, as we will see, leaves a man with no hope. The book does not say. What it does is set this scene beside the end, when the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind (38:1): openly, in person, to the man himself. God does not need to creep up on anyone. A believer who is told "God showed me in the night what your suffering means" is right to ask what Scripture says.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Can mortal man be in the right before God? Can a man be pure before his Maker?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can mortal man be in the right before God? Can a man be pure before his Maker?

That is the voice's message, and it is true. No one can stand before God on his own merits. Job will ask the same question himself, how can a man be in the right before God? (9:2), and Bildad will ask it again (25:4). It is the question the whole Bible asks.

That is what makes the friends so dangerous, and the reader must hold it firmly: they speak true sentences in a false speech. Eliphaz uses a true doctrine to reach a false verdict. Because no one is pure before God, he reasons, Job's suffering must be the fruit of Job's sin. But the question was never meant to condemn one man above others. It is the question that the gospel answers. God set forth Christ so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Rom 3:26). Eliphaz asks how a man can be right with God and leaves the question hanging over Job like a sword. The cross answers it.

verseByVerse.quote: Even in his servants he puts no trust, and his angels he charges with error; how much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed like the moth. Between morning and evening they are beaten to pieces; they perish forever without anyone regarding it. Is not their tent-cord plucked up within them, do they not die, and that without wisdom?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even in his servants he puts no trust, and his angels he charges with error; how much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed like the moth.

If even angels fall short before God, what hope for men of clay? It is a picture of how frail we are: bodies of mud, founded on dust, as easily crushed as a moth. Between morning and evening they are beaten to pieces; they perish forever without anyone regarding it. Is not their tent-cord plucked up within them, do they not die, and that without wisdom? The body is a tent; pull up the cord and it collapses.

Paul uses the same pictures, and the difference is the gospel. We have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God (2 Cor 4:7). If the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens (2 Cor 5:1). Eliphaz's vision ends with men dying without wisdom, unnoticed, for ever. Paul's ends with a house in heaven. Same clay, same tent. The difference is Christ, raised from the dust.

5.title: Blessed Is the One Whom God Reproves
5.text: <sup>1</sup>"Call now; is there anyone who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?<sup>2</sup>Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple.<sup>3</sup>I have seen the fool taking root, but suddenly I cursed his dwelling.<sup>4</sup>His children are far from safety; they are crushed in the gate, and there is no one to deliver them.<sup>5</sup>The hungry eat his harvest, and he takes it even out of thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth.<sup>6</sup>For affliction does not come from the dust, nor does trouble sprout from the ground,<sup>7</sup>but man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward.<sup>8</sup>"As for me, I would seek God, and to God would I commit my cause,<sup>9</sup>who does great things and unsearchable, marvelous things without number:<sup>10</sup>he gives rain on the earth and sends waters on the fields;<sup>11</sup>he sets on high those who are lowly, and those who mourn are lifted to safety.<sup>12</sup>He frustrates the devices of the crafty, so that their hands achieve no success.<sup>13</sup>He catches the wise in their own craftiness, and the schemes of the wily are brought to a quick end.<sup>14</sup>They meet with darkness in the daytime and grope at noonday as in the night.<sup>15</sup>But he saves the needy from the sword of their mouth and from the hand of the mighty.<sup>16</sup>So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts her mouth.<sup>17</sup>"Behold, blessed is the one whom God reproves; therefore despise not the discipline of the Almighty.<sup>18</sup>For he wounds, but he binds up; he shatters, but his hands heal.<sup>19</sup>He will deliver you from six troubles; in seven no evil shall touch you.<sup>20</sup>In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword.<sup>21</sup>You shall be hidden from the lash of the tongue, and shall not fear destruction when it comes.<sup>22</sup>At destruction and famine you shall laugh, and shall not fear the beasts of the earth.<sup>23</sup>For you shall be in league with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with you.<sup>24</sup>You shall know that your tent is at peace, and you shall inspect your fold and miss nothing.<sup>25</sup>You shall know also that your offspring shall be many, and your descendants as the grass of the earth.<sup>26</sup>You shall come to your grave in ripe old age, like a sheaf gathered up in its season.<sup>27</sup>Behold, this we have searched out; it is true. Hear, and know it for your good."
5.overview: Eliphaz goes on. No heavenly being will answer Job; vexation kills the fool, whose house is cursed, whose children are crushed and whose harvest others eat, for trouble does not sprout from the ground: man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward (vv. 1-7). He would seek God, who does unsearchable things, lifts the lowly, catches the wise in their own craftiness and gives the poor hope (vv. 8-16). Blessed is the one whom God reproves: God wounds and heals, and if Job accepts his discipline he will be kept from every trouble and will see his tent at peace, his children many and his grave in ripe old age. This we have searched out; it is true (vv. 17-27).
5.theology:
Eliphaz speaks true things falsely. God does catch the wise in their craftiness (quoted as Scripture, 1 Cor 3:19), does discipline those he loves (Prov 3:11-12; Heb 12:5-6), does wound and heal (Deut 32:39). But he applies them to a man God has declared innocent, and God will say he did not speak rightly (42:7). The wise man caught in his own wisdom is the speaker.

God's works are unsearchable (v. 9; Rom 11:33); Eliphaz claims to have searched out Job's case (v. 27). The comforter must hold both what God has revealed and the limits of what he knows.
5.examples:
The fool's children are crushed; Job's were.

I would seek God: Job does; the friends never speak to God at all.

The first Almighty in the book is on Eliphaz's lips.

Paul quotes Eliphaz as Scripture, and turns the line on the man who thinks himself wise.

No evil shall touch you, to a man evil has touched twice.

Unsearchable (v. 9) and searched out (v. 27) are the same Hebrew word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Man Is Born to Trouble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Call now; is there anyone who will answer you? (v. 1). Vexation kills the fool; Eliphaz has seen the fool's house cursed, his children crushed in the gate, his harvest eaten by others (vv. 2-5). Trouble does not sprout from the ground: man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Every picture Eliphaz chooses of the fool's end is a picture of what has happened to Job.

verseByVerse.quote: "Call now; is there anyone who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Call now; is there anyone who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?

The holy ones are heavenly beings, the angels. Eliphaz is mocking the idea that Job might find anyone in heaven to take his side: cry out if you like, no one will answer. He has just said that God puts no trust even in his angels (4:18). Who, then, would stand up for a man like Job?

It is a cruel question, and Job will spend the rest of the book reaching for an answer. He will wish for an arbiter between himself and God (9:33); he will say my witness is in heaven (16:19); he will say I know that my Redeemer lives (19:25). Eliphaz says there is no one. The Christian knows the name of the one there is: we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple. I have seen the fool taking root, but suddenly I cursed his dwelling. His children are far from safety; they are crushed in the gate, and there is no one to deliver them. The hungry eat his harvest, and he takes it even out of thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple. Vexation is exactly what Job poured out in chapter 3. Eliphaz is warning him that this kind of complaining is what fools die of. Job will pick the word up and throw it back: Oh that my vexation were weighed (6:2). Weigh my trouble before you judge my words.

I have seen the fool taking root, but suddenly I cursed his dwelling. His children are far from safety; they are crushed in the gate, and there is no one to deliver them. The hungry eat his harvest, and he takes it even out of thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth.

Eliphaz has seen a fool prosper and then fall: his home cursed, his children crushed, his harvest carried off by others. And he says I cursed his dwelling: he pronounced the fool's house cursed when he saw it. The friend who came to comfort is a man ready to pronounce curses, where Job, in chapter 1, pronounced a blessing. He tells it as a general lesson. But Job's children were crushed when a house fell on them, and his flocks were carried off by raiders. Eliphaz does not need to say "you are the fool". Every detail says it for him. This is how the friends will work throughout: they will describe "the wicked" and paint Job's portrait.

verseByVerse.quote: For affliction does not come from the dust, nor does trouble sprout from the ground, but man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For affliction does not come from the dust, nor does trouble sprout from the ground, but man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward.

The last line is often quoted as a sad truth about life: we are all born to trouble, as sure as sparks fly up from a fire. That is true, and it is part of what Eliphaz means. But look at the line before. Trouble does not grow out of the ground like a weed; it has a root, and the root is in man. Eliphaz means: your trouble came from somewhere, and it came from you.

Trouble is Job's own word again, 'amal, from 3:10. Job said he wished he had not been born to see trouble. Eliphaz answers that trouble is what human beings earn. Scripture agrees that suffering entered the world through sin (Rom 5:12). It refuses to say that each sufferer's pain can be traced to his own sin. That is the step Eliphaz takes, and it is the step God will judge.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As for me, I would seek God (v. 8), who does unsearchable things, sends rain, lifts the lowly and the mourners (vv. 9-11), frustrates the crafty and catches the wise in their own craftiness (vv. 12-14), and saves the needy, so that the poor have hope (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: A true and beautiful hymn. Paul quotes a line of it as Scripture (1 Cor 3:19). Job, not Eliphaz, is the one who will actually take it to God.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for me, I would seek God, and to God would I commit my cause, who does great things and unsearchable, marvelous things without number: he gives rain on the earth and sends waters on the fields; he sets on high those who are lowly, and those who mourn are lifted to safety.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for me, I would seek God, and to God would I commit my cause, who does great things and unsearchable, marvelous things without number.

This is good advice. Take it to God. And here is the irony of the whole debate: Job is the one who does it. Again and again in the chapters to come he will turn from the friends and speak to God directly, pleading, protesting, asking for a hearing. Not once in the whole debate do the friends speak to God. They only speak about him. When the LORD judges between them, that difference will matter.

He gives rain on the earth and sends waters on the fields; he sets on high those who are lowly, and those who mourn are lifted to safety. Lovely lines, and Mary will sing their gospel fulfilment: he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate (Luke 1:52). God does lift the mourner. He will lift this one, and Eliphaz will be standing by with a sacrifice in his hands when he does (42:8).

But look again at the first line. God gives rain on the earth. Jesus drew a lesson from the rain that cuts straight across Eliphaz's system: God makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust (Matt 5:45). Rain is not a wage paid to the good. It falls on everyone's field, out of kindness. If God's gifts are not handed out strictly by merit, neither are his losses. Eliphaz has quoted the evidence against his own case.

verseByVerse.quote: He frustrates the devices of the crafty, so that their hands achieve no success. He catches the wise in their own craftiness, and the schemes of the wily are brought to a quick end. They meet with darkness in the daytime and grope at noonday as in the night. But he saves the needy from the sword of their mouth and from the hand of the mighty. So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts her mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He frustrates the devices of the crafty, so that their hands achieve no success. He catches the wise in their own craftiness, and the schemes of the wily are brought to a quick end.

Paul quotes this line: For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, He catches the wise in their craftiness (1 Cor 3:19). It is one of only two places where the New Testament clearly quotes the book of Job, and it quotes Eliphaz. How can a man God rebuked be cited as Scripture? Because the book is inspired as a whole, it records his words truly, and this sentence is true. God does bring clever schemers to nothing. Eliphaz's error was never the sentence. It was aiming it at Job.

And Paul aims it rightly, at the man who thinks that he is wise (1 Cor 3:18). Read to the end of Job and see who that is. The wise man caught in his own wisdom is Eliphaz, who closes this speech with this we have searched out; it is true (v. 27), and to whom God says, My anger burns against you (42:7).

They meet with darkness in the daytime and grope at noonday as in the night. It is Deuteronomy's curse on the disobedient, you shall grope at noonday, as the blind grope in darkness (Deut 28:29), from the same chapter as the sores of 2:7. Job is sitting in the dark at noon. The friends will keep reaching for the curses of the covenant to describe the wicked, and each time the description fits the man in front of them.

But he saves the needy from the sword of their mouth and from the hand of the mighty. So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts her mouth. God rescues the needy from the sword of their mouth. Before long, the sword aimed at this needy man will be the friends' own words.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–27 — Blessed Is the One Whom God Reproves
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Blessed is the one whom God reproves; therefore despise not the discipline of the Almighty (v. 17). He wounds and heals; he will deliver from six troubles, from famine, sword, slander and wild beasts (vv. 18-23); your tent will be safe, your children many, your grave in ripe old age (vv. 24-26). This we have searched out; it is true (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: Much of it will come true for Job. None of it will come true for the reason Eliphaz gives.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, blessed is the one whom God reproves; therefore despise not the discipline of the Almighty. For he wounds, but he binds up; he shatters, but his hands heal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, blessed is the one whom God reproves; therefore despise not the discipline of the Almighty.

This is the first time the book calls God the Almighty (Hebrew Shaddai), the name it will use thirty-one times in all. And the sentence is true. Proverbs says it: the LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights (Prov 3:12). Hebrews quotes Proverbs to Christians under pressure: the Lord disciplines the one he loves (Heb 12:6). God does use suffering to correct and train his children, and a believer in trouble may rightly ask whether God is showing him something to put right.

But notice the difference. Hebrews gives this truth to sons as comfort: your pain is not a sign that you are unloved. Eliphaz gives it to Job as a diagnosis: your pain is a rebuke, so you must have done something to deserve it. The truth is the same. Its use is opposite. And in Job's case it is false, because God has already said his suffering was without reason (2:3).

For he wounds, but he binds up; he shatters, but his hands heal. Moses sang it (Deut 32:39) and Hosea preached it (Hos 6:1), and it will prove true of Job. The wounding hand is the healing hand. But it will not heal him by the route Eliphaz prescribes.

verseByVerse.quote: He will deliver you from six troubles; in seven no evil shall touch you. In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword. You shall be hidden from the lash of the tongue, and shall not fear destruction when it comes. At destruction and famine you shall laugh, and shall not fear the beasts of the earth. For you shall be in league with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will deliver you from six troubles; in seven no evil shall touch you. Six, then seven: a way of saying every trouble, however many. No evil shall touch you. Touch is Satan's word: touch all that he has (1:11), touch his bone and his flesh (2:5). Evil has touched Job, twice, and Job will cry to these same friends, Have mercy on me ... for the hand of God has touched me! (19:21).

In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword. You shall be hidden from the lash of the tongue, and shall not fear destruction when it comes. At destruction and famine you shall laugh, and shall not fear the beasts of the earth. For you shall be in league with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with you.

A picture of perfect safety: no famine, no sword, no stone in the plough-land, no wild beast. It is the peace God promised Israel for obedience. One line stands out. Job will be hidden from the lash of the tongue. He is being lashed by one now.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall know that your tent is at peace, and you shall inspect your fold and miss nothing. You shall know also that your offspring shall be many, and your descendants as the grass of the earth. You shall come to your grave in ripe old age, like a sheaf gathered up in its season.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall know that your tent is at peace, and you shall inspect your fold and miss nothing. You shall know also that your offspring shall be many, and your descendants as the grass of the earth. You shall come to your grave in ripe old age, like a sheaf gathered up in its season.

Imagine hearing this beside ten new graves. Your offspring shall be many. Eliphaz means it kindly; it is the reward he offers if Job will only confess. But Job has nothing true to confess, and every line of the promise names something he has just lost.

The last picture is the loveliest: like a sheaf gathered up in its season. A good death is a harvest, the grain brought in when it is ripe and not before. Job's children were cut down green. Eliphaz holds out the ripe sheaf as the reward of the righteous, and does not see the field behind Job.

And here is the strangest thing: it comes true. At the end of the book Job will have seven sons and three daughters again, and Job died, an old man, and full of days (42:17). Eliphaz promised the right blessings for the wrong reason. They came to Job not as the wage for a false confession, but as the free gift of a God who had vindicated him. God's kindness is larger than the friends' theology, and it does not run on their terms.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, this we have searched out; it is true. Hear, and know it for your good."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, this we have searched out; it is true. Hear, and know it for your good.

We: Eliphaz speaks for the three of them, for the whole tradition. Searched out: they have studied the matter and settled it. But listen to what he said in verse 9: God does things unsearchable. In Hebrew it is the same word. God's ways cannot be searched out, says Eliphaz; and we have searched this out, says Eliphaz. He has not noticed the contradiction.

Job will take up the line about God's unsearchable works and say it almost word for word himself (9:10). Paul will cry, How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! (Rom 11:33). That is the right response to the God of Job. Every believer who sits with a sufferer should be slow to say, "we have searched this out." There is a proper confidence about what God has said, and a proper humility about what he has not. The friends had the first without the second.

6.title: Oh That My Vexation Were Weighed
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Oh that my vexation were weighed, and all my calamity laid in the balances!<sup>3</sup>For then it would be heavier than the sand of the sea; therefore my words have been rash.<sup>4</sup>For the arrows of the Almighty are in me; my spirit drinks their poison; the terrors of God are arrayed against me.<sup>5</sup>Does the wild donkey bray when he has grass, or the ox low over his fodder?<sup>6</sup>Can that which is tasteless be eaten without salt, or is there any taste in the juice of the mallow?<sup>7</sup>My appetite refuses to touch them; they are as food that is loathsome to me.<sup>8</sup>"Oh that I might have my request, and that God would fulfill my hope,<sup>9</sup>that it would please God to crush me, that he would let loose his hand and cut me off!<sup>10</sup>This would be my comfort; I would even exult in pain unsparing, for I have not denied the words of the Holy One.<sup>11</sup>What is my strength, that I should wait? And what is my end, that I should be patient?<sup>12</sup>Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh bronze?<sup>13</sup>Have I any help in me, when resource is driven from me?<sup>14</sup>"He who withholds kindness from a friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty.<sup>15</sup>My brothers are treacherous as a torrent-bed, as torrential streams that pass away,<sup>16</sup>which are dark with ice, and where the snow hides itself.<sup>17</sup>When they melt, they disappear; when it is hot, they vanish from their place.<sup>18</sup>The caravans turn aside from their course; they go up into the waste and perish.<sup>19</sup>The caravans of Tema look, the travelers of Sheba hope.<sup>20</sup>They are ashamed because they were confident; they come there and are disappointed.<sup>21</sup>For you have now become nothing; you see my calamity and are afraid.<sup>22</sup>Have I said, 'Make me a gift'? Or, 'From your wealth offer a bribe for me'?<sup>23</sup>Or, 'Deliver me from the adversary's hand'? Or, 'Redeem me from the hand of the ruthless'?<sup>24</sup>"Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand how I have gone astray.<sup>25</sup>How forceful are upright words! But what does reproof from you reprove?<sup>26</sup>Do you think that you can reprove words, when the speech of a despairing man is wind?<sup>27</sup>You would even cast lots over the fatherless, and bargain over your friend.<sup>28</sup>"But now, be pleased to look at me, for I will not lie to your face.<sup>29</sup>Please turn; let no injustice be done. Turn now; my vindication is at stake.<sup>30</sup>Is there any injustice on my tongue? Cannot my palate discern the cause of calamity?
6.overview: Job answers Eliphaz. If his calamity were weighed it would outweigh the sand of the sea, and that is why his words were rash; the arrows of the Almighty are in him, and a donkey does not bray without cause (vv. 1-7). He asks God to crush him; his comfort would be that he has not denied the words of the Holy One; he has no strength left to wait (vv. 8-13). He accuses his friends of withholding loyal love: they are like a desert stream that fails the caravans in summer, and they are afraid at what they see, though he asked them for nothing (vv. 14-23). Teach me, and I will be silent: they rebuke a despairing man's words, which are wind; let them look at him and turn, for his vindication is at stake (vv. 24-30).
6.theology:
Loyal love (chesed) to a suffering friend belongs to the fear of God (v. 14); the friends, not Job, are failing it. Christ is the spring that does not fail (John 4:14).

Job feels God's arrows and is right that God's hand is in his trouble (2:3), and wrong about its intent. His comfort is that he has not denied God's word (v. 10); his strength is gone, and God's power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:9).
6.examples:
Weigh the pain before you judge the words.

Job admits his words were rash.

The only time he calls God the Holy One is while asking to die.

A wadi: full in winter, dry in summer.

You see my calamity and are afraid: the friends need him to be guilty.

He asked them for nothing but themselves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Oh That My Vexation Were Weighed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job answers: weigh my calamity and it would outweigh the sand of the sea, therefore my words have been rash (vv. 1-3). The arrows of the Almighty are in me (v. 4). A donkey does not bray over grass; there is a reason for his cry, and what he is given to eat is loathsome to him (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Job admits his words are rash and asks that his pain be weighed before his words are judged. That is a fair request, and the friends never grant it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "Oh that my vexation were weighed, and all my calamity laid in the balances! For then it would be heavier than the sand of the sea; therefore my words have been rash.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Job answered and said: Oh that my vexation were weighed, and all my calamity laid in the balances! For then it would be heavier than the sand of the sea; therefore my words have been rash.

Eliphaz warned that vexation kills the fool (5:2). Job takes the word and asks for it to be weighed. Put my trouble on the scales before you judge what I said. It would outweigh the sand of every shore. Later he will ask God for the same thing: Let me be weighed in a just balance (31:6).

And he admits it: my words have been rash. He does not claim that chapter 3 was measured speech. He says it was wild, and that the wildness is the size of the pain. That is honesty, not defiance. Anyone who has sat with the bereaved knows it. The first thing to do with rash words from a crushed person is to weigh the crushing, not the words.

verseByVerse.quote: For the arrows of the Almighty are in me; my spirit drinks their poison; the terrors of God are arrayed against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the arrows of the Almighty are in me; my spirit drinks their poison; the terrors of God are arrayed against me.

For the first time Job says plainly who he thinks is behind it: not raiders, not bad luck, but the Almighty. He pictures God as an archer and himself as the target, the arrows tipped with poison, God's terrors drawn up against him like an army. The poet of Lamentations would say the same: he bent his bow and set me as a target for his arrow (Lam 3:12).

Job is right that God's hand is in it; the LORD said so in heaven (2:3). He is wrong about what the hand intends. He thinks he is God's enemy. The reader knows he is God's delight. Many believers have felt exactly this, that God has turned against them, and the book lets them say it, while showing them what Job could not see: the arrows he feels are not the verdict of an enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: Does the wild donkey bray when he has grass, or the ox low over his fodder? Can that which is tasteless be eaten without salt, or is there any taste in the juice of the mallow? My appetite refuses to touch them; they are as food that is loathsome to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does the wild donkey bray when he has grass, or the ox low over his fodder? Animals do not complain when they are fed. When a donkey brays, something is wrong. Job's cries have a cause, and it is not a weak character.

Can that which is tasteless be eaten without salt, or is there any taste in the juice of the mallow? My appetite refuses to touch them; they are as food that is loathsome to me. The mallow's juice was slimy and flavourless, perhaps like raw egg white. Job may mean the food of suffering he is forced to eat every day; or he may mean the advice he has just been served, which has no salt in it. Either way he cannot swallow it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — That It Would Please God to Crush Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He asks God to end his life (vv. 8-9), and his one comfort would be that I have not denied the words of the Holy One (v. 10). He has no strength left to wait: he is not stone or bronze (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Even wishing to die, Job holds on to the one thing Satan tried to take: he has not denied God's word.

verseByVerse.quote: "Oh that I might have my request, and that God would fulfill my hope, that it would please God to crush me, that he would let loose his hand and cut me off! This would be my comfort; I would even exult in pain unsparing, for I have not denied the words of the Holy One.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh that I might have my request, and that God would fulfill my hope, that it would please God to crush me, that he would let loose his hand and cut me off!

His one request is that God would finish it. Cut me off is a weaver's word: cut the finished cloth from the loom. King Hezekiah, sick to death, used the same picture: like a weaver I have rolled up my life; he cuts me off from the loom (Isa 38:12). Job does not reach for the knife himself. He asks God, because his life is God's to end.

This would be my comfort; I would even exult in pain unsparing, for I have not denied the words of the Holy One. Here is the one thing he still has. If he died now, he would die without having denied God's word. That was exactly what Satan wanted him to do (1:11; 2:5), and he has not done it. It is the only time in the book that Job calls God the Holy One. Even while asking to die, he names God by his holiness and clings to his word. That is not the speech of a man who has lost his faith. It is faith at the end of its strength.

verseByVerse.quote: What is my strength, that I should wait? And what is my end, that I should be patient? Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh bronze? Have I any help in me, when resource is driven from me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is my strength, that I should wait? And what is my end, that I should be patient? Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh bronze? Have I any help in me, when resource is driven from me?

Eliphaz told him to be patient. Job says: with what? I am not made of stone. My body is not bronze. There is nothing left in me to hold on with.

He is right that the strength is not in him, and Scripture never says it should be. They who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength (Isa 40:31); the strength comes from the one waited for. Paul learned it in his own weakness: My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:9). Job has reached the end of himself. That is not the end of the road.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He who withholds kindness from a friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty (v. 14). His friends are like a desert stream that vanishes in summer and fails the caravans that came looking for it (vv. 15-20). You see my calamity and are afraid (v. 21). He asked them for nothing, no gift, no ransom (vv. 22-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The friends are afraid of what Job's suffering would mean if he were innocent. So they need him to be guilty.

verseByVerse.quote: "He who withholds kindness from a friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who withholds kindness from a friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty.

Kindness is chesed, loyal love, the faithfulness that holds when holding is costly. Eliphaz told Job that his fear of God should be his confidence (4:6). Job turns it round. A man who withholds loyal love from a suffering friend is the one who has abandoned the fear of the Almighty. The friends think they are defending God. In failing their friend, they are failing him.

There is a test in that for every church. The measure of our fear of God is not how firmly we hold our doctrine while a brother suffers. It is whether we stay with him.

The Hebrew of this verse is compressed, and it can also be read another way, which several translations follow: "a despairing man should have kindness from his friend, even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty". On that reading Job says something even more searching. Suppose my faith did falter under this. That is exactly when a friend's loyalty is owed. Both readings land in the same place: the one who is going under needs love, not a verdict, and he needs it most when his grip on God is weakest.

verseByVerse.quote: My brothers are treacherous as a torrent-bed, as torrential streams that pass away, which are dark with ice, and where the snow hides itself. When they melt, they disappear; when it is hot, they vanish from their place. The caravans turn aside from their course; they go up into the waste and perish. The caravans of Tema look, the travelers of Sheba hope. They are ashamed because they were confident; they come there and are disappointed. For you have now become nothing; you see my calamity and are afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My brothers are treacherous as a torrent-bed, as torrential streams that pass away, which are dark with ice, and where the snow hides itself. When they melt, they disappear; when it is hot, they vanish from their place.

A desert wadi: a gully that roars with water in winter, when no one needs it, and is bone dry in the summer heat, when everyone does. The caravans turn aside from their course; they go up into the waste and perish. The caravans of Tema look, the travelers of Sheba hope. Traders from the Arabian desert, Sheba among them, the country of the raiders who took his oxen (1:15), leave their route to reach the stream they remember, and find stones. They are ashamed because they were confident; they come there and are disappointed. So are his friends. Full when he was prospering; dry now.

Jeremiah once said the same thing to God himself: Will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail? (Jer 15:18). God is not. Jesus offered a woman at a well water ... welling up to eternal life (John 4:14), a spring that does not dry up in the heat.

For you have now become nothing; you see my calamity and are afraid. Here is the heart of it. They are afraid. If a man like Job can lose everything without having done anything to deserve it, then so can they. Their theology is their shelter, and Job's innocence would blow the roof off. So they need him to be guilty. That is still why people blame the sufferer: it keeps them safe.

The Hebrew makes the point with a play on sound: see and be afraid are almost the same word. They looked, and what they saw frightened them. The friend who is afraid of what your suffering means for him cannot help you with it. The Christian can afford to look, because his safety was never in having deserved his blessings. It is in Christ, and nothing that happens to a brother can take it away.

verseByVerse.quote: Have I said, 'Make me a gift'? Or, 'From your wealth offer a bribe for me'? Or, 'Deliver me from the adversary's hand'? Or, 'Redeem me from the hand of the ruthless'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have I said, Make me a gift? Or, From your wealth offer a bribe for me? Or, Deliver me from the adversary's hand? Or, Redeem me from the hand of the ruthless?

What did I ask you for? Not money. Not a payment to buy me out of trouble. Not a rescue. I asked you for nothing but yourselves. The friends cannot even give that, and it cost nothing.

Notice the last word, redeem. Job is not asking the friends to redeem him. He will look much higher for that, and find it: I know that my Redeemer lives (19:25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — Teach Me, and I Will Be Silent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand how I have gone astray (v. 24). They rebuke the words of a despairing man, which are wind (vv. 25-27). Be pleased to look at me, for I will not lie to your face; my vindication is at stake (vv. 28-30).
verseByVerse.theology: Job is willing to be corrected. He asks only to be shown, not presumed.

verseByVerse.quote: "Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand how I have gone astray. How forceful are upright words! But what does reproof from you reprove? Do you think that you can reprove words, when the speech of a despairing man is wind? You would even cast lots over the fatherless, and bargain over your friend.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand how I have gone astray. Job is teachable. Show me where I went wrong and I will stop talking. It is the prayer of Psalm 139 turned to his friends: see if there be any grievous way in me (Ps 139:24). He does not claim to be sinless. He asks to be shown, not presumed.

How forceful are upright words! But what does reproof from you reprove? Do you think that you can reprove words, when the speech of a despairing man is wind? Honest words have force. Theirs prove nothing, because they are aimed at the wrong thing. They are correcting Job's words as if they were a lecture on doctrine, when they were the cry of a man in despair. Bildad will throw the word straight back at him: the words of your mouth are a great wind (8:2). The lesson stands for every counsellor: hear grief as grief before you correct it as theology.

You would even cast lots over the fatherless, and bargain over your friend. The harshest line in the chapter. People who can treat a suffering friend as a case to be argued would gamble for an orphan's goods. Remember the line. Job had been the man who delivered ... the fatherless who had none to help him (29:12), and in his last speech he will stake his whole life on it (31:17, 21). Before the debate is over, Eliphaz will accuse him of exactly this: the arms of the fatherless were crushed (22:9). The charge that fits the accusers will be laid on the accused.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now, be pleased to look at me, for I will not lie to your face. Please turn; let no injustice be done. Turn now; my vindication is at stake. Is there any injustice on my tongue? Cannot my palate discern the cause of calamity?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now, be pleased to look at me, for I will not lie to your face. Please turn; let no injustice be done. Turn now; my vindication is at stake.

Look at me. They have been looking at a theory. Job asks them to look at a man. To your face is the phrase Satan used when he said Job would curse God to his face (1:11). Job will not curse God to his face, and he will not lie to his friends' faces either. My vindication is his righteousness, his standing as an innocent man. That, not his health, is what he is fighting for from here on.

Is there any injustice on my tongue? Cannot my palate discern the cause of calamity? The palate that knew the mallow's juice was tasteless (v. 6) can taste the difference between a lie and the truth. Job knows his own heart better than they do. And the reader knows he is right, because God has said so (2:3).

7.title: What Is Man, That You Make So Much of Him?
7.text: <sup>1</sup>"Has not man a hard service on earth, and are not his days like the days of a hired hand?<sup>2</sup>Like a slave who longs for the shadow, and like a hired hand who looks for his wages,<sup>3</sup>so I am allotted months of emptiness, and nights of misery are apportioned to me.<sup>4</sup>When I lie down I say, 'When shall I arise?' But the night is long, and I toss and turn till the dawn.<sup>5</sup>My flesh is clothed with worms and dirt; my skin hardens, then breaks out afresh.<sup>6</sup>My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle and come to their end without hope.<sup>7</sup>"Remember that my life is a breath; my eye will never again see good.<sup>8</sup>The eye of him who sees me will behold me no more; while your eyes are on me, I shall be gone.<sup>9</sup>As the cloud fades and vanishes, so he who goes down to Sheol does not come up;<sup>10</sup>he returns no more to his house, nor does his place know him anymore.<sup>11</sup>"Therefore I will not restrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.<sup>12</sup>Am I the sea, or a sea monster, that you set a guard over me?<sup>13</sup>When I say, 'My bed will comfort me, my couch will ease my complaint,'<sup>14</sup>then you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions,<sup>15</sup>so that I would choose strangling and death rather than my bones.<sup>16</sup>I loathe my life; I would not live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are a breath.<sup>17</sup>What is man, that you make so much of him, and that you set your heart on him,<sup>18</sup>visit him every morning and test him every moment?<sup>19</sup>How long will you not look away from me, nor leave me alone till I swallow my spit?<sup>20</sup>If I sin, what do I do to you, you watcher of mankind? Why have you made me your mark? Why have I become a burden to you?<sup>21</sup>Why do you not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity? For now I shall lie in the earth; you will seek me, but I shall not be."
7.overview: Job describes human life as hard service, and his own as months of emptiness and nights of misery, tossing till dawn, his skin broken and crawling, his days running out without hope (vv. 1-6). Then he turns to God: remember that my life is a breath; I will go down to Sheol and not return (vv. 7-10). He will not restrain his mouth. Is he the sea, that God must set a guard over him? His bed gives him nightmares, and he would choose death; leave me alone, for my days are a breath (vv. 11-16). What is man, that you make so much of him, testing him every moment? If he has sinned, why does God not pardon him before he lies in the earth and God seeks him and he is gone (vv. 17-21)?
7.theology:
Job's first words to God are complaint, and they are prayer; the friends never pray at all. He turns Psalm 8's wonder at God's attention into a groan at God's scrutiny, and Hebrews finds the psalm fulfilled in Jesus, made lower than the angels to taste death for everyone (Heb 2:6-9).

Job asks for pardon and assumes God will seek him. His two cries, hard service and unpardoned sin, are answered together: her warfare is ended, that her iniquity is pardoned (Isa 40:2); the Lamb of God takes away sin (John 1:29).
7.examples:
Hard service is a soldier's term of duty.

The shuttle runs out of thread; hope and thread are one Hebrew word.

Remember: Job's first words to God.

God sets bars for the sea (38:8-11); Job is not the sea.

Psalm 8's wonder becomes Job's groan.

You will seek me: faith inside the complaint.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A Hard Service on Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Human life is a hard service, a hired man's day, a slave longing for shade (vv. 1-2). Job has been given months of emptiness and nights of misery (v. 3); he tosses till dawn, his skin crawling with worms and breaking out afresh (vv. 4-5), his days running out without hope (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Job describes the life of a sufferer from the inside: the long night, the body, the days that go nowhere.

verseByVerse.quote: "Has not man a hard service on earth, and are not his days like the days of a hired hand? Like a slave who longs for the shadow, and like a hired hand who looks for his wages, so I am allotted months of emptiness, and nights of misery are apportioned to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Has not man a hard service on earth, and are not his days like the days of a hired hand? Like a slave who longs for the shadow, and like a hired hand who looks for his wages, so I am allotted months of emptiness, and nights of misery are apportioned to me.

Hard service is the Hebrew word for military service, a soldier's term of duty. Life is a conscription. A labourer in the field longs for evening and his pay; a slave in the sun longs for a patch of shade. They at least have something to wait for. Job's shift has no end and no wage. He has been allotted emptiness, month after month. The illness has gone on for months now, not days.

Hold on to that first word, service or warfare, and to the last request of this chapter, why do you not pardon my transgression? (v. 21). Isaiah was sent with a message that answers both at once: cry to her that her warfare is ended, that her iniquity is pardoned (Isa 40:2). That is the gospel in one sentence, and it is spoken to exhausted people. In Christ the service is over and the pardon is given.

verseByVerse.quote: When I lie down I say, 'When shall I arise?' But the night is long, and I toss and turn till the dawn. My flesh is clothed with worms and dirt; my skin hardens, then breaks out afresh. My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle and come to their end without hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I lie down I say, When shall I arise? But the night is long, and I toss and turn till the dawn. Anyone who has been ill or grieving knows this night. He goes to bed longing for morning; the hours do not move; he turns over and over until grey light comes. Scripture does not think sleeplessness too small to record.

My flesh is clothed with worms and dirt; my skin hardens, then breaks out afresh. The sores of 2:7, described by the man who has them: crusting, cracking, weeping again, and maggots in the wounds.

My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle and come to their end without hope. The shuttle flies back and forth across the loom until the thread runs out. And there is a play on words here: the Hebrew for hope, tiqvah, also means a cord or thread; it is the word for the scarlet cord Rahab tied in her window (Josh 2:18). Job's days run on like the shuttle and come to the end of the thread. Out of thread; out of hope.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–16 — Remember That My Life Is a Breath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job turns to God: Remember that my life is a breath (v. 7). Soon he will be gone like a cloud, and his place will not know him (vv. 8-10). Therefore I will not restrain my mouth (v. 11). Am I the sea, or a sea monster, that you set a guard over me? (v. 12). Even sleep brings terrors; he loathes his life: Leave me alone, for my days are a breath (vv. 13-16).
verseByVerse.theology: For the first time in the book Job speaks to God rather than about him. It is a complaint, and it is prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember that my life is a breath; my eye will never again see good. The eye of him who sees me will behold me no more; while your eyes are on me, I shall be gone. As the cloud fades and vanishes, so he who goes down to Sheol does not come up; he returns no more to his house, nor does his place know him anymore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember that my life is a breath; my eye will never again see good.

Here the chapter turns, and so does the book. Remember is spoken to God. These are the first words Job addresses to God directly since his troubles began, and from here on he will keep doing it. Eliphaz said, I would seek God (5:8). Job does. The friends never once will.

And his first prayer is: remember what I am. A breath. The psalmist says God does remember it: He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again (Ps 78:39). The eye of him who sees me will behold me no more; while your eyes are on me, I shall be gone. As the cloud fades and vanishes, so he who goes down to Sheol does not come up; he returns no more to his house, nor does his place know him anymore. Sheol is the Hebrew name for the grave, the place of the dead. Psalm 103 says the same of us, that the wind passes over us and its place knows it no more (Ps 103:16), and adds the comfort Job cannot yet see: he remembers that we are dust (Ps 103:14).

Job sees no way back from the grave, only a door that closes. Later he will begin to hope past it (14:14; 19:25-27). The Christian stands where Job could not, on the far side of an empty tomb.

Notice the eyes in verse 8. While your eyes are on me, I shall be gone. God is looking at him, and he will vanish while God looks. It is the first half of a frame that closes the chapter: you will seek me, but I shall not be (v. 21). Job cannot stop believing that God's eyes are on him. His fear is only that God will look away too long, or look again too late. James takes up the cloud and asks, What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes, and draws a different lesson from it: say If the Lord wills (James 4:14-15). The shortness of life is not a reason to despair of God but to lean on him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore I will not restrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul. Am I the sea, or a sea monster, that you set a guard over me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I will not restrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul. Therefore: since life is this short, he will not waste it in silence. This is a decision, not an outburst. He will speak, and he will speak to God. Better an honest complaint to God than a polite silence that has given up on him.

Am I the sea, or a sea monster, that you set a guard over me? The ancient world pictured the sea as chaos that God had to hold back. Job feels treated like that: watched, penned in, as if he were a danger to creation. When God answers, he will speak of exactly this: who shut in the sea with doors and said, Thus far shall you come, and no farther (38:8, 11). God does set bars for the sea. Job is not the sea. He is a man God is holding.

verseByVerse.quote: When I say, 'My bed will comfort me, my couch will ease my complaint,' then you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions, so that I would choose strangling and death rather than my bones. I loathe my life; I would not live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are a breath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I say, My bed will comfort me, my couch will ease my complaint, then you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions, so that I would choose strangling and death rather than my bones.

Even sleep, when it comes, is not rest. It brings nightmares, and Job lays them at God's door too. He would rather choke than go on in this body.

Set this beside Eliphaz. He too had visions of the night (4:13), and came away from his with a doctrine he was sure of. Job's come to him as terror, and teach him nothing. Neither man's nights are a safe guide to what God is doing. The book will not let either the confident dreamer or the frightened one have the last word; God will speak openly, from the storm (38:1).

I loathe my life; I would not live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are a breath. A breath here is hevel, the word Ecclesiastes uses for everything that vanishes like vapour. Leave me alone is his first request to God, and it is a desperate one. He does not want God to go away for good. He wants him to stop pressing. The same man will soon be begging God to come near and answer (13:22; 23:3).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What is man, that you make so much of him, and that you set your heart on him? (vv. 17-18). Why will God not look away even long enough to swallow (v. 19)? If I sin, what do I do to you, you watcher of mankind? Why do you not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity? Soon you will seek me, but I shall not be (vv. 20-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Job turns the psalm of wonder at God's care into a complaint at God's scrutiny. The answer to both is a Son of Man who was tested for us, and a God who takes iniquity away.

verseByVerse.quote: What is man, that you make so much of him, and that you set your heart on him, visit him every morning and test him every moment? How long will you not look away from me, nor leave me alone till I swallow my spit?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is man, that you make so much of him, and that you set your heart on him, visit him every morning and test him every moment?

Readers of the Psalms will hear Psalm 8 turned inside out: what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him? (Ps 8:4). The psalmist marvels that God pays attention to tiny man. Job groans that God will not stop paying attention. The same fact, God's close attention, is wonder in one mouth and torment in another.

And there is an echo only the reader can hear. Set your heart on him is the idiom the LORD used in heaven: Have you considered my servant Job? (1:8) is literally "have you set your heart on" him. Job is right that he is being watched and tested every moment. He does not know that it began in the council, or that God's own heart was set on him in delight.

How long will you not look away from me, nor leave me alone till I swallow my spit? Not even a moment's pause, not long enough to swallow.

Hebrews takes up Psalm 8 and finds its answer in one man: we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death (Heb 2:9). What is man? The Son of Man was tested every moment, on our behalf, and did not fail.

verseByVerse.quote: If I sin, what do I do to you, you watcher of mankind? Why have you made me your mark? Why have I become a burden to you? Why do you not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity? For now I shall lie in the earth; you will seek me, but I shall not be."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I sin, what do I do to you, you watcher of mankind? Why have you made me your mark? Why have I become a burden to you?

Even if I have sinned, how could that harm you? Why aim at me? Your mark is the archer's target of 6:4. Watcher is a word for a keeper or guard; Job gives God the name and hears it as surveillance.

Why do you not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity? For now I shall lie in the earth; you will seek me, but I shall not be.

Two things here that every reader should hold on to. First, Job does not claim to be sinless. He asks for pardon. His complaint is not that he has never done wrong but that nothing he has done can account for this, and that God, if he is holding something against him, could forgive it.

Second, listen to the last line. You will seek me. Even in his complaint Job assumes that God will come looking for him, and grieves that he will be gone. It is the faith hidden inside the protest: he believes God cares enough to search. He was right. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). And the prayer to take away my iniquity was answered by name on the banks of the Jordan: Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! (John 1:29).

8.title: Does God Pervert Justice?
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"How long will you say these things, and the words of your mouth be a great wind?<sup>3</sup>Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert the right?<sup>4</sup>If your children have sinned against him, he has delivered them into the hand of their transgression.<sup>5</sup>If you will seek God and plead with the Almighty for mercy,<sup>6</sup>if you are pure and upright, surely then he will rouse himself for you and restore your rightful habitation.<sup>7</sup>And though your beginning was small, your latter days will be very great.<sup>8</sup>"For inquire, please, of bygone ages, and consider what the fathers have searched out.<sup>9</sup>For we are but of yesterday and know nothing, for our days on earth are a shadow.<sup>10</sup>Will they not teach you and tell you and utter words out of their understanding?<sup>11</sup>"Can papyrus grow where there is no marsh? Can reeds flourish where there is no water?<sup>12</sup>While yet in flower and not cut down, they wither before any other plant.<sup>13</sup>Such are the paths of all who forget God; the hope of the godless shall perish.<sup>14</sup>His confidence is severed, and his trust is a spider's web.<sup>15</sup>He leans against his house, but it does not stand; he lays hold of it, but it does not endure.<sup>16</sup>He is a lush plant before the sun, and his shoots spread over his garden.<sup>17</sup>His roots entwine the stone heap; he looks upon a house of stones.<sup>18</sup>If he is destroyed from his place, then it will deny him, saying, 'I have never seen you.'<sup>19</sup>Behold, this is the joy of his way, and out of the soil others will spring.<sup>20</sup>"Behold, God will not reject a blameless man, nor take the hand of evildoers.<sup>21</sup>He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with shouting.<sup>22</sup>Those who hate you will be clothed with shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more."
8.overview: Bildad calls Job's words a great wind and asks whether God perverts justice. If Job's children sinned, God gave them over to their transgression; if Job is pure and upright and pleads for mercy, God will restore him and his latter days will be very great (vv. 1-7). Ask the fathers, for we are of yesterday: the papyrus withers without water, so do all who forget God; the godless man's trust is a spider's web and his house will not stand; the lush plant is uprooted and forgotten (vv. 8-19). God will not reject a blameless man; he will fill Job's mouth with laughter, and those who hate him will be clothed with shame (vv. 20-22).
8.theology:
God does not pervert justice (Gen 18:25), but his justice is not read off each person's circumstances. Bildad's inference that Job's children died for their sins is the speech the LORD rejects (42:7-8); Jesus refused the same reasoning (Luke 13:4-5). Tradition deserves honour (Deut 32:7) and cannot overrule God's word (Mark 7:13).

Bildad's promises come true (42:12) for the opposite of his reasons: God keeps the promise and discards the reasoning, and the friends end up needing Job's prayers.
8.examples:
Does God pervert justice? Job answers with the same verb at 19:6.

Bildad blames the dead children.

Your latter days will be very great is fulfilled in the words of 42:12.

We know nothing, says Bildad, and knows why ten people died.

In Jesus' parable the storm beats on both houses.

God will not reject a blameless man: the truest thing Bildad says.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bildad calls Job's words a great wind (vv. 1-2) and asks, Does God pervert justice? (v. 3). If your children have sinned against him, he has delivered them into the hand of their transgression (v. 4). If Job is pure and upright and pleads for mercy, God will restore him, and your latter days will be very great (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: God is just; Bildad is right. From that he concludes that Job's children died for their sins, and the LORD will say he did not speak rightly (42:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: "How long will you say these things, and the words of your mouth be a great wind?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: How long will you say these things, and the words of your mouth be a great wind?

The second friend has none of Eliphaz's courtesy. Job asked them to hear the speech of a despairing man as wind (6:26), a cry and not a doctrine. Bildad takes the word and turns it into an insult: your words are a gale of hot air. The friends' case was set out in chapter 4, and Bildad will repeat it. What he adds is harder: he brings in the dead, and he brings in the fathers. And he too is among the three of whom God will say, you have not spoken of me what is right (42:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert the right?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert the right?

The answer is no, and Bildad is right to insist on it. Abraham said the same at Sodom: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Gen 18:25). God never perverts justice. Every believer in Job's position needs to keep hold of that.

But see what Bildad does with it. God is just; Job is suffering; therefore Job deserves it. The first two are true and the third does not follow, because God's justice is not measured out day by day in each man's circumstances. The whole debate turns on this one verb. Job will answer it later with the same word turned round: God has put me in the wrong (19:6), the verb Bildad uses here. Bildad says God cannot pervert justice; so Job must be guilty. Job says he is not guilty; so God seems to have perverted justice. Both men are trapped by the same assumption, that suffering is a verdict. The prologue has already told the reader it is not.

verseByVerse.quote: If your children have sinned against him, he has delivered them into the hand of their transgression.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If your children have sinned against him, he has delivered them into the hand of their transgression.

The cruellest sentence yet. The if is a courtesy; Bildad means since. Your children are dead; God is just; therefore they had it coming. God simply handed them over to the consequences of their own sin.

Say it to a father who rose early after every feast to offer a burnt offering for each of them (1:5), and who has ten graves to visit. Bildad has no evidence at all. His system requires it, so he says it. The narrator never suggests it, and the LORD will name what Bildad has done: you have not spoken of me what is right (42:8). Jesus refused the same reasoning about eighteen people killed when a tower fell: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others ...? No, I tell you (Luke 13:4-5).

If you have been told that someone you loved died because of their sin, or yours, hear the verdict of this book. That was Bildad's speech, and God did not accept it.

verseByVerse.quote: If you will seek God and plead with the Almighty for mercy, if you are pure and upright, surely then he will rouse himself for you and restore your rightful habitation. And though your beginning was small, your latter days will be very great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you will seek God and plead with the Almighty for mercy, if you are pure and upright, surely then he will rouse himself for you and restore your rightful habitation.

Now the offer: seek God, plead for mercy, be pure and upright, and God will wake up and act for you. It sounds like the gospel and is a bargain. And there is an irony Bildad cannot see. Upright is the narrator's word for Job in 1:1. By Bildad's own conditions, God should restore Job. He will.

And though your beginning was small, your latter days will be very great. Read the last chapter: And the LORD blessed the latter days of Job more than his beginning (42:12). Bildad's promise comes true in almost the same words. But it does not come true because Job confessed the sins Bildad imagined. It comes true after God has declared Bildad wrong and Job right. God kept the promise and threw away the reasoning.

Notice too he will rouse himself for you, as though God were asleep toward Job and would wake only when Job repented. There is a psalm that uses Bildad's very verb and turns his theology upside down. Psalm 44 is the prayer of people who have not sinned their way into trouble: All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten you, and we have not been false to your covenant (Ps 44:17). And they cry, Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself! (Ps 44:23). Paul quotes that psalm of innocent suffering about Christians, For your sake we are being killed all the day long, and answers it: in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us (Rom 8:36-37). God never sleeps (Ps 121:4). When the disciples woke Jesus in the storm and asked, do you not care that we are perishing? (Mark 4:38), he had been in the boat with them all along.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ask the fathers, says Bildad, for we are but of yesterday and know nothing (vv. 8-10). Papyrus without water withers; such are the paths of all who forget God (vv. 11-13). The godless man's trust is a spider's web; his house does not stand (vv. 14-15). The lush plant is torn up, and its place says, I have never seen you (vv. 16-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Every picture is true of the godless. Every picture is also a portrait of Job, and that is the point of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For inquire, please, of bygone ages, and consider what the fathers have searched out. For we are but of yesterday and know nothing, for our days on earth are a shadow. Will they not teach you and tell you and utter words out of their understanding?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For inquire, please, of bygone ages, and consider what the fathers have searched out. For we are but of yesterday and know nothing, for our days on earth are a shadow. Will they not teach you and tell you and utter words out of their understanding?

Eliphaz appealed to his experience and a vision. Bildad appeals to the fathers. We are young, we live a short time, we know little; ask the generations before us. Searched out is Eliphaz's confident word again (5:27).

There is real wisdom in that. Scripture tells us to ask your father, and he will show you (Deut 32:7), and it is foolish to think no one understood anything until we arrived. But tradition cannot overrule what God has said. Jesus rebuked men for making void the word of God by your tradition (Mark 7:13). Notice too the contradiction: Bildad says we know nothing, and in the same breath knows exactly why ten young people died. Humility about himself did not make him humble about Job. David used the same words in prayer: Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding (1 Chr 29:15). In David's mouth they lead to humble dependence on God. In Bildad's they lead to a lecture.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can papyrus grow where there is no marsh? Can reeds flourish where there is no water? While yet in flower and not cut down, they wither before any other plant. Such are the paths of all who forget God; the hope of the godless shall perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can papyrus grow where there is no marsh? Can reeds flourish where there is no water? While yet in flower and not cut down, they wither before any other plant. Such are the paths of all who forget God; the hope of the godless shall perish.

The papyrus reed of the Nile grows tall and green, but only in the marsh. Take away the water and it withers overnight, before it can even be harvested. So, says Bildad, the man who forgets God: flourishing one day, dead the next.

True, and the Psalms and prophets say it better: the man who trusts in the LORD is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes (Jer 17:8). But the point of Bildad's reed is its sudden withering, and Job has withered suddenly. The hidden sentence is: you must have forgotten God. Job has not. He is the one still speaking to him, and he could pray with the psalmist, though we have not forgotten you (Ps 44:17).

verseByVerse.quote: His confidence is severed, and his trust is a spider's web. He leans against his house, but it does not stand; he lays hold of it, but it does not endure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His confidence is severed, and his trust is a spider's web. In Hebrew it is a spider's house: something built with care, beautiful in the morning light, and useless when you lean on it. Isaiah uses the web for the works of the wicked: their webs will not serve as clothing (Isa 59:6).

He leans against his house, but it does not stand; he lays hold of it, but it does not endure. Job's house did not stand. It fell on his children (1:19). Bildad could hardly have chosen a sharper picture.

Jesus told a story about two houses, and it answers Bildad. One was built on rock, one on sand. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, and almost the same words are said of both (Matt 7:25, 27). The storm came to the wise man as well as the fool. What showed the difference was not whether the storm came but what stood when it had passed. Job's roof fell in; his faith did not. By Jesus' measure, he built on the rock.

verseByVerse.quote: He is a lush plant before the sun, and his shoots spread over his garden. His roots entwine the stone heap; he looks upon a house of stones. If he is destroyed from his place, then it will deny him, saying, 'I have never seen you.' Behold, this is the joy of his way, and out of the soil others will spring.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is a lush plant before the sun, and his shoots spread over his garden. His roots entwine the stone heap; he looks upon a house of stones. Another plant: a creeper spreading green in the sun, its roots wrapped round the stones, looking settled and strong.

If he is destroyed from his place, then it will deny him, saying, I have never seen you. Behold, this is the joy of his way, and out of the soil others will spring. Pull it up and the garden forgets it was ever there; something else grows in its place. This is the joy of his way is bitter irony: this is all his flourishing came to. Job himself said of the man who goes down to the grave, nor does his place know him anymore (7:10). Bildad agrees, and adds that the wicked deserve to be forgotten.

The Christian holds a better promise than either of them. The one who does the will of God abides forever (1 John 2:17), and God does not forget his own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — God Will Not Reject a Blameless Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behold, God will not reject a blameless man (v. 20). He will yet fill your mouth with laughter (v. 21), and those who hate Job will be clothed with shame (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Bildad has said the truest thing in his speech without knowing it. God will not reject Job, because he is blameless.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, God will not reject a blameless man, nor take the hand of evildoers. He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with shouting. Those who hate you will be clothed with shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, God will not reject a blameless man, nor take the hand of evildoers.

Blameless is the very word God used of Job (1:1, 8; 2:3). Bildad means it as a warning: God does not abandon the blameless, so if you have been abandoned, you are not blameless. But his sentence is simply true, and it is the truest thing he says. God will not reject Job, because Job is exactly what Bildad doubts he is.

He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with shouting. Those who hate you will be clothed with shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more. The laughter of the restored, as in the psalm of the returning exiles: Then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with shouts of joy (Ps 126:2). It will happen. And the ones clothed with shame at the end of the book will not be Job's enemies but his friends, sent to him with seven bulls and seven rams so that he can pray for them, not to deal with you according to your folly (42:8). God is kinder to Bildad than Bildad was to Job.

9.title: There Is No Arbiter Between Us
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Truly I know that it is so: But how can a man be in the right before God?<sup>3</sup>If one wished to contend with him, one could not answer him once in a thousand times.<sup>4</sup>He is wise in heart and mighty in strength— who has hardened himself against him, and succeeded?—<sup>5</sup>he who removes mountains, and they know it not, when he overturns them in his anger,<sup>6</sup>who shakes the earth out of its place, and its pillars tremble;<sup>7</sup>who commands the sun, and it does not rise; who seals up the stars;<sup>8</sup>who alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea;<sup>9</sup>who made the Bear and Orion, the Pleiades and the chambers of the south;<sup>10</sup>who does great things beyond searching out, and marvelous things beyond number.<sup>11</sup>Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not; he moves on, but I do not perceive him.<sup>12</sup>Behold, he snatches away; who can turn him back? Who will say to him, 'What are you doing?'<sup>13</sup>"God will not turn back his anger; beneath him bowed the helpers of Rahab.<sup>14</sup>How then can I answer him, choosing my words with him?<sup>15</sup>Though I am in the right, I cannot answer him; I must appeal for mercy to my accuser.<sup>16</sup>If I summoned him and he answered me, I would not believe that he was listening to my voice.<sup>17</sup>For he crushes me with a tempest and multiplies my wounds without cause;<sup>18</sup>he will not let me get my breath, but fills me with bitterness.<sup>19</sup>If it is a contest of strength, behold, he is mighty! If it is a matter of justice, who can summon him?<sup>20</sup>Though I am in the right, my own mouth would condemn me; though I am blameless, he would prove me perverse.<sup>21</sup>I am blameless; I regard not myself; I loathe my life.<sup>22</sup>It is all one; therefore I say, 'He destroys both the blameless and the wicked.'<sup>23</sup>When disaster brings sudden death, he mocks at the calamity of the innocent.<sup>24</sup>The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; he covers the faces of its judges— if it is not he, who then is it?<sup>25</sup>"My days are swifter than a runner; they flee away; they see no good.<sup>26</sup>They go by like skiffs of reed, like an eagle swooping on the prey.<sup>27</sup>If I say, 'I will forget my complaint, I will put off my sad face, and be of good cheer,'<sup>28</sup>I become afraid of all my suffering, for I know you will not hold me innocent.<sup>29</sup>I shall be condemned; why then do I labor in vain?<sup>30</sup>If I wash myself with snow and cleanse my hands with lye,<sup>31</sup>yet you will plunge me into a pit, and my own clothes will abhor me.<sup>32</sup>For he is not a man, as I am, that I might answer him, that we should come to trial together.<sup>33</sup>There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both.<sup>34</sup>Let him take his rod away from me, and let not dread of him terrify me.<sup>35</sup>Then I would speak without fear of him, for I am not so in myself.
9.overview: Job agrees that no man can be in the right before God, but means that no one could win a case against him. God moves mountains, commands the sun, tramples the sea and made the stars; he passes by unseen and no one can ask what he is doing (vv. 1-13). Though in the right, Job could only plead for mercy; God crushes him and multiplies his wounds without cause; no court can summon God. Job is blameless, yet God destroys the blameless and the wicked alike; if it is not he, who then is it? (vv. 14-24). His days flee; he cannot put on a cheerful face; though he washed with snow, God would plunge him in the pit. God is not a man, and there is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both. If God took away his rod, he could speak without fear (vv. 25-35).
9.theology:
Job's cry for an arbiter who could lay a hand on God and on man describes the mediator God provided: the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim 2:5). The God who walks on the sea and passes by unseen (vv. 8, 11) walked on the sea in the flesh and spoke (Mark 6:48-50).

Job is right that his wounds are without cause (v. 17; 2:3), and wrong that God mocks the innocent (v. 23; 38:2; 40:8). No one can wash himself clean (v. 30; Jer 2:22); God washes whiter than snow (Isa 1:18; Ps 51:7).
9.examples:
Job repeats Eliphaz's hymn to God's power, and draws the opposite conclusion.

God walks on the waves and passes by: Mark 6:48.
