The prophet Habakkuk would pray almost the same words: O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? Or cry to you Violence! and you will not save? (Hab 1:2). God did answer Habakkuk, and he will answer Job. But not yet, and the waiting is part of the trial.

He has walled up my way, so that I cannot pass, and he has set darkness upon my paths. In chapter 3 he said God had hedged him in (3:23). Now it is a wall. The poet of Lamentations knew it: He has walled me about so that I cannot escape (Lam 3:7). Every road out is blocked, and he cannot see where to walk.

verseByVerse.quote: He has stripped from me my glory and taken the crown from my head. He breaks me down on every side, and I am gone, and my hope has he pulled up like a tree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has stripped from me my glory and taken the crown from my head. The honour Job once had, the respect of his city (29:7-11), is gone, as if God had pulled the crown from his head in public.

That is exactly what men did to Christ, in mockery. They stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him, and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on his head (Matt 27:28-29). And that is the road by which he came to be crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death (Heb 2:9). The glory stripped from Job will be given back. The glory Christ laid down was taken up again, for us.

He breaks me down on every side, and I am gone, and my hope has he pulled up like a tree. In chapter 14 Job said there is hope for a tree: cut it down and the stump will sprout (14:7). Now he feels that even that hope has been torn out by the roots. No stump left, nothing to sprout. It is the lowest point his hope has reached, and it comes fifteen verses before the highest.

verseByVerse.quote: He has kindled his wrath against me and counts me as his adversary. His troops come on together; they have cast up their siege ramp against me and encamp around my tent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has kindled his wrath against me and counts me as his adversary. His troops come on together; they have cast up their siege ramp against me and encamp around my tent.

God as a general and Job as a besieged town: the troops arrive, the earth ramp is built against the wall, the camp is pitched around him. And all of it against one tent, one sick man. The scale is absurd, and Job knows it. Counts me as his adversary is the complaint of 13:24 again. Job still believes God is his enemy. The reader knows God said the opposite: there is none like him on the earth (1:8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — Have Mercy on Me, O You My Friends
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Brothers, acquaintances, relatives, friends, guests, maidservants all treat him as a stranger (vv. 13-15); his servant ignores him, his wife recoils, his brothers find him repulsive, children mock him, and those he loved have turned against him (vv. 16-19). He has escaped by the skin of my teeth (v. 20). Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, O you my friends, for the hand of God has touched me! (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The loneliness of the sufferer, described from the inside. The Son of God knew it: He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11).

verseByVerse.quote: "He has put my brothers far from me, and those who knew me are wholly estranged from me. My relatives have failed me, my close friends have forgotten me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has put my brothers far from me, and those who knew me are wholly estranged from me. My relatives have failed me, my close friends have forgotten me.

Now the siege moves inside. Job begins to count, circle by circle, the people who have abandoned him: brothers first, then everyone who knew him, then relatives, then close friends. He lays even this at God's door: he has put them far from me. When a man is ill and disgraced, people stop coming. Some are embarrassed, some afraid, some have simply drawn their own conclusions. Job has lost his wealth and his children; now he loses everyone else.

verseByVerse.quote: The guests in my house and my maidservants count me as a stranger; I have become a foreigner in their eyes. I call to my servant, but he gives me no answer; I must plead with him with my mouth for mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The guests in my house and my maidservants count me as a stranger; I have become a foreigner in their eyes. I call to my servant, but he gives me no answer; I must plead with him with my mouth for mercy.

In his own house he is a stranger. The guests he once fed and the maids who served him treat him as a foreigner. The master calls his servant, and the servant does not come; the master has to beg. It is a complete inversion of the world of chapter 1, and it is humiliating.

Keep the word stranger. It will come back at the summit of the chapter, in verse 27.

verseByVerse.quote: My breath is strange to my wife, and I am a stench to the children of my own mother. Even young children despise me; when I rise they talk against me. All my intimate friends abhor me, and those whom I loved have turned against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My breath is strange to my wife, and I am a stench to the children of my own mother. Even young children despise me; when I rise they talk against me. All my intimate friends abhor me, and those whom I loved have turned against me.

His wife cannot bear his breath. His own brothers find him disgusting. Children jeer when he tries to stand. His closest friends, the ones he loved, have turned their backs. There is no one left.

Set the children beside the memory Job will describe in chapter 29: the young men saw me and withdrew, and the aged rose and stood (29:8). The man before whom the young once stepped aside respectfully is now jeered at by children when he struggles to his feet. And his wife, who told him to curse God and die (2:9), cannot come near him. He does not curse her. He grieves that she has gone from him too.

The psalms know this loneliness in almost the same words: I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother's sons (Ps 69:8). The New Testament quotes the next verse of that psalm of Jesus (John 2:17), and the whole of it was lived by him. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). In Gethsemane, they all left him and fled (Mark 14:50). He was despised and rejected by men ... as one from whom men hide their faces (Isa 53:3). Whoever reads this chapter alone, abandoned by family and friends, may know that the Son of God has stood exactly there, and does not abandon his own.

verseByVerse.quote: My bones stick to my skin and to my flesh, and I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My bones stick to my skin and to my flesh, and I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.

He is skin and bone, wasted to nothing. By the skin of my teeth has passed into English as the phrase for the narrowest escape. What Job meant is not certain; teeth have no skin, and that may be the point: he has escaped with nothing at all, or he has only his gums left. Either way, he is barely alive. And barely is enough. God said to Satan, only spare his life (2:6), and his life has been spared, just.

verseByVerse.quote: Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, O you my friends, for the hand of God has touched me! Why do you, like God, pursue me? Why are you not satisfied with my flesh?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, O you my friends, for the hand of God has touched me!

For the only time in the debate, Job begs the friends for pity, and he says it twice. He is not arguing now. He is pleading. The hand of God has touched me: touch is the word Satan used when he asked God to touch his bone and his flesh (2:5). Job does not know about Satan. He knows that the hand on him is God's, and he asks his friends not to add their hands to it.

A man with a skin disease crying have mercy and getting none. Centuries later ten men with a skin disease stood at a distance from Jesus and lifted up their voices, saying, Jesus, Master, have mercy on us (Luke 17:13), and he did. The friends had no mercy for the man whose skin was rotting. The Lord had nothing else for such men.

Why do you, like God, pursue me? Why are you not satisfied with my flesh? They are hunting him as he feels God hunts him. Not satisfied with my flesh is probably an idiom for slander; in the Aramaic of Daniel, to "eat pieces" of a man means to accuse him maliciously (Dan 3:8). They are devouring him with accusations. Enough.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–29 — I Know That My Redeemer Lives
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oh that my words were written! Engraved in rock forever (vv. 23-24). For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth. And after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God, whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another (vv. 25-27). Let the friends beware of judgment (vv. 28-29).
verseByVerse.theology: From the bottom of the pit, the summit of the book's faith: a living Redeemer, standing at the last on the dust where Job will lie, and Job seeing God with his own eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: "Oh that my words were written! Oh that they were inscribed in a book! Oh that with an iron pen and lead they were engraved in the rock forever!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh that my words were written! Oh that they were inscribed in a book! Oh that with an iron pen and lead they were engraved in the rock forever!

The chapter turns. Job wants what he is about to say preserved: written in a book, and better, cut into rock with an iron chisel and the letters filled with lead, like the great royal inscriptions carved into cliff faces, so that it would outlast him and outlast the friends. He is sure that he will die unvindicated. So he wants his testimony on record.

His wish was granted beyond anything he imagined. His words were written in a book, and that book is Scripture. They have been read in more languages and by more people than any inscription ever cut into a cliff. The man who thought his voice would die with him is still speaking.

verseByVerse.quote: For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth.

Bildad said Job was a man who knows not God (18:21). Job says: I know. Not I hope, not I wish. And what he knows is this: he has a Redeemer, and his Redeemer is alive.

The Hebrew word is go'el, and every Israelite knew what it meant. The go'el was your nearest kinsman, the relative whose duty was to rescue you when you could not rescue yourself. If you fell into debt and sold your land, he bought it back (Lev 25:25). If you were sold as a slave, he redeemed you (Lev 25:48-49). If you were murdered, he was the avenger of your blood (Num 35:19), which is why Job cried, O earth, cover not my blood (16:18). Boaz was Ruth's go'el, and the women of Bethlehem blessed the LORD who has not left you this day without a redeemer (Ruth 4:14). But the word belongs above all to God: your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel (Isa 41:14). Job has no kinsman left who will stand up for him (vv. 13-19). He knows he has one who will.

Who is this Redeemer? Job does not name him, and the question has been asked for as long as the book has been read. Most likely Job means God himself: the God who seems to be his enemy in verses 6-12 is the God he appeals to as his kinsman and defender in verse 25, God against God, the same appeal as in 16:19. But a go'el has to be a kinsman, one of the family. How can God be that? The New Testament answers. The Son of God is not ashamed to call them brothers (Heb 2:11); since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things (Heb 2:14). God became our kinsman so that he could be our Redeemer. Job's words reached further than he could see.

And notice where this sentence comes. Not after Job has been healed or answered. Nothing has changed. Fifteen verses ago he said God had torn up his hope like a tree (v. 10), and fourteen verses ago that God counted him an enemy (v. 11). The harshest things Job says about God and the greatest thing he says about God stand in the same speech. That is how faith often speaks in real suffering. It does not wait for the dark to lift before it says I know. It does not rest on how things look. It rests on who God is. A believer who can only say, today, he has walled up my way, is still allowed to say, in the next breath, my Redeemer lives. Job did.

Look at the rest of the line. At the last is the Hebrew acharon, and Isaiah puts Job's two words side by side in one sentence: Thus says the LORD, the King of Israel and his Redeemer ... I am the first and I am the last (Isa 44:6). The Redeemer is the Last. And the risen Christ took that title as his own, with the other word of Job's line: Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore (Rev 1:17-18). My Redeemer lives. And as he said it, John writes, he laid his right hand on me. In chapter 9 Job cried that there was no arbiter who might lay his hand on us both (9:33). Here is the hand, and the living Redeemer, and the Last, in one person.

He will stand upon the earth. The word for earth is the dust of the grave. Job said, For now I shall lie in the earth (7:21), the same word; he asked whether his hope would descend together into the dust (17:16). His Redeemer will stand up on that very dust, over the place where Job lies, like a kinsman rising in court to speak for the dead. Christ did stand on that dust: he went into the grave and rose from it, and he will stand upon the earth again at the last day.

verseByVerse.quote: And after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God, whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. My heart faints within me!
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God, whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. My heart faints within me!

Job expects to die. His skin, already rotting, will be destroyed. And yet he will see God. The Hebrew of in my flesh can also be read "without my flesh", and the ESV notes it; some take Job to mean he will see God as a spirit after death. But he goes on, my eyes shall behold, and eyes belong to a body. The Christian reads here the hope of the resurrection of the body, which Paul spelled out: It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory (1 Cor 15:43). The wasted flesh on the ash heap will be raised, and with those eyes Job will see his God.

And then two words that the English hides. And not another is, in Hebrew, "and not a stranger": the word of verse 15, where his own servants count me as a stranger. His household looks at him as a stranger. He will look at God, and it will not be as a stranger. He will see God for myself, face to face, as one who belongs to him. We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8). They will see his face (Rev 22:4).

My heart faints within me! Literally, his inmost being is spent with longing. This is not calm doctrine. It is a man overwhelmed by what he has just said. Every believer who has stood by a grave and said these words knows the feeling. And Job will taste the first of it before he dies: now my eye sees you (42:5).

verseByVerse.quote: If you say, 'How we will pursue him!' and, 'The root of the matter is found in him,' be afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishment of the sword, that you may know there is a judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you say, How we will pursue him! and, The root of the matter is found in him, be afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishment of the sword, that you may know there is a judgment.

Job turns back to the friends with a warning. You are hunting me, sure that the root of my trouble is in me. Be careful. If there is a Redeemer who will stand up at the last, there is also a judgment, and it may fall on you. It did: My anger burns against you and against your two friends (42:7). The man they condemned would be the one who prayed for them (42:8).

That is the shape of the gospel. We who condemned Christ were saved by the prayers of the one we condemned: Father, forgive them. Job's Redeemer lives, and he lives to intercede.

20.title: The Wicked Man's Portion
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Therefore my thoughts answer me, because of my haste within me.<sup>3</sup>I hear censure that insults me, and out of my understanding a spirit answers me.<sup>4</sup>Do you not know this from of old, since man was placed on earth,<sup>5</sup>that the exulting of the wicked is short, and the joy of the godless but for a moment?<sup>6</sup>Though his height mount up to the heavens, and his head reach to the clouds,<sup>7</sup>he will perish forever like his own dung; those who have seen him will say, 'Where is he?'<sup>8</sup>He will fly away like a dream and not be found; he will be chased away like a vision of the night.<sup>9</sup>The eye that saw him will see him no more, nor will his place any more behold him.<sup>10</sup>His children will seek the favor of the poor, and his hands will give back his wealth.<sup>11</sup>His bones are full of his youthful vigor, but it will lie down with him in the dust.<sup>12</sup>"Though evil is sweet in his mouth, though he hides it under his tongue,<sup>13</sup>though he is loath to let it go and holds it in his mouth,<sup>14</sup>yet his food is turned in his stomach; it is the venom of cobras within him.<sup>15</sup>He swallows down riches and vomits them up again; God casts them out of his belly.<sup>16</sup>He will suck the poison of cobras; the tongue of a viper will kill him.<sup>17</sup>He will not look upon the rivers, the streams flowing with honey and curds.<sup>18</sup>He will give back the fruit of his toil and will not swallow it down; from the profit of his trading he will get no enjoyment.<sup>19</sup>For he has crushed and abandoned the poor; he has seized a house that he did not build.<sup>20</sup>"Because he knew no contentment in his belly, he will not let anything in which he delights escape him.<sup>21</sup>There was nothing left after he had eaten; therefore his prosperity will not endure.<sup>22</sup>In the fullness of his sufficiency he will be in distress; the hand of everyone in misery will come against him.<sup>23</sup>To fill his belly to the full, God will send his burning anger against him and rain it upon him into his body.<sup>24</sup>He will flee from an iron weapon; a bronze arrow will strike him through.<sup>25</sup>It is drawn forth and comes out of his body; the glittering point comes out of his gallbladder; terrors come upon him.<sup>26</sup>Utter darkness is laid up for his treasures; a fire not fanned will devour him; what is left in his tent will be consumed.<sup>27</sup>The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him.<sup>28</sup>The possessions of his house will be carried away, dragged off in the day of God's wrath.<sup>29</sup>This is the wicked man's portion from God, the heritage decreed for him by God."
20.overview: Zophar, stung by what he hears as an insult, says the triumph of the wicked has always been short: though he reach the clouds, he perishes like dung and vanishes like a dream, his children beg from the poor, and his vigour lies down in the dust (vv. 1-11). Evil is sweet in his mouth and turns to venom; he vomits up his riches, for he crushed the poor. God rains anger into his belly; an arrow pierces his gall; fire consumes his tent. The heavens reveal his iniquity and the earth rises against him: this is the wicked man's portion from God (vv. 12-29).
20.theology:
Zophar's last speech ignores Job's confession of a living Redeemer and turns Job's own appeals to the earth and to heaven (16:18-19; 19:25) against him. God judged the speech false (42:7).

Sin is sweet in the mouth and deadly in the stomach (vv. 12-16; James 1:14-15), a true warning. Christ received the wicked man's portion though he knew no sin (2 Cor 5:21), and the believer's portion is God himself (Ps 73:26).
20.examples:
Zophar's last speech; he says nothing in the third round.

He never mentions the Redeemer.

Evil sweet in the mouth, venom in the stomach.

Heaven and earth, Job's witnesses, turned against him.

The wicked man's portion: Job will quote it back at 27:13.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Exulting of the Wicked Is Short
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zophar is stung by what he hears as an insult (vv. 1-3). From of old, the exulting of the wicked is short, and the joy of the godless but for a moment (vv. 4-5). Though he reach the clouds, he will perish like his own dung and vanish like a dream (vv. 6-9); his children will beg from the poor, and his vigour will lie down in the dust (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Job has just confessed a living Redeemer. Zophar does not mention it. He has heard only the warning aimed at him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said: "Therefore my thoughts answer me, because of my haste within me. I hear censure that insults me, and out of my understanding a spirit answers me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is Zophar's last speech. In the third round he will say nothing at all. His case was set out in chapter 11 and the round's subject, the end of the wicked, in chapter 15; what follows repeats both. What is new is what he does not say.

Therefore my thoughts answer me, because of my haste within me. I hear censure that insults me, and out of my understanding a spirit answers me. Job has just said, I know that my Redeemer lives (19:25), the highest confession of faith in the book so far. Zophar does not mention it. What he heard was the last two verses, the warning that judgment might fall on the friends (19:28-29), and he is offended. It is a very human failure. People in an argument often hear only the sentence that stings them, and miss the one that could have changed everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know this from of old, since man was placed on earth, that the exulting of the wicked is short, and the joy of the godless but for a moment? Though his height mount up to the heavens, and his head reach to the clouds, he will perish forever like his own dung; those who have seen him will say, 'Where is he?' He will fly away like a dream and not be found; he will be chased away like a vision of the night. The eye that saw him will see him no more, nor will his place any more behold him. His children will seek the favor of the poor, and his hands will give back his wealth. His bones are full of his youthful vigor, but it will lie down with him in the dust.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know this from of old, since man was placed on earth, that the exulting of the wicked is short, and the joy of the godless but for a moment? The wicked man's triumph is brief. That is true in the end, and the psalms say it: until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end ... How they are destroyed in a moment (Ps 73:17-19). But Zophar means that it is always short in this life, and Job will spend the next chapter showing that it often is not.

Though his height mount up to the heavens, and his head reach to the clouds, he will perish forever like his own dung. The proud man who climbs to the sky, like the king of Babylon who said I will ascend to heaven (Isa 14:13), ends on the dung heap. He will fly away like a dream ... The eye that saw him will see him no more, nor will his place any more behold him. Job said the same of every man (7:8-10); Zophar says it only of the wicked.

His children will seek the favor of the poor, and his hands will give back his wealth. His bones are full of his youthful vigor, but it will lie down with him in the dust. Children begging, wealth handed back, a strong body in the dust: once more, the portrait of the wicked is drawn from Job's own life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–29 — The Wicked Man's Portion from God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Evil is sweet in his mouth and turns to venom in his stomach; he vomits up his riches (vv. 12-16). He will not enjoy the land's honey, for he crushed the poor and seized houses (vv. 17-19). His greed is never satisfied, so God rains anger into his belly; an arrow pierces his gall (vv. 20-25); fire consumes his tent (v. 26). The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him. This is the wicked man's portion from God (vv. 27-29).
verseByVerse.theology: Zophar turns Job's own words, the earth and the witness in heaven, against him. God will turn them back (42:7).

verseByVerse.quote: "Though evil is sweet in his mouth, though he hides it under his tongue, though he is loath to let it go and holds it in his mouth, yet his food is turned in his stomach; it is the venom of cobras within him. He swallows down riches and vomits them up again; God casts them out of his belly. He will suck the poison of cobras; the tongue of a viper will kill him. He will not look upon the rivers, the streams flowing with honey and curds. He will give back the fruit of his toil and will not swallow it down; from the profit of his trading he will get no enjoyment. For he has crushed and abandoned the poor; he has seized a house that he did not build.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though evil is sweet in his mouth, though he hides it under his tongue, though he is loath to let it go and holds it in his mouth, yet his food is turned in his stomach; it is the venom of cobras within him.

This is the one new picture in the speech, and it is a true one. Sin is like a sweet in the mouth: the sinner rolls it round his tongue, cannot bear to let it go, and swallows it, and in the stomach it turns to snake venom. Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel (Prov 20:17). James traces the same course: desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death (James 1:15). Every believer should hear the warning.

He swallows down riches and vomits them up again; God casts them out of his belly ... For he has crushed and abandoned the poor; he has seized a house that he did not build. The greedy man gorges on wealth and God makes him bring it all back up, like the rich fool who heard, This night your soul is required of you (Luke 12:20). And here, for the first time, a friend hints at a specific charge: Job oppressed the poor. Eliphaz will say it outright (22:6-9). It is false. Job was the man who delivered the poor who cried for help (29:12).

verseByVerse.quote: "Because he knew no contentment in his belly, he will not let anything in which he delights escape him. There was nothing left after he had eaten; therefore his prosperity will not endure. In the fullness of his sufficiency he will be in distress; the hand of everyone in misery will come against him. To fill his belly to the full, God will send his burning anger against him and rain it upon him into his body. He will flee from an iron weapon; a bronze arrow will strike him through. It is drawn forth and comes out of his body; the glittering point comes out of his gallbladder; terrors come upon him. Utter darkness is laid up for his treasures; a fire not fanned will devour him; what is left in his tent will be consumed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because he knew no contentment in his belly ... To fill his belly to the full, God will send his burning anger against him and rain it upon him into his body. The man who was always hungry for more will be filled at last, with God's wrath. Zophar pictures sickness in the body as anger rained down from heaven. He is looking at Job's body when he says it.

He will flee from an iron weapon; a bronze arrow will strike him through. It is drawn forth and comes out of his body; the glittering point comes out of his gallbladder; terrors come upon him. Job had described his suffering in exactly these terms: God's archers, and he pours out my gall on the ground (16:13). Zophar takes Job's picture of his own pain and makes it the death of the wicked. A fire not fanned will devour him: no human hand lit it, as no hand lit the fire of God that fell on Job's flocks (1:16).

verseByVerse.quote: The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him. The possessions of his house will be carried away, dragged off in the day of God's wrath. This is the wicked man's portion from God, the heritage decreed for him by God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him.

Here Zophar answers Job directly, and it is cleverly done. Job had cried, O earth, cover not my blood, and my witness is in heaven (16:18-19); and just now, that his Redeemer will stand upon the earth (19:25). Zophar turns all three round: heaven will witness against you, and the earth will rise up, the same verb as stand, not for you but against you. Job's hope is thrown back at him as his doom.

The possessions of his house will be carried away, dragged off in the day of God's wrath. This is the wicked man's portion from God, the heritage decreed for him by God. Zophar's last words are a verdict. Job will quote the line back almost word for word (27:13).

The heavens did reveal the truth in the end, and it was not Job's iniquity. God spoke from heaven and said that Job had spoken rightly and Zophar had not (42:7). There was one man who received the wicked man's portion from God though he was not wicked: For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21). Because he took that portion, the believer's portion is God himself: God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever (Ps 73:26).

21.title: Why Do the Wicked Live?
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Keep listening to my words, and let this be your comfort.<sup>3</sup>Bear with me, and I will speak, and after I have spoken, mock on.<sup>4</sup>As for me, is my complaint against man? Why should I not be impatient?<sup>5</sup>Look at me and be appalled, and lay your hand over your mouth.<sup>6</sup>When I remember, I am dismayed, and shuddering seizes my flesh.<sup>7</sup>Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power?<sup>8</sup>Their offspring are established in their presence, and their descendants before their eyes.<sup>9</sup>Their houses are safe from fear, and no rod of God is upon them.<sup>10</sup>Their bull breeds without fail; their cow calves and does not miscarry.<sup>11</sup>They send out their little boys like a flock, and their children dance.<sup>12</sup>They sing to the tambourine and the lyre and rejoice to the sound of the pipe.<sup>13</sup>They spend their days in prosperity, and in peace they go down to Sheol.<sup>14</sup>They say to God, 'Depart from us! We do not desire the knowledge of your ways.<sup>15</sup>What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? And what profit do we get if we pray to him?'<sup>16</sup>Behold, is not their prosperity in their hand? The counsel of the wicked is far from me.<sup>17</sup>"How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? That their calamity comes upon them? That God distributes pains in his anger?<sup>18</sup>That they are like straw before the wind, and like chaff that the storm carries away?<sup>19</sup>You say, 'God stores up their iniquity for their children.' Let him pay it out to them, that they may know it.<sup>20</sup>Let their own eyes see their destruction, and let them drink of the wrath of the Almighty.<sup>21</sup>For what do they care for their houses after them, when the number of their months is cut off?<sup>22</sup>Will any teach God knowledge, seeing that he judges those who are on high?<sup>23</sup>One dies in his full vigor, being wholly at ease and secure,<sup>24</sup>his pails full of milk and the marrow of his bones moist.<sup>25</sup>Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity.<sup>26</sup>They lie down alike in the dust, and the worms cover them.<sup>27</sup>"Behold, I know your thoughts and your schemes to wrong me.<sup>28</sup>For you say, 'Where is the house of the prince? Where is the tent in which the wicked lived?'<sup>29</sup>Have you not asked those who travel the roads, and do you not accept their testimony<sup>30</sup>that the evil man is spared in the day of calamity, that he is rescued in the day of wrath?<sup>31</sup>Who declares his way to his face, and who repays him for what he has done?<sup>32</sup>When he is carried to the grave, watch is kept over his tomb.<sup>33</sup>The clods of the valley are sweet to him; all mankind follows after him, and those who go before him are innumerable.<sup>34</sup>How then will you comfort me with empty nothings? There is nothing left of your answers but falsehood."
21.overview: Job asks the friends to listen; that would be their comfort. His complaint is with God; let them look at him and put their hands over their mouths (vv. 1-6). Why do the wicked live to old age in power, their children dancing, their herds breeding, dying in peace, though they tell God to depart and see no profit in prayer? Their counsel is far from him (vv. 7-16). How often is the lamp of the wicked put out? If God punishes their children, what do they care? No one can teach God; one dies at ease and another in bitterness, and the worms cover both (vv. 17-26). Ask any traveller: the evil man is spared and buried with honour. Their comfort is empty and their answers falsehood (vv. 27-34).
21.theology:
Job answers the second round with the facts: the wicked often prosper and die in peace. Scripture agrees (Jer 12:1; Ps 73) and places the reckoning beyond death: after that comes judgment (Heb 9:27; Luke 16:25). The friends' neat system is empty nothings, and God will say so (42:7).

The wicked reject God because prayer brings no profit (v. 15); Satan accused Job of serving God for profit (1:9). Job serves God when it has cost him everything.
21.examples:
Let this be your comfort: just listen.

Lay your hand over your mouth: Job will do it himself (40:4).

The children of the wicked dance; Job's are dead.

What profit do we get if we pray? Satan's premise, inside out.

How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? Bildad's words answered.

Empty nothings and falsehood: hevel and ma'al.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Lay Your Hand over Your Mouth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Keep listening to my words, and let this be your comfort (vv. 1-3). His complaint is not against man (v. 4). Look at me and be appalled, and lay your hand over your mouth (v. 5); when he remembers, he shudders (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The friends' best comfort would have been to listen. And the gesture Job asks of them is the one he will make himself before God (40:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "Keep listening to my words, and let this be your comfort. Bear with me, and I will speak, and after I have spoken, mock on.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Job answered and said: Keep listening to my words, and let this be your comfort. Bear with me, and I will speak, and after I have spoken, mock on.

Zophar has made his last speech. Job answers with something new: not a lament, but a sustained argument from the facts. And he begins with a request that every comforter should hear. Let this be your comfort: the comfort you could give me is simply to listen. That is all he asks. Hear me out, and then mock if you must.

The friends came to comfort (2:11) and have done everything but listen. The ministry Job asks for is the cheapest there is and the rarest.

verseByVerse.quote: As for me, is my complaint against man? Why should I not be impatient? Look at me and be appalled, and lay your hand over your mouth. When I remember, I am dismayed, and shuddering seizes my flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for me, is my complaint against man? Why should I not be impatient? His quarrel is not with the friends, or with any man. It is with God. That is why he cannot simply calm down: a man can ignore a human critic, but not the Almighty.

Look at me and be appalled, and lay your hand over your mouth. Look at what has happened to me, and be silent. Put your hand over your mouth. Remember this gesture. When God has spoken from the whirlwind, Job himself will say, I lay my hand on my mouth (40:4). The silence he asks of the friends before his suffering, he will give to God before his glory.

When I remember, I am dismayed, and shuddering seizes my flesh. What he is about to say frightens him. He is going to describe the world as it actually is, and it does not fit what anyone has been taught.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–16 — Why Do the Wicked Live?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power? (v. 7). Their children flourish, their houses are safe, their herds breed, their children dance, and they die in peace (vv. 8-13). They tell God, Depart from us! and ask what profit prayer brings (vv. 14-15). The counsel of the wicked is far from me (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Job answers the whole second round with plain facts. And he refuses the wicked's creed even though it seems to work.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power? Their offspring are established in their presence, and their descendants before their eyes. Their houses are safe from fear, and no rod of God is upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power? Their offspring are established in their presence, and their descendants before their eyes. Their houses are safe from fear, and no rod of God is upon them.

Zophar said the exulting of the wicked is short (20:5). Job asks: then why do so many of them live to a ripe old age, powerful, with their grandchildren around them? Their houses are safe; God's rod never falls on them. Job knows the rod; it is on him (9:34).

He is not the only servant of God to ask this. Jeremiah began, Righteous are you, O LORD, when I complain to you; yet I would plead my case before you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper? (Jer 12:1). Notice what both men do: they hold that God is righteous and they bring the question to him. Honest believers have always noticed that the world does not run the way the friends say it does. Faith does not require pretending otherwise.

verseByVerse.quote: Their bull breeds without fail; their cow calves and does not miscarry. They send out their little boys like a flock, and their children dance. They sing to the tambourine and the lyre and rejoice to the sound of the pipe. They spend their days in prosperity, and in peace they go down to Sheol.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their bull breeds without fail; their cow calves and does not miscarry. They send out their little boys like a flock, and their children dance. They sing to the tambourine and the lyre and rejoice to the sound of the pipe. They spend their days in prosperity, and in peace they go down to Sheol.

Herds that breed; little boys let out to play like lambs; children dancing to tambourine and pipe. Every line hurts, because Job's own children once feasted together in their brother's house (1:4), and they are dead. The wicked's children dance. His are in the ground.

And the wicked die in peace. No long illness, no ash heap: in peace they go down to Sheol. Jesus told a story that answers this line exactly. A rich man feasted every day; a poor man lay at his gate covered with sores. Both died, and Abraham said to the rich man, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish (Luke 16:25). The peaceful death is not the end of the story.

verseByVerse.quote: They say to God, 'Depart from us! We do not desire the knowledge of your ways. What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? And what profit do we get if we pray to him?' Behold, is not their prosperity in their hand? The counsel of the wicked is far from me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They say to God, Depart from us! We do not desire the knowledge of your ways. What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? And what profit do we get if we pray to him?

Here is the creed of the prosperous wicked. They tell God to go away, and they give their reason: religion does not pay. What would we gain by praying?

Hear how this matches the first chapter. Satan accused Job of serving God for profit: Does Job fear God for no reason? (1:9). The wicked reject God because serving him brings no profit. Job serves him when it has brought him nothing but loss. The whole book is in that contrast. And the wicked's Depart from us will be answered in their own words at the last: I never knew you; depart from me (Matt 7:23).

Behold, is not their prosperity in their hand? The counsel of the wicked is far from me. Their success seems to be in their own hands. But Job wants no part of their philosophy, however well it seems to work. It is the first line of the Psalter: Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked (Ps 1:1). And the line was noticed: Eliphaz will quote it back at him, word for word, in his next speech (22:18).

That refusal is the pastoral point of the chapter for anyone who watches the wicked do well. The temptation is not only to doubt God but to envy them, and to wonder whether their way is wiser. Fret not yourself because of evildoers; be not envious of wrongdoers! For they will soon fade like the grass (Ps 37:1-2). Asaph nearly slipped on exactly this, and found his footing only when he saw that what he had was God himself: Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you (Ps 73:25). Job has lost everything the wicked still have, and he still says, their counsel is far from me. He would rather have God with nothing than their prosperity without him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–26 — How Often Is the Lamp of the Wicked Put Out?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? (vv. 17-18). If God punishes their children, what do they care (vv. 19-21)? No one can teach God (v. 22). One dies at ease, another in bitterness; they lie down alike in the dust (vv. 23-26).
verseByVerse.theology: In this life the lamp of the wicked often burns to the end. The book's answer, and the gospel's, lies beyond the grave: after that comes judgment (Heb 9:27).

verseByVerse.quote: "How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? That their calamity comes upon them? That God distributes pains in his anger? That they are like straw before the wind, and like chaff that the storm carries away?
verseByVerse.commentary:
How often is it that the lamp of the wicked is put out? That their calamity comes upon them? That God distributes pains in his anger? That they are like straw before the wind, and like chaff that the storm carries away?

Bildad said, the light of the wicked is put out ... his lamp above him is put out (18:5-6). Job takes his words and asks: how often? Honestly, how often do you see it? The psalm says the wicked are like chaff that the wind drives away (Ps 1:4), and it is true. But in this life, how often do we watch it happen? Not often. Job is not denying that God judges. He is denying that you can see the judgment on schedule, in time for your argument.

verseByVerse.quote: You say, 'God stores up their iniquity for their children.' Let him pay it out to them, that they may know it. Let their own eyes see their destruction, and let them drink of the wrath of the Almighty. For what do they care for their houses after them, when the number of their months is cut off?
verseByVerse.commentary:
You say, God stores up their iniquity for their children. Let him pay it out to them, that they may know it. Let their own eyes see their destruction, and let them drink of the wrath of the Almighty. For what do they care for their houses after them, when the number of their months is cut off?

Job anticipates the reply: God punishes the children instead. But what does the wicked man care, once he is dead? If justice means anything, it must reach the man himself. Ezekiel would say it as God's own word: The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezek 18:20). And Job has heard where that argument leads, for Bildad said his own children died for their sins (8:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Will any teach God knowledge, seeing that he judges those who are on high? One dies in his full vigor, being wholly at ease and secure, his pails full of milk and the marrow of his bones moist. Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity. They lie down alike in the dust, and the worms cover them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will any teach God knowledge, seeing that he judges those who are on high? The friends are trying to tell God how his justice must work. Who taught him the path of justice? asks Isaiah (Isa 40:14), and Paul, who has been his counselor? (Rom 11:34). No one teaches God. That cuts against the friends' neat system, and it will cut against Job's demands too when God speaks.

One dies in his full vigor, being wholly at ease and secure, his pails full of milk and the marrow of his bones moist. Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity. They lie down alike in the dust, and the worms cover them.

Two deaths: one well fed and comfortable to the last, the other bitter all his days. And the grave makes no distinction; the worms take both. If this life were all, there would be no justice at all. The New Testament answers where Job's argument points: it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Heb 9:27). The dust is not the verdict.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job knows what they are thinking: where is the prince's house now (vv. 27-28)? Ask any traveller: the evil man is spared in the day of calamity (vv. 29-30); no one confronts him; he is buried with honour and a crowd follows him (vv. 31-33). How then will you comfort me with empty nothings? There is nothing left of your answers but falsehood (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's verdict on the friends' comfort: vapour and treachery. God will agree (42:7).

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I know your thoughts and your schemes to wrong me. For you say, 'Where is the house of the prince? Where is the tent in which the wicked lived?' Have you not asked those who travel the roads, and do you not accept their testimony that the evil man is spared in the day of calamity, that he is rescued in the day of wrath?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I know your thoughts and your schemes to wrong me. For you say, Where is the house of the prince? Where is the tent in which the wicked lived? Job knows exactly whose house they mean. His own lies in ruins. They have been describing it for three chapters.

Have you not asked those who travel the roads, and do you not accept their testimony that the evil man is spared in the day of calamity, that he is rescued in the day of wrath? Ask anyone who has travelled and seen the world. They will tell you that disaster often passes the evil man by. Job appeals to common experience against a theory that ignores it.

verseByVerse.quote: Who declares his way to his face, and who repays him for what he has done? When he is carried to the grave, watch is kept over his tomb. The clods of the valley are sweet to him; all mankind follows after him, and those who go before him are innumerable. How then will you comfort me with empty nothings? There is nothing left of your answers but falsehood."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who declares his way to his face, and who repays him for what he has done? The powerful wicked man is never confronted; no one dares tell him the truth to his face.

When he is carried to the grave, watch is kept over his tomb. The clods of the valley are sweet to him; all mankind follows after him, and those who go before him are innumerable. A grand funeral, a guard of honour at the grave, the earth lying lightly on him, crowds in the procession. There was one tomb in history that was guarded for a different reason. The authorities made the tomb secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard (Matt 27:66), to keep the Righteous One in. It could not.

How then will you comfort me with empty nothings? There is nothing left of your answers but falsehood.

Job's verdict on the friends' whole case. Empty nothings is hevel, vapour, the word of Ecclesiastes. And falsehood is the word Chronicles uses again and again for unfaithfulness to God, as when Judah had been unfaithful to the LORD (2 Chr 12:2). Their comfort is vapour, and their answers are a kind of treachery. God will give the same verdict at the end: you have not spoken of me what is right (42:7).

22.title: Is Not Your Evil Abundant?
22.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he who is wise is profitable to himself.<sup>3</sup>Is it any pleasure to the Almighty if you are in the right, or is it gain to him if you make your ways blameless?<sup>4</sup>Is it for your fear of him that he reproves you and enters into judgment with you?<sup>5</sup>Is not your evil abundant? There is no end to your iniquities.<sup>6</sup>For you have exacted pledges of your brothers for nothing and stripped the naked of their clothing.<sup>7</sup>You have given no water to the weary to drink, and you have withheld bread from the hungry.<sup>8</sup>The man with power possessed the land, and the favored man lived in it.<sup>9</sup>You have sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless were crushed.<sup>10</sup>Therefore snares are all around you, and sudden terror overwhelms you,<sup>11</sup>or darkness, so that you cannot see, and a flood of water covers you.<sup>12</sup>"Is not God high in the heavens? See the highest stars, how lofty they are!<sup>13</sup>But you say, 'What does God know? Can he judge through the deep darkness?<sup>14</sup>Thick clouds veil him, so that he does not see, and he walks on the vault of heaven.'<sup>15</sup>Will you keep to the old way that wicked men have trod?<sup>16</sup>They were snatched away before their time; their foundation was washed away.<sup>17</sup>They said to God, 'Depart from us,' and 'What can the Almighty do to us?'<sup>18</sup>Yet he filled their houses with good things— but the counsel of the wicked is far from me.<sup>19</sup>The righteous see it and are glad; the innocent one mocks at them,<sup>20</sup>saying, 'Surely our adversaries are cut off, and what they left the fire has consumed.'<sup>21</sup>"Agree with God, and be at peace; thereby good will come to you.<sup>22</sup>Receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart.<sup>23</sup>If you return to the Almighty you will be built up; if you remove injustice far from your tents,<sup>24</sup>if you lay gold in the dust, and gold of Ophir among the stones of the torrent-bed,<sup>25</sup>then the Almighty will be your gold and your precious silver.<sup>26</sup>For then you will delight yourself in the Almighty and lift up your face to God.<sup>27</sup>You will make your prayer to him, and he will hear you, and you will pay your vows.<sup>28</sup>You will decide on a matter, and it will be established for you, and light will shine on your ways.<sup>29</sup>For when they are humbled you say, 'It is because of pride'; but he saves the lowly.<sup>30</sup>He delivers even the one who is not innocent, who will be delivered through the cleanness of your hands."
22.overview: Eliphaz says God gains nothing from man's righteousness; surely God is not reproving Job for his piety. Job's evil must be great: he has taken pledges for nothing, stripped the naked, refused water and bread, sent widows away and crushed orphans; so snares and darkness surround him (vv. 1-11). God is high, but Job says God cannot see; will he follow the wicked who told God to depart? The counsel of the wicked is far from Eliphaz, and the righteous rejoice at their fall (vv. 12-20). Let Job agree with God and be at peace, receive his words, return, throw away his gold and have the Almighty as his treasure; he will pray and be heard, and God will deliver even the one who is not innocent through the cleanness of Job's hands (vv. 21-30).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Is Not Your Evil Abundant?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gains nothing from a man's righteousness (vv. 1-3). Is it for your fear of him that he reproves you? (v. 4). Is not your evil abundant? Eliphaz lists Job's sins: pledges exacted for nothing, the naked stripped, the thirsty and hungry refused, widows sent away empty, orphans crushed (vv. 5-9). That is why snares and darkness surround him (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: With no evidence, Eliphaz invents Job's crimes. They are the opposite of what the narrator and God have said of him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: "Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he who is wise is profitable to himself. Is it any pleasure to the Almighty if you are in the right, or is it gain to him if you make your ways blameless? Is it for your fear of him that he reproves you and enters into judgment with you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third round begins, and Eliphaz speaks for the last time. His case was set out in chapters 4-5 and hardened in chapter 15. What is new in this speech is that he stops hinting and starts inventing, and that his last words say more than he knows.

Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he who is wise is profitable to himself. Is it any pleasure to the Almighty if you are in the right, or is it gain to him if you make your ways blameless? God gains nothing from us. Half of that is true: God needs nothing, and Paul asks, who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid? (Rom 11:35), quoting this very book (41:11). But the other half is false. God does take pleasure in the righteous. He said so in heaven: Have you considered my servant Job? (1:8). He will rejoice over you with gladness (Zeph 3:17). Eliphaz's God is too remote to care.

Is it for your fear of him that he reproves you and enters into judgment with you? Eliphaz means it as sarcasm: surely God is not punishing you for being godly! The reader, who has been in the council, knows the answer. Yes. It was precisely because of Job's fear of God that the trial came: Does Job fear God for no reason? (1:9). Eliphaz has asked the question the whole book turns on, and got the answer backwards.

verseByVerse.quote: Is not your evil abundant? There is no end to your iniquities. For you have exacted pledges of your brothers for nothing and stripped the naked of their clothing. You have given no water to the weary to drink, and you have withheld bread from the hungry. The man with power possessed the land, and the favored man lived in it. You have sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless were crushed. Therefore snares are all around you, and sudden terror overwhelms you, or darkness, so that you cannot see, and a flood of water covers you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is not your evil abundant? There is no end to your iniquities. For you have exacted pledges of your brothers for nothing and stripped the naked of their clothing. You have given no water to the weary to drink, and you have withheld bread from the hungry ... You have sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless were crushed.

Here is what is new. Eliphaz has no evidence, so he supplies it. Job must have taken the cloak of a poor man as security for a debt and left him naked; refused water to a traveller and bread to the hungry; turned widows away and trampled orphans. None of it is true. Job will answer every item: I delivered the poor who cried for help, and the fatherless who had none to help him (29:12); if I have seen anyone perish for lack of clothing ... if he was not warmed with the fleece of my sheep (31:19-20). And the orphans are Job's own charge against the friends turned round (6:27).

Notice two things. First, for nothing is chinnam, Satan's word: Does Job fear God for no reason? (1:9). God said Job's suffering was without reason (2:3). Now Eliphaz says Job took pledges from his brothers for nothing. The word that marks Job's innocence is used to accuse him. Second, the list is the very list by which Christ will judge the nations: I was hungry and you gave me no food, I was thirsty and you gave me no drink ... naked and you did not clothe me (Matt 25:42-43). Eliphaz has charged Job with the sins of the goats. Job was a sheep.

Therefore snares are all around you, and sudden terror overwhelms you, or darkness, so that you cannot see, and a flood of water covers you. This is how the friends' theology ends when the facts will not fit: the facts are invented. A counsellor who "knows" what a sufferer must have done, without evidence, is doing what Eliphaz did, and God will call it what he called it (42:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is high above the stars, but you say, What does God know? (vv. 12-14). Will Job walk the old path of the wicked, who were swept away and who told God, Depart from us (vv. 15-17)? The counsel of the wicked is far from me; the righteous rejoice at their end (vv. 18-20).
verseByVerse.theology: Eliphaz puts the words of the wicked in Job's mouth, and borrows Job's own words to do it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is not God high in the heavens? See the highest stars, how lofty they are! But you say, 'What does God know? Can he judge through the deep darkness? Thick clouds veil him, so that he does not see, and he walks on the vault of heaven.' Will you keep to the old way that wicked men have trod? They were snatched away before their time; their foundation was washed away. They said to God, 'Depart from us,' and 'What can the Almighty do to us?' Yet he filled their houses with good things— but the counsel of the wicked is far from me. The righteous see it and are glad; the innocent one mocks at them, saying, 'Surely our adversaries are cut off, and what they left the fire has consumed.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is not God high in the heavens? See the highest stars, how lofty they are! But you say, What does God know? Can he judge through the deep darkness? Thick clouds veil him, so that he does not see.

Eliphaz now puts words in Job's mouth, and they are the wicked man's words: How can God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High? (Ps 73:11). Job has said the opposite all along. His complaint is that God sees too much: he said God would watch all my paths (13:27) and test him every moment (7:18). Eliphaz is not listening; he is answering the man his theory needs Job to be.

Will you keep to the old way that wicked men have trod? They were snatched away before their time; their foundation was washed away. The generation of the flood, swept away with their foundations (2 Pet 2:5). They said to God, Depart from us, and What can the Almighty do to us? Yet he filled their houses with good things — but the counsel of the wicked is far from me.

Listen closely. Depart from us is Job's own description of the wicked (21:14), and the counsel of the wicked is far from me is Job's own sentence, word for word (21:16). Eliphaz takes Job's words and sets them in his own mouth: I, Eliphaz, am the one far from the wicked. He has turned Job's confession into his accusation. The righteous see it and are glad when the wicked fall; the fire consumes what they left, as it consumed Job's flocks (1:16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–30 — Agree with God, and Be at Peace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Agree with God, and be at peace; receive his words, return to the Almighty, put away injustice (vv. 21-23). Throw gold in the dust, and the Almighty will be your gold (vv. 24-25). Job will delight in God, pray and be heard (vv. 26-28); God saves the lowly and delivers even the one who is not innocent ... through the cleanness of your hands (vv. 29-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The loveliest words Eliphaz ever speaks, and his last. Their final line comes true exactly: God delivers the man who was not innocent, Eliphaz himself, through Job's prayer (42:8).

verseByVerse.quote: "Agree with God, and be at peace; thereby good will come to you. Receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart. If you return to the Almighty you will be built up; if you remove injustice far from your tents, if you lay gold in the dust, and gold of Ophir among the stones of the torrent-bed, then the Almighty will be your gold and your precious silver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Agree with God, and be at peace; thereby good will come to you. Receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart.

These are lovely words, and in another setting they would be the gospel's own invitation: be reconciled to God (2 Cor 5:20); I have stored up your word in my heart (Ps 119:11). But Job has not been disagreeing with God. He has been disagreeing with Eliphaz about God. And he has done exactly what Eliphaz tells him to do; his next speech will say, I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my portion of food (23:12). In the end God will say which of them agreed with him (42:7).

If you return to the Almighty you will be built up; if you remove injustice far from your tents, if you lay gold in the dust, and gold of Ophir among the stones of the torrent-bed, then the Almighty will be your gold and your precious silver. Throw your gold into the gravel of the stream bed like worthless stones, and God himself will be your treasure. It is true, and beautiful, and Paul lived it: I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord (Phil 3:8). Job has already lost all his gold. He is about to prove that God is his treasure without it.

verseByVerse.quote: For then you will delight yourself in the Almighty and lift up your face to God. You will make your prayer to him, and he will hear you, and you will pay your vows. You will decide on a matter, and it will be established for you, and light will shine on your ways. For when they are humbled you say, 'It is because of pride'; but he saves the lowly. He delivers even the one who is not innocent, who will be delivered through the cleanness of your hands."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For then you will delight yourself in the Almighty and lift up your face to God. You will make your prayer to him, and he will hear you, and you will pay your vows. Every word of this comes true. Job will pray and God will hear. But the prayer God hears will be Job's prayer for Eliphaz: my servant Job shall pray for you, for I will accept his prayer (42:8).

You will decide on a matter, and it will be established for you, and light will shine on your ways. For when they are humbled you say, It is because of pride; but he saves the lowly.

He delivers even the one who is not innocent, who will be delivered through the cleanness of your hands.

These are Eliphaz's last words in the book, and they are a prophecy he does not understand. He means: if Job repents, Job's clean hands will be able to rescue other sinners by his prayers. Turn to chapter 42. God is angry with Eliphaz. He tells him to take seven bulls and seven rams to Job, and says, my servant Job shall pray for you ... not to deal with you according to your folly (42:8). The one who was not innocent was Eliphaz. The clean hands were Job's. Eliphaz was delivered through the prayers of the man he had accused.

That is the gospel in a sentence Eliphaz spoke without knowing it. Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Pet 3:18). The guilty are delivered through the clean hands of another, hands that were pierced for them.

22.theology:
When the facts do not fit the friends' system, Eliphaz invents them (vv. 5-9), charging Job with the sins of Matthew 25:42-43. God judged the speech false (42:7). His sarcastic question, whether God reproves Job for his fear of God (v. 4), is answered yes by the prologue (1:8-9).

Eliphaz's last words (v. 30) are fulfilled on himself: the one who was not innocent is delivered through the clean hands of Job's intercession (42:8). The guilty are saved through the clean hands of Christ, the righteous for the unrighteous (1 Pet 3:18).
22.examples:
Is it for your fear of him that he reproves you? Yes.

For nothing: chinnam, used to accuse the innocent.

The sins of the goats (Matt 25:42-43) charged to a sheep.

Eliphaz quotes Job's own words as his own.

The Almighty will be your gold.

Eliphaz is delivered through the cleanness of Job's hands.

23.title: He Knows the Way That I Take
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Today also my complaint is bitter; my hand is heavy on account of my groaning.<sup>3</sup>Oh, that I knew where I might find him, that I might come even to his seat!<sup>4</sup>I would lay my case before him and fill my mouth with arguments.<sup>5</sup>I would know what he would answer me and understand what he would say to me.<sup>6</sup>Would he contend with me in the greatness of his power? No; he would pay attention to me.<sup>7</sup>There an upright man could argue with him, and I would be acquitted forever by my judge.<sup>8</sup>"Behold, I go forward, but he is not there, and backward, but I do not perceive him;<sup>9</sup>on the left hand when he is working, I do not behold him; he turns to the right hand, but I do not see him.<sup>10</sup>But he knows the way that I take; when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold.<sup>11</sup>My foot has held fast to his steps; I have kept his way and have not turned aside.<sup>12</sup>I have not departed from the commandment of his lips; I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my portion of food.<sup>13</sup>But he is unchangeable, and who can turn him back? What he desires, that he does.<sup>14</sup>For he will complete what he appoints for me, and many such things are in his mind.<sup>15</sup>Therefore I am terrified at his presence; when I consider, I am in dread of him.<sup>16</sup>God has made my heart faint; the Almighty has terrified me;<sup>17</sup>yet I am not silenced because of the darkness, nor because thick darkness covers my face.
23.overview: Job's complaint is still bitter. If only he knew where to find God, he would come to his seat, lay out his case and hear his answer; God would not crush him but listen, and he would be acquitted forever (vv. 1-7). He looks in every direction and cannot find God, but he knows the way that I take; when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold. He has kept God's way and treasured his words more than food (vv. 8-12). But God is unchangeable and will complete what he has appointed, and Job is terrified; yet the darkness has not silenced him (vv. 13-17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Oh, That I Knew Where I Might Find Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: His complaint is still bitter (vv. 1-2). Oh, that I knew where I might find him, that I might come even to his seat! He would lay out his case and hear God's answer (vv. 3-5). God would not crush him with power but pay attention to me, and he would be acquitted forever (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who feared God's court in chapter 9 now longs to stand in it. He believes God would listen.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "Today also my complaint is bitter; my hand is heavy on account of my groaning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Job answered and said: Today also my complaint is bitter; my hand is heavy on account of my groaning.

Today also: nothing has changed. Eliphaz has just accused him of crimes he never committed (22:5-9), and Job does not answer the charges yet. He turns away from Eliphaz altogether. The rest of this chapter is about God: where he is, and what he knows.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, that I knew where I might find him, that I might come even to his seat! I would lay my case before him and fill my mouth with arguments. I would know what he would answer me and understand what he would say to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh, that I knew where I might find him, that I might come even to his seat! I would lay my case before him and fill my mouth with arguments. I would know what he would answer me and understand what he would say to me.

Few prayers in the Bible are more honest. Job does not doubt that God exists. He does not know where to find him. If he knew the way to God's throne, he would go straight there and lay out his whole case, and listen to God's reply. It is what every believer in the dark has longed for: not an explanation from a friend but a hearing from God himself.

The Christian knows the way Job did not. We have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us (Heb 10:19-20). I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me (John 14:6). There is a road to the seat Job longed for, and it has been opened.

verseByVerse.quote: Would he contend with me in the greatness of his power? No; he would pay attention to me. There an upright man could argue with him, and I would be acquitted forever by my judge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Would he contend with me in the greatness of his power? No; he would pay attention to me. There an upright man could argue with him, and I would be acquitted forever by my judge.

Compare chapter 9. There Job was sure that God would simply overpower him: How then can I answer him? (9:14). Now he says: no, God would not crush me with his strength. He would listen. Something has changed in Job since chapter 9, and it is not his circumstances. Somewhere between the arbiter, the witness and the Redeemer, he has come to believe that God, if he could only reach him, would be fair.

Acquitted forever by my judge. That is the verdict every believer has in Christ: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1). Job hoped for it through his own innocence. We receive it through another's.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–12 — He Knows the Way That I Take
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Forward, backward, left and right, Job cannot find God (vv. 8-9). But he knows the way that I take; when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold (v. 10). He has kept God's way and treasured his words more than food (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job cannot find God, and God has never lost sight of Job. The fire is a refiner's, and he will come out as gold.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I go forward, but he is not there, and backward, but I do not perceive him; on the left hand when he is working, I do not behold him; he turns to the right hand, but I do not see him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I go forward, but he is not there, and backward, but I do not perceive him; on the left hand when he is working, I do not behold him; he turns to the right hand, but I do not see him.

East, west, north, south, and God is nowhere to be found. Job knows God is at work, when he is working, but he cannot see him. This is the hiddenness of God in suffering, and many of God's people have lived through seasons exactly like it.

Set it beside Psalm 139. There the psalmist tries every direction too, and cannot get away from God: If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there! (Ps 139:8). Job said he would make my bed in darkness in the grave (17:13); the psalm answers that God is there too. Both are true. Job cannot find God in any direction; the psalmist cannot escape him in any direction. The God Job cannot find is the God no one can get away from. Hidden is not the same as absent.

verseByVerse.quote: But he knows the way that I take; when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he knows the way that I take; when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold.

Here is the turn, and it is one of the great sentences of the book. I cannot find him. But he knows the way that I take. Job has lost sight of God; God has not lost sight of Job. It is the first psalm's promise: the LORD knows the way of the righteous (Ps 1:6). The believer who cannot find God in the dark is still completely known.

When he has tried me, I shall come out as gold. Job has used the word before: God would test him every moment (7:18), and there it was a complaint. Now he sees where the testing leads. It is a refiner's fire, not an executioner's. Gold is put into the furnace to take out what is not gold; what comes out is purer than what went in. Eliphaz had said, the Almighty will be your gold (22:25), if Job repented. Job answers: I will come out as gold, because God is testing me, not punishing me. Malachi pictures the Lord who will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver (Mal 3:3), and Peter writes to suffering Christians of the tested genuineness of your faith — more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire (1 Pet 1:7). Job came out as gold. So will every believer whose faith is in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: My foot has held fast to his steps; I have kept his way and have not turned aside. I have not departed from the commandment of his lips; I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my portion of food.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My foot has held fast to his steps; I have kept his way and have not turned aside. I have not departed from the commandment of his lips; I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my portion of food.

This is not boasting. It is the testimony God himself gave of Job (1:8). He has walked in God's footsteps and not turned off the path. And notice the last line. Eliphaz told him to receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart (22:22). Job answers in the same words: I have treasured the words of his mouth, more than my daily bread.

That is exactly the answer Jesus gave when he was tested, hungry, in the wilderness: Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matt 4:4). My food is to do the will of him who sent me (John 4:34). Job held on to God's word when he had nothing else. Christ held on to it when he could have had everything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — What He Desires, That He Does
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He is unchangeable, and who can turn him back? What he desires, that he does (v. 13). He will complete what he has appointed for Job, and Job is terrified (vv. 14-16), yet I am not silenced because of the darkness (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: God's sovereignty frightens Job, and it is also the ground of his hope. He goes on speaking in the dark.

verseByVerse.quote: But he is unchangeable, and who can turn him back? What he desires, that he does. For he will complete what he appoints for me, and many such things are in his mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he is unchangeable, and who can turn him back? What he desires, that he does. For he will complete what he appoints for me, and many such things are in his mind.

Then the fear returns. God cannot be moved. What he has decided, he will do. The psalm says it as praise: Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases (Ps 115:3). Job says it with a shiver. Whatever God has appointed for him, God will carry through to the end, and Job does not know what that is.

The Christian hears the same truth and is steadied by it, because he knows what God has appointed: he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Phil 1:6). The God who will complete what he appoints is exactly the God you want if what he has appointed is your salvation. Job could not yet see that it was his gold, not his ruin, that God was completing.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I am terrified at his presence; when I consider, I am in dread of him. God has made my heart faint; the Almighty has terrified me; yet I am not silenced because of the darkness, nor because thick darkness covers my face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I am terrified at his presence; when I consider, I am in dread of him. God has made my heart faint; the Almighty has terrified me; yet I am not silenced because of the darkness, nor because thick darkness covers my face.

Trust in verse 10 and terror in verse 15: both in the same man, in the same speech. That is real faith under pressure. It is not a steady glow; it swings between confidence and dread.

And the last line is the one to hold on to. Yet I am not silenced because of the darkness. The dark has not shut his mouth. He goes on praying, arguing, hoping, into the dark. Isaiah gives the word for such a person: Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God (Isa 50:10). That is what Job is doing, and it is what anyone in his darkness may do.

23.theology:
God may be hidden from the sufferer and never absent (vv. 8-10; Ps 139:7-10); he knows the way of the righteous (Ps 1:6). Trials are a refiner's fire, from which faith comes out as gold (v. 10; 1 Pet 1:7).

God's unchangeable will terrifies Job (vv. 13-16) and is the believer's assurance, for what God has appointed he will complete (Phil 1:6). The way to God's seat is opened in Christ (Heb 10:19-22).
23.examples:
Oh, that I knew where I might find him.

Chapter 9's fear of God's power has become confidence that God would listen.

Job cannot find God anywhere; the psalmist cannot escape him anywhere.

He knows the way that I take.

Gold: Eliphaz's promise, and Job's hope.

Yet I am not silenced because of the darkness.

24.title: Why Are Not Times of Judgment Kept?
24.text: <sup>1</sup>"Why are not times of judgment kept by the Almighty, and why do those who know him never see his days?<sup>2</sup>Some move landmarks; they seize flocks and pasture them.<sup>3</sup>They drive away the donkey of the fatherless; they take the widow's ox for a pledge.<sup>4</sup>They thrust the poor off the road; the poor of the earth all hide themselves.<sup>5</sup>Behold, like wild donkeys in the desert the poor go out to their toil, seeking game; the wasteland yields food for their children.<sup>6</sup>They gather their fodder in the field, and they glean the vineyard of the wicked man.<sup>7</sup>They lie all night naked, without clothing, and have no covering in the cold.<sup>8</sup>They are wet with the rain of the mountains and cling to the rock for lack of shelter.<sup>9</sup>(There are those who snatch the fatherless child from the breast, and they take a pledge against the poor.)<sup>10</sup>They go about naked, without clothing; hungry, they carry the sheaves;<sup>11</sup>among the olive rows of the wicked they make oil; they tread the winepresses, but suffer thirst.<sup>12</sup>From out of the city the dying groan, and the soul of the wounded cries for help; yet God charges no one with wrong.<sup>13</sup>"There are those who rebel against the light, who are not acquainted with its ways, and do not stay in its paths.<sup>14</sup>The murderer rises before it is light, that he may kill the poor and needy, and in the night he is like a thief.<sup>15</sup>The eye of the adulterer also waits for the twilight, saying, 'No eye will see me';
