and he veils his face.<sup>16</sup>In the dark they dig through houses; by day they shut themselves up; they do not know the light.<sup>17</sup>For deep darkness is morning to all of them; for they are friends with the terrors of deep darkness.<sup>18</sup>"You say, 'Swift are they on the face of the waters; their portion is cursed in the land; no treader turns toward their vineyards.<sup>19</sup>Drought and heat snatch away the snow waters; so does Sheol those who have sinned.<sup>20</sup>The womb forgets them; the worm finds them sweet; they are no longer remembered, so wickedness is broken like a tree.'<sup>21</sup>"They wrong the barren, childless woman, and do no good to the widow.<sup>22</sup>Yet God prolongs the life of the mighty by his power; they rise up when they despair of life.<sup>23</sup>He gives them security, and they are supported, and his eyes are upon their ways.<sup>24</sup>They are exalted a little while, and then are gone; they are brought low and gathered up like all others; they are cut off like the heads of grain.<sup>25</sup>If it is not so, who will prove me a liar and show that there is nothing in what I say?"
24.overview: Job asks why the Almighty does not keep times of judgment. Men move landmarks and rob orphans and widows; the poor scavenge in the wilderness, sleep naked in the rain, have their children taken for debt, and go hungry carrying the harvest; the dying groan, yet God charges no one with wrong (vv. 1-12). Murderers, adulterers and burglars love the dark (vv. 13-17). The wicked are swept away and forgotten, as the ESV puts it on the friends' lips (vv. 18-20); yet God prolongs the mighty for a while, and then they are cut off like heads of grain. Who can prove Job a liar (vv. 21-25)?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Why Are Not Times of Judgment Kept?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Why are not times of judgment kept by the Almighty? (v. 1). Men move landmarks, steal flocks, take the orphan's donkey and the widow's ox (vv. 2-4). The poor scavenge like wild donkeys, sleep naked in the cold rain and cling to rocks (vv. 5-8); children are snatched for debt; labourers go hungry among the sheaves (vv. 9-11). The dying groan in the city, yet God charges no one with wrong (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's question widens from his own suffering to the suffering of the poor. He is asking what the prophets and James will ask: when will God judge?

verseByVerse.quote: "Why are not times of judgment kept by the Almighty, and why do those who know him never see his days?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why are not times of judgment kept by the Almighty, and why do those who know him never see his days?

Chapter 23 was about Job's own case. Now he looks beyond himself. Why does God not hold court on fixed days, like a king, and put things right? Why do the people who know God live and die without ever seeing him act? It is not only a sufferer's question; it is the question of every believer who reads the news. Where is the day of the Lord?

The New Testament gives two answers, and holds them together. The delay is mercy: The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish (2 Pet 3:9). And the day is fixed: he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed (Acts 17:31). The times of judgment are kept. They are kept on God's calendar, and the Judge has already been named and raised from the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: Some move landmarks; they seize flocks and pasture them. They drive away the donkey of the fatherless; they take the widow's ox for a pledge. They thrust the poor off the road; the poor of the earth all hide themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some move landmarks; they seize flocks and pasture them. They drive away the donkey of the fatherless; they take the widow's ox for a pledge. They thrust the poor off the road; the poor of the earth all hide themselves.

Job lists the crimes of the strong against the weak. Shifting the boundary stone to steal a neighbour's land, which the law cursed (Deut 27:17). Driving off an orphan's only donkey. Taking a widow's ox as security for a debt, when the law forbade even taking her cloak (Deut 24:17). Shoving the poor off the road until they hide. These are the very sins Eliphaz accused Job of (22:6-9). Job has not done them. He has seen them done, and he is asking why God lets them go on.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, like wild donkeys in the desert the poor go out to their toil, seeking game; the wasteland yields food for their children. They gather their fodder in the field, and they glean the vineyard of the wicked man. They lie all night naked, without clothing, and have no covering in the cold. They are wet with the rain of the mountains and cling to the rock for lack of shelter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, like wild donkeys in the desert the poor go out to their toil, seeking game; the wasteland yields food for their children. They gather their fodder in the field, and they glean the vineyard of the wicked man. They lie all night naked, without clothing, and have no covering in the cold. They are wet with the rain of the mountains and cling to the rock for lack of shelter.

Read this slowly, because it is the answer to Eliphaz. He said Job had stripped the naked of their clothing (22:6). Here is Job describing the naked poor: scavenging in the wilderness like wild animals to feed their children, picking over the leftovers in a rich man's vineyard, lying all night without a blanket, soaked by mountain storms, pressing themselves against a rock for shelter. No man who had done this to them could describe them like this. It is written with compassion, from a heart that has looked at them.

Hebrews describes God's faithful people in almost the same terms: destitute, afflicted, mistreated — of whom the world was not worthy — wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth (Heb 11:37-38). The poor on the mountainside are not forgotten by God, even when they seem to be.

verseByVerse.quote: (There are those who snatch the fatherless child from the breast, and they take a pledge against the poor.) They go about naked, without clothing; hungry, they carry the sheaves; among the olive rows of the wicked they make oil; they tread the winepresses, but suffer thirst. From out of the city the dying groan, and the soul of the wounded cries for help; yet God charges no one with wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are those who snatch the fatherless child from the breast, and they take a pledge against the poor. A baby taken from its mother's arms and held as security for a debt. They go about naked, without clothing; hungry, they carry the sheaves; among the olive rows of the wicked they make oil; they tread the winepresses, but suffer thirst.

A cruel picture: men carrying armfuls of grain while they starve, pressing olive oil they will never taste, treading grapes with parched throats. Even an ox was not to be muzzled while it threshed (1 Cor 9:9). James, the New Testament writer who holds Job up to the church, writes in the same chapter: Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts (James 5:4). Job heard those cries. So does God.

From out of the city the dying groan, and the soul of the wounded cries for help; yet God charges no one with wrong.

Then comes a line that goes to the heart of the book. Charges no one with wrong uses the very word of the prologue: In all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong (1:22). Job refused to charge God with wrong. Now he complains that God does not charge the oppressors with wrong. It is the complaint of a man who still believes God is just, and cannot see the justice being done. God will answer it, not with a timetable, but with himself (chs 38-41).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Those Who Rebel Against the Light
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some rebel against the light (v. 13): the murderer at dawn, the adulterer at twilight saying No eye will see me, the burglar digging through walls in the dark (vv. 14-16). Deep darkness is morning to all of them (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Evil loves the dark because it thinks the dark hides it. It does not (Ps 139:12; John 3:19-20).

verseByVerse.quote: "There are those who rebel against the light, who are not acquainted with its ways, and do not stay in its paths. The murderer rises before it is light, that he may kill the poor and needy, and in the night he is like a thief. The eye of the adulterer also waits for the twilight, saying, 'No eye will see me'; and he veils his face. In the dark they dig through houses; by day they shut themselves up; they do not know the light. For deep darkness is morning to all of them; for they are friends with the terrors of deep darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are those who rebel against the light, who are not acquainted with its ways, and do not stay in its paths. Job turns to another kind of wickedness: not the powerful oppressor in daylight, but the criminal who works in the dark.

The murderer rises before it is light, that he may kill the poor and needy, and in the night he is like a thief. The eye of the adulterer also waits for the twilight, saying, No eye will see me; and he veils his face. In the dark they dig through houses; by day they shut themselves up; they do not know the light. The killer out before dawn, the adulterer waiting for dusk, as in Proverbs, in the twilight, in the evening (Prov 7:9), the burglar tunnelling through a mud-brick wall at night; Jesus used the same picture for thieves who break in (Matt 6:19).

For deep darkness is morning to all of them; for they are friends with the terrors of deep darkness. For them the night is the working day. Jesus said it exactly: people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil (John 3:19). And they are wrong that no eye will see: even the darkness is not dark to you; the night is bright as the day (Ps 139:12).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ESV sets vv. 18-20 as the friends' view: the wicked are swept away, cursed, forgotten, broken like a tree. They wrong the childless and the widow (v. 21); God prolongs the mighty and his eyes are on their ways (vv. 22-23). They are exalted a little while, and then are gone, cut off like heads of grain (v. 24). If it is not so, who will prove me a liar? (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: The wicked do fall at last, but on God's schedule and not the friends'. The harvest is coming (Matt 13:30).

verseByVerse.quote: "You say, 'Swift are they on the face of the waters; their portion is cursed in the land; no treader turns toward their vineyards. Drought and heat snatch away the snow waters; so does Sheol those who have sinned. The womb forgets them; the worm finds them sweet; they are no longer remembered, so wickedness is broken like a tree.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
You say, Swift are they on the face of the waters; their portion is cursed in the land; no treader turns toward their vineyards. Drought and heat snatch away the snow waters; so does Sheol those who have sinned. The womb forgets them; the worm finds them sweet; they are no longer remembered, so wickedness is broken like a tree.

These verses are one of the hard places in the book, and the reader should know why. They sound like the friends: the wicked swept away like debris on a flood, their fields cursed, swallowed by the grave as melting snow is swallowed by the heat, forgotten, broken like a tree. The Hebrew has no You say; the ESV has added it, taking these lines as Job quoting the friends' view before he answers it. Other readers think Job himself is saying that the wicked do come to a bad end in the end, which he never denied. Others think a piece of one of the friends' speeches has been misplaced here. The first two readings come to the same place: the wicked do perish, but not on the friends' timetable, and not in a way that lets anyone read a man's guilt from his troubles.

verseByVerse.quote: "They wrong the barren, childless woman, and do no good to the widow. Yet God prolongs the life of the mighty by his power; they rise up when they despair of life. He gives them security, and they are supported, and his eyes are upon their ways. They are exalted a little while, and then are gone; they are brought low and gathered up like all others; they are cut off like the heads of grain. If it is not so, who will prove me a liar and show that there is nothing in what I say?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They wrong the barren, childless woman, and do no good to the widow. Yet God prolongs the life of the mighty by his power; they rise up when they despair of life. He gives them security, and they are supported, and his eyes are upon their ways.

The powerful who prey on the childless and the widow are kept alive by God's power; when they seem to be dying, they recover. His eyes are upon their ways: God is watching them, as he is watching Job (23:10). He is not blind. He is patient.

They are exalted a little while, and then are gone; they are brought low and gathered up like all others; they are cut off like the heads of grain. In the end they die like everyone else, cut off like ears of wheat at harvest. That is Job's real answer to his own question in verse 1. Judgment comes; it comes at harvest.

Jesus told a parable that fits this chapter exactly. A man's field was sown with weeds by an enemy, and his servants wanted to pull them up at once. No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them. Let both grow together until the harvest (Matt 13:29-30). That is why the times of judgment seem not to be kept. God is protecting the wheat. The harvest is certain.

If it is not so, who will prove me a liar and show that there is nothing in what I say? Job's challenge to the friends: prove me wrong. They cannot. Bildad will try, with six verses (ch 25), and then the friends fall silent for good.

24.theology:
The delay of judgment is God's patience, and the day is fixed and the Judge named (2 Pet 3:9; Acts 17:31). God lets the wheat and weeds grow together until the harvest (Matt 13:30). Job refused to charge God with wrong (1:22) and complains that God does not charge the oppressors (v. 12).

Job describes the naked poor with the compassion Eliphaz said he lacked (22:6). The cries of defrauded labourers reach the Lord of hosts (James 5:4).
24.examples:
Why are not times of judgment kept?

The naked poor clinging to the rock: the answer to Eliphaz.

Hungry men carrying sheaves: James 5:4.

God charges no one with wrong: the word of 1:22.

The ESV's You say at verse 18 is not in the Hebrew.

Wheat and weeds together until the harvest.

25.title: How Can Man Be in the Right Before God?
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Dominion and fear are with God; he makes peace in his high heaven.<sup>3</sup>Is there any number to his armies? Upon whom does his light not arise?<sup>4</sup>How then can man be in the right before God? How can he who is born of woman be pure?<sup>5</sup>Behold, even the moon is not bright, and the stars are not pure in his eyes;<sup>6</sup>how much less man, who is a maggot, and the son of man, who is a worm!"
25.overview: In his last and shortest speech Bildad says that dominion and fear belong to God, who makes peace in the heavens, whose armies are countless and whose light rises on all. How then can man be right before God, or one born of woman be pure? If the moon and stars are not pure in his sight, how much less man, a maggot, and the son of man, a worm. The friends never speak again.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Man, Who Is a Maggot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Dominion and fear belong to God, who makes peace in the heavens; his armies are countless and his light rises on all (vv. 1-3). How then can man be in the right before God? How can he who is born of woman be pure? (v. 4). If the moon and stars are not pure in his eyes, how much less man, who is a maggot, and the son of man, who is a worm! (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The friends' last words: the right question, asked to crush, and no answer. God gives the answer, and calls his people worms in order to call himself their Redeemer (Isa 41:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: "Dominion and fear are with God; he makes peace in his high heaven. Is there any number to his armies? Upon whom does his light not arise?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: Dominion and fear are with God; he makes peace in his high heaven. Is there any number to his armies? Upon whom does his light not arise?

This is the last time any of the three friends speaks, and Bildad manages six verses. Zophar will not speak at all. Count the speeches: Eliphaz three, Bildad three, Zophar two. The cycle that began so confidently in chapter 4 has run out of breath. The friends have nothing left to say, because their system has nothing left to say to a man like Job. The LORD's verdict on everything they said still stands: you have not spoken of me what is right (42:7).

What Bildad does say is true. God rules and is to be feared; he keeps order in the heavens; his armies cannot be counted; his light reaches everyone. He makes peace in his high heaven: Bildad means he keeps the heavenly powers in order. The New Testament hears a deeper peace in those words. God was pleased through Christ to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross (Col 1:20). The God who makes peace in heaven made it on earth, at a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: How then can man be in the right before God? How can he who is born of woman be pure?
verseByVerse.commentary:
How then can man be in the right before God? How can he who is born of woman be pure?

For the third time in the book, the great question. Eliphaz's night visitor asked it (4:17). Job asked it (9:2). Now Bildad asks it, and it is the friends' last question. It is the right question, the question every human being must face before a holy God. And Bildad has no answer. He asks it to shut Job's mouth, and leaves it hanging.

The book of Job does not answer it either, not in so many words. The answer came later, and it came in a person. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Rom 3:23-24). Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God (Rom 5:1). The question Bildad used as a club, the gospel answers as good news.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, even the moon is not bright, and the stars are not pure in his eyes; how much less man, who is a maggot, and the son of man, who is a worm!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, even the moon is not bright, and the stars are not pure in his eyes; how much less man, who is a maggot, and the son of man, who is a worm!

If the moon and stars look dim beside God's holiness, what is a human being? A maggot. A worm. Bildad's last word on man is contempt, and he says it to a man whose sores are full of worms (7:5).

But Scripture uses the same word twice more, and it changes everything. God himself calls his people worms, and says it tenderly: Fear not, you worm Jacob, you men of Israel! I am the one who helps you, declares the LORD; your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel (Isa 41:14). The same God who sees how small we are calls himself our Redeemer, the word of Job's great confession (19:25). And in the psalm the cross fulfilled, the sufferer says of himself, But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind and despised by the people (Ps 22:6). Bildad called man a worm to crush him. The Son of Man became the worm, scorned and despised, to lift us. The friends' last word is contempt. God's last word is redemption.

25.theology:
The friends' debate collapses: Bildad has six verses and Zophar none. Their last question, how man can be right before God (v. 4), is the right one, and they cannot answer it; the gospel does (Rom 3:23-24; 5:1).

Bildad calls man a worm in contempt (v. 6). God calls Jacob a worm and himself their Redeemer (Isa 41:14), and the Messiah said, I am a worm and not a man (Ps 22:6).
25.examples:
Six verses, and then silence.

He makes peace in his high heaven: Colossians 1:20.

The great question asked a third time, and left unanswered.

The worm: Bildad's contempt, God's tenderness, Christ's humiliation.

26.title: The Outskirts of His Ways
26.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"How you have helped him who has no power! How you have saved the arm that has no strength!<sup>3</sup>How you have counseled him who has no wisdom, and plentifully declared sound knowledge!<sup>4</sup>With whose help have you uttered words, and whose breath has come out from you?<sup>5</sup>The dead tremble under the waters and their inhabitants.<sup>6</sup>Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering.<sup>7</sup>He stretches out the north over the void and hangs the earth on nothing.<sup>8</sup>He binds up the waters in his thick clouds, and the cloud is not split open under them.<sup>9</sup>He covers the face of the full moon and spreads over it his cloud.<sup>10</sup>He has inscribed a circle on the face of the waters at the boundary between light and darkness.<sup>11</sup>The pillars of heaven tremble and are astounded at his rebuke.<sup>12</sup>By his power he stilled the sea; by his understanding he shattered Rahab.<sup>13</sup>By his wind the heavens were made fair; his hand pierced the fleeing serpent.<sup>14</sup>Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ways, and how small a whisper do we hear of him! But the thunder of his power who can understand?"
26.overview: Job mocks Bildad's help: what strength has he given the weak, what wisdom to the ignorant, and whose spirit spoke through him (vv. 1-4)? Then he praises God's power: the dead tremble before him and Sheol is naked to him; he stretches the north over the void and hangs the earth on nothing; he binds the waters in clouds and draws the horizon on the sea; the pillars of heaven tremble at his rebuke; he stilled the sea, shattered Rahab and pierced the fleeing serpent. These are but the outskirts of his ways, and how small a whisper do we hear of him! (vv. 5-14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — How You Have Helped Him Who Has No Power!
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How you have helped him who has no power! Bildad has counselled the unwise and declared sound knowledge in abundance (vv. 1-3). With whose help have you uttered words, and whose breath has come out from you? (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Job answers the friends' last speech with sarcasm. Six verses about worms have helped no one.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "How you have helped him who has no power! How you have saved the arm that has no strength! How you have counseled him who has no wisdom, and plentifully declared sound knowledge! With whose help have you uttered words, and whose breath has come out from you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Job answered and said: How you have helped him who has no power! How you have saved the arm that has no strength! How you have counseled him who has no wisdom, and plentifully declared sound knowledge! With whose help have you uttered words, and whose breath has come out from you?

Bildad's six verses told Job he was a maggot. Job's reply drips with sarcasm. What a help you have been to the weak! What wisdom you have poured out on the ignorant! He is speaking of himself: the man with no power, no strength, and, in their eyes, no wisdom. They came to strengthen him, and they have told him he is a worm.

Whose breath has come out from you? Whose spirit is speaking through you? Not God's. Perhaps the spirit that glided past Eliphaz's face in the night (4:15). A counsellor should ask himself Job's question before he speaks: whose breath is this? Am I speaking God's word, or only my own certainty?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–14 — He Hangs the Earth on Nothing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The dead tremble under the waters; Sheol is naked before God (vv. 5-6). He stretches out the north over the void and hangs the earth on nothing (v. 7); he binds the waters in clouds, covers the moon, draws the horizon on the sea (vv. 8-10). The pillars of heaven tremble at his rebuke; he stilled the sea, shattered Rahab, pierced the fleeing serpent (vv. 11-13). Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ways, and how small a whisper do we hear of him! (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Job outdoes the friends in praising God's power, and ends where all theology must: we have heard a whisper. The thunder is coming (38:1).

verseByVerse.quote: The dead tremble under the waters and their inhabitants. Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The dead tremble under the waters and their inhabitants. Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering.

Now Job shows he can praise God's power better than the friends. He begins at the bottom of the world. The dead, the shades below the waters, tremble before God. Sheol is the grave; Abaddon means destruction, the place of ruin. Neither is hidden from him. Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of the children of man! (Prov 15:11).

Hebrews says the same of every one of us: no creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account (Heb 4:13). For the friends that is a threat. For Job it is a hope. If even the grave is naked before God, then Job's innocence is not hidden from him either.

verseByVerse.quote: He stretches out the north over the void and hangs the earth on nothing. He binds up the waters in his thick clouds, and the cloud is not split open under them. He covers the face of the full moon and spreads over it his cloud. He has inscribed a circle on the face of the waters at the boundary between light and darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He stretches out the north over the void and hangs the earth on nothing.

A breathtaking line. The ancient world usually pictured the earth resting on pillars or on the back of something. Job says God hangs it on nothing. It is poetry, not a science lesson, but the point is exact: nothing holds the world up except God. The New Testament names the one who does it: the Son upholds the universe by the word of his power (Heb 1:3); in him all things hold together (Col 1:17). The same hands that hold up the earth hold up the believer who has nothing left under him.

He binds up the waters in his thick clouds, and the cloud is not split open under them. He covers the face of the full moon and spreads over it his cloud. He has inscribed a circle on the face of the waters at the boundary between light and darkness. Tons of water carried in a cloud that does not burst; the moon veiled; the horizon drawn like a compass line where sea meets sky, the edge of day and night. Wisdom says it too: when he drew a circle on the face of the deep (Prov 8:27). Everything Job points to is ordinary and astonishing at once.

verseByVerse.quote: The pillars of heaven tremble and are astounded at his rebuke. By his power he stilled the sea; by his understanding he shattered Rahab. By his wind the heavens were made fair; his hand pierced the fleeing serpent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pillars of heaven tremble and are astounded at his rebuke. By his power he stilled the sea; by his understanding he shattered Rahab. By his wind the heavens were made fair; his hand pierced the fleeing serpent.

The mountains that seem to hold up the sky shake when he rebukes them. He calmed the raging sea. Rahab is the sea monster of 9:13, and the fleeing serpent is Leviathan, whom Isaiah calls Leviathan the fleeing serpent (Isa 27:1), the monster Job once wanted roused against his birthday (3:8). The powers of chaos are nothing to God. His wind clears the sky after the storm.

Then read the Gospel. A storm on the lake, the boat filling with water, and Jesus asleep. And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, Peace! Be still! And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm (Mark 4:39). His rebuke; the sea stilled. The disciples asked, Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? (Mark 4:41). Job has told us. Only God stills the sea. The man in the boat was God.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ways, and how small a whisper do we hear of him! But the thunder of his power who can understand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ways, and how small a whisper do we hear of him! But the thunder of his power who can understand?

After all that, Job says: this is only the edge. The underworld, the sky, the sea, the stars: all of it is the fringe of God's garment, the outskirts of his ways, a faint whisper of who he is. If this is the whisper, who could stand the thunder?

This verse judges every neat explanation of suffering, the friends' and ours. They thought they had God's ways mapped: sin brings trouble, righteousness brings blessing, and Job's case can be read off the chart. Job says: we have heard a whisper. Paul says the same of the Christian's knowledge now: For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face (1 Cor 13:12). Humility is not a lack of faith; it is faith that knows how big God is.

And the thunder is coming. In twelve chapters the LORD will answer Job out of the whirlwind (38:1), and Job will hear more than a whisper. It will not explain his suffering. It will show him God.

26.theology:
God upholds the world with nothing beneath it (v. 7), and the Son upholds the universe by his word (Heb 1:3; Col 1:17). He stills the sea by his rebuke (vv. 11-12), and Jesus did (Mark 4:39-41).

All that can be seen of God is the outskirts of his ways, a whisper (v. 14). No theology, the friends' or ours, has him mapped (1 Cor 13:12).
26.examples:
Whose breath has come out from you?

Sheol is naked before God, and so are we (Heb 4:13).

The earth hung on nothing.

The sea stilled at his rebuke: Mark 4:39.

The outskirts of his ways; a whisper; the thunder to come.

27.title: I Will Not Put Away My Integrity
27.text: <sup>1</sup>And Job again took up his discourse, and said:<sup>2</sup>"As God lives, who has taken away my right, and the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter,<sup>3</sup>as long as my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils,<sup>4</sup>my lips will not speak falsehood, and my tongue will not utter deceit.<sup>5</sup>Far be it from me to say that you are right; till I die I will not put away my integrity from me.<sup>6</sup>I hold fast my righteousness and will not let it go; my heart does not reproach me for any of my days.<sup>7</sup>"Let my enemy be as the wicked, and let him who rises up against me be as the unrighteous.<sup>8</sup>For what is the hope of the godless when God cuts him off, when God takes away his life?<sup>9</sup>Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him?<sup>10</sup>Will he take delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times?<sup>11</sup>I will teach you concerning the hand of God; what is with the Almighty I will not conceal.<sup>12</sup>Behold, all of you have seen it yourselves; why then have you become altogether vain?<sup>13</sup>"This is the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage that oppressors receive from the Almighty:<sup>14</sup>If his children are multiplied, it is for the sword, and his descendants have not enough bread.<sup>15</sup>Those who survive him the pestilence buries, and his widows do not weep.<sup>16</sup>Though he heap up silver like dust, and pile up clothing like clay,<sup>17</sup>he may pile it up, but the righteous will wear it, and the innocent will divide the silver.<sup>18</sup>He builds his house like a moth's, like a booth that a watchman makes.<sup>19</sup>He goes to bed rich, but will do so no more; he opens his eyes, and his wealth is gone.<sup>20</sup>Terrors overtake him like a flood; in the night a whirlwind carries him off.<sup>21</sup>The east wind lifts him up and he is gone; it sweeps him out of his place.<sup>22</sup>It hurls at him without pity; he flees from its power in headlong flight.<sup>23</sup>It claps its hands at him and hisses at him from its place.
27.overview: With the friends silent, Job takes up his discourse again. He swears by the God who has taken away his right that he will not speak falsehood, will not say the friends are right, and will not put away his integrity; his heart does not reproach him (vv. 1-6). Let his enemy be as the wicked, who has no hope when God takes his life and does not delight in the Almighty; Job will teach them about God's hand (vv. 7-12). This is the portion of the wicked: children for the sword, silver inherited by the innocent, a house like a moth's, wealth gone overnight, swept away by the east wind (vv. 13-23).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — I Will Not Put Away My Integrity
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job takes up his discourse again (v. 1). As God lives, who has taken away my right, as long as he has breath, he will not speak falsehood (vv. 2-4). Till I die I will not put away my integrity from me. I hold fast my righteousness and will not let it go (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Job swears by the God he is protesting to. He will not buy peace with a false confession.

verseByVerse.quote: And Job again took up his discourse, and said:
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Job again took up his discourse, and said:

The friends are silent. After Bildad's six verses, it would be Zophar's turn, and Zophar says nothing. So Job speaks again, and a new heading marks the change: he took up his discourse, a word used for a solemn speech or parable. From here to chapter 31, with the great poem on wisdom in the middle, Job speaks alone. The debate is over. What follows is his closing statement.

verseByVerse.quote: "As God lives, who has taken away my right, and the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter, as long as my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils, my lips will not speak falsehood, and my tongue will not utter deceit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As God lives, who has taken away my right, and the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter, as long as my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils, my lips will not speak falsehood, and my tongue will not utter deceit.

Job swears an oath, and he swears it by God. As God lives was the most solemn oath there was. And notice by whom he swears: the God who has taken away my right, who has made my soul bitter. Job is protesting against God and swearing by him in the same breath. He has no one else to swear by. Even his grievance is addressed to God.

Those words have been heard before, in the mouth of a widow who came home from Moab with nothing: call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me (Ruth 1:20). The same two words, the Almighty and bitterness. And Naomi's story ends with a kinsman-redeemer, a go'el, the very word of Job's great confession (19:25). Both of them felt the Almighty's hand as bitter. Both were being led, without knowing it, to a redeemer.

As long as my breath is in me: every breath he uses to speak is God's gift (12:10), and he will not use it to lie. As at the beginning, Job did not sin with his lips (2:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Far be it from me to say that you are right; till I die I will not put away my integrity from me. I hold fast my righteousness and will not let it go; my heart does not reproach me for any of my days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Far be it from him, Job says, to agree with the friends. Till I die I will not put away my integrity from me. I hold fast my righteousness and will not let it go; my heart does not reproach me for any of my days.

Here is the answer to a question asked in chapter 2. God said, He still holds fast his integrity (2:3). Job's wife said, Do you still hold fast your integrity? Curse God and die (2:9). Now Job answers, on oath, with the same word and the same verb: I will not put away my integrity ... I hold fast my righteousness. He will not agree with the friends to buy peace. A false confession would end the argument and be a lie, and he will not tell it. That is what God saw in him from the start.

My heart does not reproach me. His conscience is clear. John writes, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God (1 John 3:21). But Paul adds a caution every believer needs: I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me (1 Cor 4:4). A clear conscience is a gift; it is not the final verdict. Job's defence of his innocence is true, and it will be vindicated (42:7). But Elihu will accuse him of justifying himself rather than God (32:2), and God will ask him, Will you condemn me that you may be in the right? (40:8). Holding fast to one's integrity is right. Using it to put God in the wrong is not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Let My Enemy Be as the Wicked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let his accusers be treated as the wicked (v. 7). What hope has the godless when God takes his life? Will God hear him, will he delight in the Almighty (vv. 8-10)? Job will teach them about God's hand; why have they become so empty (vv. 11-12)?
verseByVerse.theology: Job does not deny that God judges the wicked. He denies that he is one.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let my enemy be as the wicked, and let him who rises up against me be as the unrighteous. For what is the hope of the godless when God cuts him off, when God takes away his life? Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him? Will he take delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let my enemy be as the wicked, and let him who rises up against me be as the unrighteous. Job turns the friends' doctrine on them. They have risen up against him like false witnesses. The law said a false witness should receive what he meant for his brother (Deut 19:18-19). Let them have the portion they have been assigning to him.

For what is the hope of the godless when God cuts him off, when God takes away his life? Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him? Will he take delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times? The godless man has no hope at death, God does not hear him, he takes no delight in God, he does not keep praying. Every one of those questions is a quiet claim about Job. He has hope (19:25); he cries to God and expects to be heard (23:3-7); Eliphaz told him to delight yourself in the Almighty (22:26), and he has never stopped calling on God. That is not how a godless man behaves.

verseByVerse.quote: I will teach you concerning the hand of God; what is with the Almighty I will not conceal. Behold, all of you have seen it yourselves; why then have you become altogether vain?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will teach you concerning the hand of God; what is with the Almighty I will not conceal. Behold, all of you have seen it yourselves; why then have you become altogether vain?

Job will teach the teachers. They have seen the same world he has, the wicked prospering and the righteous suffering. Why then have they filled the air with hevel, vapour, empty talk (21:34)? Their answers do not fit what their own eyes have seen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — The Portion of a Wicked Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This is the portion of a wicked man with God (v. 13): his children fall to the sword, his widows do not weep (vv. 14-15); the innocent will divide his silver (vv. 16-17); his house is like a moth's, his wealth gone overnight (vv. 18-19); terror and the east wind sweep him away, and the wind hisses at him (vv. 20-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Zophar's words (20:29), now in Job's mouth. Job holds the same truth about the wicked; he refuses the friends' use of it against him.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage that oppressors receive from the Almighty: If his children are multiplied, it is for the sword, and his descendants have not enough bread. Those who survive him the pestilence buries, and his widows do not weep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage that oppressors receive from the Almighty.

These words are almost exactly Zophar's last line (20:29), and the paragraph that follows sounds like the friends: the wicked man's children fall by the sword, his survivors die of plague, his widows do not mourn him. Some readers think this is Zophar's missing third speech, misplaced in the copying of the book. Others think Job is quoting the friends' doctrine back to them. But the text gives it to Job, and it fits what he has just said: let my enemy be as the wicked (v. 7). Job has never denied that God judges the wicked. He has denied that everyone who suffers is wicked. He believes this portion is real, and he warns the men who have falsely accused him that it is theirs to fear.

If his children are multiplied, it is for the sword, and his descendants have not enough bread. Those who survive him the pestilence buries, and his widows do not weep. It is hard to read these words from a man whose children are dead. Job does not turn them round and apply them to himself. That was the friends' mistake: reading the harvest back into the seed.

verseByVerse.quote: Though he heap up silver like dust, and pile up clothing like clay, he may pile it up, but the righteous will wear it, and the innocent will divide the silver. He builds his house like a moth's, like a booth that a watchman makes. He goes to bed rich, but will do so no more; he opens his eyes, and his wealth is gone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though he heap up silver like dust, and pile up clothing like clay, he may pile it up, but the righteous will wear it, and the innocent will divide the silver. The oppressor hoards silver and clothes, and in the end the righteous inherit them. The sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous (Prov 13:22). Job himself will one day be given silver and gold by those who come to him (42:11).

He builds his house like a moth's, like a booth that a watchman makes. He goes to bed rich, but will do so no more; he opens his eyes, and his wealth is gone. A moth's cocoon, a watchman's shelter of branches in a vineyard: flimsy things that vanish in a season. The rich man goes to sleep secure and wakes up with nothing, like the man in Jesus' parable who heard, This night your soul is required of you (Luke 12:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Terrors overtake him like a flood; in the night a whirlwind carries him off. The east wind lifts him up and he is gone; it sweeps him out of his place. It hurls at him without pity; he flees from its power in headlong flight. It claps its hands at him and hisses at him from its place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Terrors overtake him like a flood; in the night a whirlwind carries him off. The east wind lifts him up and he is gone; it sweeps him out of his place. It hurls at him without pity; he flees from its power in headlong flight. It claps its hands at him and hisses at him from its place.

The end of the wicked is a storm in the night: the hot east wind from the desert picks him up and throws him away, and then claps its hands and hisses at him, the gesture of derision passers-by made at ruined Jerusalem (Lam 2:15). A great wind took Job's children (1:19), and the friends drew their conclusion. Job says: the storm that sweeps away the wicked is real, and it is God's; but not every man a storm has struck is wicked.

The difference between Job and the wicked man is not what has happened to them. It is where their hope is. The wicked man's hope ends when God takes his life (v. 8). Job's does not: I know that my Redeemer lives.

27.theology:
Job holds fast his integrity (vv. 5-6; 2:3, 9) and will not buy peace with a false confession. A clear conscience is a gift, not the final verdict (1 Cor 4:4); God will vindicate Job's honesty (42:7) and correct his self-justification (40:8).

Job affirms the judgment of the wicked (vv. 13-23) while denying that suffering proves wickedness. The difference between him and the wicked is where hope lies when God takes a man's life (v. 8; 19:25).
27.examples:
The friends fall silent; Zophar never speaks a third time.

The Almighty, who has made my soul bitter: Naomi's words.

Job's sworn answer to his wife's question.

A clear conscience, and the Lord who judges.

Zophar's words in Job's mouth: three readings.

28.title: Where Shall Wisdom Be Found?
28.text: <sup>1</sup>"Surely there is a mine for silver, and a place for gold that they refine.<sup>2</sup>Iron is taken out of the earth, and copper is smelted from the ore.<sup>3</sup>Man puts an end to darkness and searches out to the farthest limit the ore in gloom and deep darkness.<sup>4</sup>He opens shafts in a valley away from where anyone lives; they are forgotten by travelers; they hang in the air, far away from mankind; they swing to and fro.<sup>5</sup>As for the earth, out of it comes bread, but underneath it is turned up as by fire.<sup>6</sup>Its stones are the place of sapphires, and it has dust of gold.<sup>7</sup>"That path no bird of prey knows, and the falcon's eye has not seen it.<sup>8</sup>The proud beasts have not trodden it; the lion has not passed over it.<sup>9</sup>"Man puts his hand to the flinty rock and overturns mountains by the roots.<sup>10</sup>He cuts out channels in the rocks, and his eye sees every precious thing.<sup>11</sup>He dams up the streams so that they do not trickle, and the thing that is hidden he brings out to light.<sup>12</sup>"But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding?<sup>13</sup>Man does not know its worth, and it is not found in the land of the living.<sup>14</sup>The deep says, 'It is not in me,' and the sea says, 'It is not with me.'<sup>15</sup>It cannot be bought for gold, and silver cannot be weighed as its price.<sup>16</sup>It cannot be valued in the gold of Ophir, in precious onyx or sapphire.<sup>17</sup>Gold and glass cannot equal it, nor can it be exchanged for jewels of fine gold.<sup>18</sup>No mention shall be made of coral or of crystal; the price of wisdom is above pearls.<sup>19</sup>The topaz of Ethiopia cannot equal it, nor can it be valued in pure gold.<sup>20</sup>"From where, then, does wisdom come? And where is the place of understanding?<sup>21</sup>It is hidden from the eyes of all living and concealed from the birds of the air.<sup>22</sup>Abaddon and Death say, 'We have heard a rumor of it with our ears.'<sup>23</sup>"God understands the way to it, and he knows its place.<sup>24</sup>For he looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens.<sup>25</sup>When he gave to the wind its weight and apportioned the waters by measure,<sup>26</sup>when he made a decree for the rain and a way for the lightning of the thunder,<sup>27</sup>then he saw it and declared it; he established it, and searched it out.<sup>28</sup>And he said to man, 'Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.'"
28.overview: Men know where to mine silver, gold, iron and copper; they sink shafts into darkness far from everyone, hanging on ropes, breaking rock with fire, going where no hawk or lion has been, bringing hidden things to light (vv. 1-11). But where shall wisdom be found? It is not in the land of the living, not in the deep or the sea; no gold, onyx, sapphire, coral, crystal or pearls can buy it; it is hidden from all living, and Death has only heard a rumour of it (vv. 12-22). God understands the way to it; when he weighed the wind and made a way for the rain and lightning, he saw wisdom and established it. And he said to man, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding (vv. 23-28).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There is a mine for silver, a place for gold, iron and copper (vv. 1-2). Man drives his shafts into darkness far from where anyone lives, hanging on ropes (vv. 3-4); bread grows on the earth while fire turns it up below (vv. 5-6). No hawk or lion knows the path (vv. 7-8). He overturns mountains, cuts channels in the rock, and the thing that is hidden he brings out to light (vv. 9-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Human beings can get treasure out of the heart of a mountain. The poem admires it, and is about to ask what they cannot get.

verseByVerse.quote: "Surely there is a mine for silver, and a place for gold that they refine. Iron is taken out of the earth, and copper is smelted from the ore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Surely there is a mine for silver, and a place for gold that they refine. Iron is taken out of the earth, and copper is smelted from the ore.

After twenty-five chapters of argument, the voice changes. There is no accusation in this chapter, no complaint, no raised voice. It is a quiet poem, and it asks the question underneath the whole debate: where is wisdom? Who really understands how God runs the world?

Who speaks it? The chapter runs straight on from Job's discourse (27:1), and the ESV sets it as his. But its calm is so unlike the speeches around it, and chapter 29 begins again with And Job again took up his discourse (29:1), that many readers take it as the author's own interlude, a pause between the debate and Job's last defence. Either way, it stands in the middle of the book like a hinge. Everything before it has been men claiming wisdom. Everything after it will lead to God speaking.

It begins underground. Silver has its mine; gold has its place, and men know how to refine it. Iron is dug from the earth; copper is melted out of rock. People know where treasure is, and how to get it out.

verseByVerse.quote: Man puts an end to darkness and searches out to the farthest limit the ore in gloom and deep darkness. He opens shafts in a valley away from where anyone lives; they are forgotten by travelers; they hang in the air, far away from mankind; they swing to and fro.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Man puts an end to darkness and searches out to the farthest limit the ore in gloom and deep darkness. The miner carries his lamp into the dark and pushes to the end of the seam. Gloom and deep darkness are the very words Job called down on his birthday (3:5). Here men go into that darkness on purpose, looking for something precious. And notice the verb: he searches out the ore. It is the word the poem will use at the end, where God searched ... out wisdom (v. 27). Man can search out silver to the end of the seam. Only God can search out wisdom.

He opens shafts in a valley away from where anyone lives; they are forgotten by travelers; they hang in the air, far away from mankind; they swing to and fro. A picture of real mining in the ancient world: shafts sunk in lonely valleys, and the miners let down on ropes, swinging in the dark, far from anyone. It is dangerous, clever, costly work. Human beings will risk their lives for silver.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the earth, out of it comes bread, but underneath it is turned up as by fire. Its stones are the place of sapphires, and it has dust of gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for the earth, out of it comes bread, but underneath it is turned up as by fire. Its stones are the place of sapphires, and it has dust of gold.

On the surface, a quiet wheat field. Underneath, men are breaking the rock with fire, splitting it open to reach the sapphire and the gold dust. The same ground feeds us on top and hides treasure below, and man has learned to get at both. Keep that picture of hidden treasure in the ground. Job once said the suffering dig for death more than for hidden treasures (3:21). This poem goes down into the same mines, and asks what is more precious than any of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "That path no bird of prey knows, and the falcon's eye has not seen it. The proud beasts have not trodden it; the lion has not passed over it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That path no bird of prey knows, and the falcon's eye has not seen it. The proud beasts have not trodden it; the lion has not passed over it.

The hawk sees a mouse from the sky and has never seen a mine. The lion goes anywhere it likes and has never walked these tunnels. Man goes where the sharpest-eyed bird and the boldest beast cannot. The poem is building its case: human beings are astonishing. Remember this path that no bird knows. Wisdom will be concealed from the birds of the air too (v. 21), and it will be hidden from the miner.

The proud beasts is literally "the sons of pride", a phrase that appears again only once, at the end of God's description of Leviathan: he is king over all the sons of pride (41:34). The proud creatures that never found the miner's path are the creatures God will parade before Job, and he is their Master.

verseByVerse.quote: "Man puts his hand to the flinty rock and overturns mountains by the roots. He cuts out channels in the rocks, and his eye sees every precious thing. He dams up the streams so that they do not trickle, and the thing that is hidden he brings out to light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Man puts his hand to the flinty rock and overturns mountains by the roots. He cuts out channels in the rocks, and his eye sees every precious thing. He dams up the streams so that they do not trickle, and the thing that is hidden he brings out to light.

Flint, mountains, channels cut through stone, underground streams dammed so the miners can work: there seems to be nothing man cannot do with the earth. The thing that is hidden he brings out to light. Job said that about God: He uncovers the deeps out of darkness (12:22). Man can do something like it with rock and ore.

Watch the eyes in this poem. Man's eye sees every precious thing in the rock (v. 10). Wisdom is hidden from the eyes of all living (v. 21). And God sees everything under the heavens (v. 24). Human sight reaches the sapphire and stops. Only God's reaches wisdom.

That is exactly the point. Our cleverness with things is real, and every age has had more of it than the one before. And it has never been enough to make anyone wise. The next verse turns on that.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — Where Shall Wisdom Be Found?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding? (v. 12). It is not in the land of the living, the deep or the sea (vv. 13-14). No gold, silver, onyx, sapphire, coral, crystal or pearls can buy it (vv. 15-19). It is hidden from every living thing; Abaddon and Death say, We have heard a rumor of it (vv. 20-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The one thing that matters most cannot be dug up or bought. It has to be given.

verseByVerse.quote: "But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding? Man does not know its worth, and it is not found in the land of the living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding?

Here is the question, and the whole book has been asking it. The friends thought they had found wisdom: in visions (4:12), in the fathers (8:8), in their own long experience (15:10). Job has searched for it too, and for God. Men can find silver in a mountain. Where can they find the wisdom to understand God's ways with a suffering man?

Man does not know its worth, and it is not found in the land of the living. We do not even know what it would cost. It is not anywhere on earth. The question will be asked again in almost the same words (v. 20), like a refrain.

verseByVerse.quote: The deep says, 'It is not in me,' and the sea says, 'It is not with me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The deep says, It is not in me, and the sea says, It is not with me.

The poem sends the question to the deepest places the ancient world knew, and they answer: not here. The ocean floor, the waters under the earth, the places no miner could reach, have not got it either. Wisdom is not somewhere further down. It is not a matter of digging deeper.

verseByVerse.quote: It cannot be bought for gold, and silver cannot be weighed as its price. It cannot be valued in the gold of Ophir, in precious onyx or sapphire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It cannot be bought for gold, and silver cannot be weighed as its price. It cannot be valued in the gold of Ophir, in precious onyx or sapphire.

If it cannot be dug up, can it be bought? No. Silver was weighed out on scales in a sale; there is not enough silver in the world for this. The gold of Ophir was the finest gold there was. Onyx and sapphire, the treasures the miners risked their lives for (v. 6), are worthless as payment.

Eliphaz had told Job to throw his gold of Ophir among the stones of the torrent-bed, and God would be his gold (22:24-25). He was right that God is more precious than Ophir's gold. The poem adds what Eliphaz forgot: so is wisdom, and Eliphaz did not have it either.

verseByVerse.quote: Gold and glass cannot equal it, nor can it be exchanged for jewels of fine gold. No mention shall be made of coral or of crystal; the price of wisdom is above pearls. The topaz of Ethiopia cannot equal it, nor can it be valued in pure gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gold and glass cannot equal it, nor can it be exchanged for jewels of fine gold. No mention shall be made of coral or of crystal; the price of wisdom is above pearls. The topaz of Ethiopia cannot equal it, nor can it be valued in pure gold.

Glass was a luxury in that world, as precious as jewellery. Coral from the sea, rock crystal, pearls, topaz from far-off Cush: the poem piles up the whole jeweller's window and says, do not even mention them. Proverbs says the same: She is more precious than jewels, and nothing you desire can compare with her (Prov 3:15).

Jesus told of a man who found something more precious than everything he had: on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it (Matt 13:46). Wisdom is above pearls, and the kingdom is the pearl. The friends had plenty of learning. They did not have this.

verseByVerse.quote: "From where, then, does wisdom come? And where is the place of understanding? It is hidden from the eyes of all living and concealed from the birds of the air. Abaddon and Death say, 'We have heard a rumor of it with our ears.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
From where, then, does wisdom come? And where is the place of understanding? It is hidden from the eyes of all living and concealed from the birds of the air. The refrain again. Hidden from every living eye, even the falcon's (v. 7).

Abaddon and Death say, We have heard a rumor of it with our ears. The poem goes below the sea, to Destruction and Death themselves, the places Job said lie naked before God (26:6). They have only heard a rumour of wisdom. Death knows many secrets, and not this one. Not the living, not the dead, not the deep, not the sky: no one in all creation holds it. There is only one place left to look.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–28 — The Fear of the Lord, That Is Wisdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God understands the way to it, and he knows its place (v. 23). He sees the whole earth; when he weighed the wind, measured the waters and set a way for the rain and lightning, he saw wisdom, established it and searched it out (vv. 24-27). And he said to man, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom belongs to God, and man's share in it is to fear him. That is exactly what the narrator said of Job on the first page (1:1).

verseByVerse.quote: "God understands the way to it, and he knows its place. For he looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God understands the way to it, and he knows its place. For he looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens.

Here is the answer. Wisdom is not lost; it is with God. He knows the road to it and where it lives, because he sees everything, to the ends of the earth. What man cannot find by digging, God has always known.

This is the book's turning point. The friends spoke as if they had wisdom and could apply it to Job's case. Job spoke as if he could summon God and argue it. Both were looking for wisdom in the wrong place, in themselves. It belongs to God. Any wisdom a human being will ever have must come from him, as a gift. If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him (James 1:5), written by the apostle who holds Job up to the church.

verseByVerse.quote: When he gave to the wind its weight and apportioned the waters by measure, when he made a decree for the rain and a way for the lightning of the thunder, then he saw it and declared it; he established it, and searched it out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he gave to the wind its weight and apportioned the waters by measure, when he made a decree for the rain and a way for the lightning of the thunder, then he saw it and declared it; he established it, and searched it out.

When God made the world he weighed the wind, measured out the seas, gave the rain its law and the lightning its path. And at that moment, the poem says, he looked at wisdom, spoke it, set it in place. Wisdom is the pattern God built into creation. Proverbs pictures Wisdom present at the making of the world: The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his work, the first of his acts of old (Prov 8:22). The New Testament gives that Wisdom a name and a face: In the beginning was the Word ... All things were made through him (John 1:1, 3). The wisdom by which God made the world is the Son by whom he made it.

Notice too how the poem pictures God's wisdom: as measuring. He gives weight to the wind, which seems to weigh nothing, and measures out the seas. Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand ... and weighed the mountains in scales? (Isa 40:12). A God who weighs the wind has weighed Job's trouble too, to the ounce. Job asked for his calamity to be laid in the balances (6:2). It had been, by the only one who could.

Two words here reach across the book. A way for the lightning of the thunder is the same Hebrew phrase God himself will use when he speaks from the whirlwind (38:25, where the ESV has a way for the thunderbolt). The poem is pointing ahead: when God speaks, he will speak about exactly this. And searched it out is Eliphaz's proud word, this we have searched out; it is true (5:27), and Bildad's, what the fathers have searched out (8:8). They claimed to have searched it out. Only God has.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to man, 'Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to man, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.

After the mines, the jewels, the deep and death itself, the answer is short. Man cannot possess God's wisdom. But God has told man what wisdom looks like for him: to fear the Lord, and to turn from evil. Not to understand everything, but to reverence the one who does, and to live accordingly. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (Ps 111:10; cf. Prov 1:7). It is the only place in the book where God is called the Lord in the sense of Master, and it is fitting: wisdom begins with knowing who is Master.

Now turn back to the first verse of the book. That man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil (1:1). The same two things. By the definition God gives here, Job was the wise man all along: not the three wise men from Teman and Shuah with their visions and traditions, but the man on the ash heap who feared God and would not let go of him. Jesus thanked his Father that he had hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children (Matt 11:25).

And the New Testament tells us where the hidden treasure finally is. Job said the suffering dig for death more than for hidden treasures (3:21). The miners dig for treasure and cannot find wisdom. Paul points to Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3). Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24), who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30). The wisdom no one could dig out of the earth came down to it. To fear the Lord now is to trust him.

What does this mean for someone in Job's place? The fear of the Lord is not terror; it is the reverent trust of a creature who knows God is God. In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence (Prov 14:26). It is not an explanation of suffering, and the poem does not pretend it is. It is a way of living when there is no explanation: hold God in awe, keep turning from evil, and leave the understanding with him. That is exactly what Job did on the first day of his troubles, before any friend had spoken, when he fell on the ground and worshiped (1:20). He did not understand then either. He was wise.

28.theology:
Wisdom belongs to God alone; man cannot dig it out or buy it, and the friends' claim to have searched it out (5:27) is false (v. 27). Man's share in wisdom is to fear the Lord and turn from evil (v. 28), the very description of Job in 1:1: the man on the ash heap is the wise man.

The hidden treasures of wisdom are in Christ (Col 2:3), the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24, 30), and God gives wisdom to those who ask (James 1:5).
28.examples:
Miners on ropes in the dark, where no hawk has looked.

Bread above, fire below.

No jewel can buy it: the pearl of great value.

Death has only heard a rumour.

Searched it out: Eliphaz's boast, God's alone.

The fear of the Lord, and turning from evil: 1:1.

Hidden treasures: 3:21, the mines, Colossians 2:3.

29.title: Oh, That I Were as in the Months of Old
29.text: <sup>1</sup>And Job again took up his discourse, and said:<sup>2</sup>"Oh, that I were as in the months of old, as in the days when God watched over me,<sup>3</sup>when his lamp shone upon my head, and by his light I walked through darkness,<sup>4</sup>as I was in my prime, when the friendship of God was upon my tent,<sup>5</sup>when the Almighty was yet with me, when my children were all around me,<sup>6</sup>when my steps were washed with butter, and the rock poured out for me streams of oil!<sup>7</sup>When I went out to the gate of the city, when I prepared my seat in the square,<sup>8</sup>the young men saw me and withdrew, and the aged rose and stood;<sup>9</sup>the princes refrained from talking and laid their hand on their mouth;<sup>10</sup>the voice of the nobles was hushed, and their tongue stuck to the roof of their mouth.<sup>11</sup>When the ear heard, it called me blessed, and when the eye saw, it approved,<sup>12</sup>because I delivered the poor who cried for help, and the fatherless who had none to help him.<sup>13</sup>The blessing of him who was about to perish came upon me, and I caused the widow's heart to sing for joy.<sup>14</sup>I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; my justice was like a robe and a turban.<sup>15</sup>I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame.<sup>16</sup>I was a father to the needy, and I searched out the cause of him whom I did not know.<sup>17</sup>I broke the fangs of the unrighteous and made him drop his prey from his teeth.<sup>18</sup>Then I thought, 'I shall die in my nest, and I shall multiply my days as the sand,<sup>19</sup>my roots spread out to the waters, with the dew all night on my branches,<sup>20</sup>my glory fresh with me, and my bow ever new in my hand.'<sup>21</sup>"Men listened to me and waited and kept silence for my counsel.<sup>22</sup>After I spoke they did not speak again, and my word dropped upon them.<sup>23</sup>They waited for me as for the rain, and they opened their mouths as for the spring rain.<sup>24</sup>I smiled on them when they had no confidence, and the light of my face they did not cast down.<sup>25</sup>I chose their way and sat as chief, and I lived like a king among his troops, like one who comforts mourners.
29.overview: Job longs for the months when God watched over him, when God's lamp shone on his head, when the friendship of God was over his tent and his children were around him (vv. 1-6). At the city gate the young and old and princes honoured him, because he delivered the poor and the fatherless, made the widow sing, wore righteousness like a robe, was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame and a father to the needy, and broke the power of the oppressor (vv. 7-17). He expected to die old in his nest; men waited for his words like rain, and he lived like a king, like one who comforts mourners (vv. 18-25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Days When God Watched Over Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oh, that I were as in the months of old, as in the days when God watched over me (vv. 1-2): when God's lamp shone on his head (v. 3), when the friendship of God was upon my tent, when the Almighty was with him and his children were around him (vv. 4-5), and the rock poured out oil (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: What Job misses most is not his wealth but God's nearness, and his children.

verseByVerse.quote: And Job again took up his discourse, and said: "Oh, that I were as in the months of old, as in the days when God watched over me, when his lamp shone upon my head, and by his light I walked through darkness,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Job again took up his discourse, and said: Oh, that I were as in the months of old, as in the days when God watched over me, when his lamp shone upon my head, and by his light I walked through darkness.

Job's closing defence runs through three chapters. In this one he looks back, in the next he looks at the present, and in chapter 31 he swears his innocence before God. It begins with longing: if only it were like it used to be.

Listen to what he misses first. Not his flocks. The days when God watched over me, when his lamp shone upon my head. The words sound like the blessing Israel's priests pronounced: The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you (Num 6:24-25). Job had lived under that blessing: kept, and shone upon. And with God's lamp over him he could walk through dark places unafraid. For it is you who light my lamp; the LORD my God lightens my darkness (Ps 18:28).

Many believers know this ache: the memory of a season when God seemed close, set against a present in which he seems far. Job does not pretend the memory is not there. But the reader knows something Job does not: God has not stopped watching over him. The limit set in heaven, only spare his life (2:6), is God's watch still being kept.

verseByVerse.quote: as I was in my prime, when the friendship of God was upon my tent, when the Almighty was yet with me, when my children were all around me, when my steps were washed with butter, and the rock poured out for me streams of oil!
verseByVerse.commentary:
As I was in my prime, when the friendship of God was upon my tent, when the Almighty was yet with me, when my children were all around me, when my steps were washed with butter, and the rock poured out for me streams of oil!

The friendship of God is a striking phrase. The Hebrew is exactly the phrase Eliphaz used when he mocked Job: Have you listened in the council of God? (15:8). The same words mean God's council and God's intimate friendship. Job says: I had it once, over my own tent. The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him (Ps 25:14). Jesus gives it to his disciples: I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you (John 15:15).

When my children were all around me. It is the line that hurts most. Your children will be like olive shoots around your table (Ps 128:3), and his were, and they are gone. Then the abundance: paths so rich they seemed washed in butter, oil flowing from the rock (Deut 32:13). His life overflowed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–17 — I Was Eyes to the Blind
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the city gate the young stepped aside, the old stood, the princes fell silent (vv. 7-10), because I delivered the poor who cried for help, and the fatherless who had none to help him (vv. 11-12). He made the widow sing, wore righteousness like a robe, was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame, a father to the needy, and broke the jaws of the oppressor (vv. 13-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Every charge Eliphaz invented (22:6-9) is answered by the life Job actually lived. It is a portrait of the King the psalms long for, and Christ is.

verseByVerse.quote: When I went out to the gate of the city, when I prepared my seat in the square, the young men saw me and withdrew, and the aged rose and stood; the princes refrained from talking and laid their hand on their mouth; the voice of the nobles was hushed, and their tongue stuck to the roof of their mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I went out to the gate of the city, when I prepared my seat in the square, the young men saw me and withdrew, and the aged rose and stood; the princes refrained from talking and laid their hand on their mouth; the voice of the nobles was hushed, and their tongue stuck to the roof of their mouth.

The city gate was the court, the council chamber and the town square of an ancient city, where the elders sat to judge and decide. When Job came, the young men stepped back respectfully, the old men got to their feet, and even princes stopped talking. Compare 19:18: now children jeer when he tries to stand.

Laid their hand on their mouth. The great men of the city did before Job what Job will do before God. When the LORD has spoken from the whirlwind, Job will say, I lay my hand on my mouth (40:4). Respect for a man silences the princes. The glory of God silences the man.

verseByVerse.quote: When the ear heard, it called me blessed, and when the eye saw, it approved, because I delivered the poor who cried for help, and the fatherless who had none to help him. The blessing of him who was about to perish came upon me, and I caused the widow's heart to sing for joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the ear heard, it called me blessed, and when the eye saw, it approved, because I delivered the poor who cried for help, and the fatherless who had none to help him. The blessing of him who was about to perish came upon me, and I caused the widow's heart to sing for joy.

Why did they honour him? Not for his money. Because he rescued the poor who cried out and the orphan who had no one. Dying men blessed him; widows sang because of him. This is the answer to Eliphaz, who said Job sent widows away empty and crushed the fatherless (22:9). Job does not argue the charge. He describes his life, and the life answers it.

verseByVerse.quote: I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; my justice was like a robe and a turban. I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. I was a father to the needy, and I searched out the cause of him whom I did not know. I broke the fangs of the unrighteous and made him drop his prey from his teeth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; my justice was like a robe and a turban. I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. I was a father to the needy, and I searched out the cause of him whom I did not know. I broke the fangs of the unrighteous and made him drop his prey from his teeth.

Righteousness was what he wore every day, as a judge wears his robe. He was the eyes of the blind man, the feet of the lame; he was a father to the destitute. And I searched out the cause of him whom I did not know: when a stranger's case came before him, he investigated it properly. Searched out is the verb Eliphaz used for his confident conclusions (5:27). Job used it for the hard work of finding out the truth about a stranger, which is exactly what the friends never did for him.

This is the picture of the king Israel longed for: he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper ... From oppression and violence he redeems their life (Ps 72:12, 14). It is the picture of God himself, who put on righteousness as a breastplate (Isa 59:17). And it is Christ. When John the Baptist asked whether Jesus was the one, Jesus answered, the blind receive their sight and the lame walk (Matt 11:5). Job was eyes to the blind. Christ gave the blind their own.

I broke the fangs of the unrighteous and made him drop his prey from his teeth. The oppressor is pictured as a wild beast with a victim in its jaws, and Job as the man who wrenched the victim out. It is what the psalmist asks God to do: you break the teeth of the wicked (Ps 3:7). Job's justice was God's justice at work through a human judge. That is what earthly authority is for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — Like One Who Comforts Mourners
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He expected to die old in his nest, like a well-watered tree (vv. 18-20). Men waited for his words as for rain; his smile gave them courage (vv. 21-24); I chose their way and sat as chief, and I lived like a king among his troops, like one who comforts mourners (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: Job had been the comforter the friends failed to be. The comforter of all who mourn is the Messiah (Isa 61:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I thought, 'I shall die in my nest, and I shall multiply my days as the sand, my roots spread out to the waters, with the dew all night on my branches, my glory fresh with me, and my bow ever new in my hand.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I thought, I shall die in my nest, and I shall multiply my days as the sand, my roots spread out to the waters, with the dew all night on my branches, my glory fresh with me, and my bow ever new in my hand.

He expected to die at home, old and surrounded by his family, like a bird in its nest. He pictured himself as a tree with roots in the water and dew on its leaves every night: the blessed man of the first psalm, like a tree planted by streams of water (Ps 1:3). He is not proud to have expected it. Any godly man might have.

And the strange thing is that it came true. After this Job lived 140 years ... And Job died, an old man, and full of days (42:16-17). The tree he thought uprooted (19:10) put down its roots again. But not before he had been through the fire.

verseByVerse.quote: "Men listened to me and waited and kept silence for my counsel. After I spoke they did not speak again, and my word dropped upon them. They waited for me as for the rain, and they opened their mouths as for the spring rain. I smiled on them when they had no confidence, and the light of my face they did not cast down. I chose their way and sat as chief, and I lived like a king among his troops, like one who comforts mourners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men listened to me and waited and kept silence for my counsel. After I spoke they did not speak again, and my word dropped upon them. They waited for me as for the rain, and they opened their mouths as for the spring rain.

People waited for his advice the way a dry field waits for rain, and when he spoke there was no more to be said. Moses prayed, May my teaching drop as the rain (Deut 32:2). Job's counsel was like that.

I smiled on them when they had no confidence, and the light of my face they did not cast down. I chose their way and sat as chief, and I lived like a king among his troops, like one who comforts mourners. When others lost heart, his smile gave them courage.
