He led like a king, and he was one who comforts mourners.

Notice the light of my face. At the start of the chapter God's lamp shone on Job (v. 3). Here Job's face shines on others, the discouraged and frightened. He passed on what he received. That is the believer's calling still: let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven (Matt 5:16).

That is the last line of the chapter, and it is pointed. The friends came to comfort him (2:11). Job had been, for years, the man who comforted mourners, and they could not do for him what he had done for others. The Messiah's mission is described in the same words: the Spirit of the Lord is upon him to bind up the brokenhearted ... to comfort all who mourn (Isa 61:1-2), and Jesus read the opening of that passage in Nazareth and said it was fulfilled in him (Luke 4:18-21). The comforter Job was, Christ is, to everyone who mourns.

29.theology:
What Job misses most is God's watching care and friendship (vv. 2-4), the blessing of Numbers 6:24-25 and the friendship of the LORD for those who fear him (Ps 25:14; John 15:15). God had not stopped watching (2:6).

Job's life answers Eliphaz's invented charges (22:6-9) and sketches the righteous King who delivers the needy (Ps 72:12-14), whom Christ fulfils (Matt 11:5), the comforter of all who mourn (Isa 61:1-2; Luke 4:18).
29.examples:
When God watched over me, when his lamp shone: the priestly blessing.

The friendship of God: the phrase Eliphaz mocked (15:8).

When my children were all around me.

Princes laid their hands on their mouths before Job; Job will before God.

Eyes to the blind and feet to the lame.

Like one who comforts mourners: Isaiah 61:2.

30.title: But Now They Laugh at Me
30.text: <sup>1</sup>"But now they laugh at me, men who are younger than I, whose fathers I would have disdained to set with the dogs of my flock.<sup>2</sup>What could I gain from the strength of their hands, men whose vigor is gone?<sup>3</sup>Through want and hard hunger they gnaw the dry ground by night in waste and desolation;<sup>4</sup>they pick saltwort and the leaves of bushes, and the roots of the broom tree for their food.<sup>5</sup>They are driven out from human company; they shout after them as after a thief.<sup>6</sup>In the gullies of the torrents they must dwell, in holes of the earth and of the rocks.<sup>7</sup>Among the bushes they bray; under the nettles they huddle together.<sup>8</sup>A senseless, a nameless brood, they have been whipped out of the land.<sup>9</sup>"And now I have become their song; I am a byword to them.<sup>10</sup>They abhor me; they keep aloof from me; they do not hesitate to spit at the sight of me.<sup>11</sup>Because God has loosed my cord and humbled me, they have cast off restraint in my presence.<sup>12</sup>On my right hand the rabble rise; they push away my feet; they cast up against me their ways of destruction.<sup>13</sup>They break up my path; they promote my calamity; they need no one to help them.<sup>14</sup>As through a wide breach they come; amid the crash they roll on.<sup>15</sup>Terrors are turned upon me; my honor is pursued as by the wind, and my prosperity has passed away like a cloud.<sup>16</sup>"And now my soul is poured out within me; days of affliction have taken hold of me.<sup>17</sup>The night racks my bones, and the pain that gnaws me takes no rest.<sup>18</sup>With great force my garment is disfigured; it binds me about like the collar of my tunic.<sup>19</sup>God has cast me into the mire, and I have become like dust and ashes.<sup>20</sup>I cry to you for help and you do not answer me; I stand, and you only look at me.<sup>21</sup>You have turned cruel to me; with the might of your hand you persecute me.<sup>22</sup>You lift me up on the wind; you make me ride on it, and you toss me about in the roar of the storm.<sup>23</sup>For I know that you will bring me to death and to the house appointed for all living.<sup>24</sup>"Yet does not one in a heap of ruins stretch out his hand, and in his disaster cry for help?<sup>25</sup>Did not I weep for him whose day was hard? Was not my soul grieved for the needy?<sup>26</sup>But when I hoped for good, evil came, and when I waited for light, darkness came.<sup>27</sup>My inward parts are in turmoil and never still; days of affliction come to meet me.<sup>28</sup>I go about darkened, but not by the sun; I stand up in the assembly and cry for help.<sup>29</sup>I am a brother of jackals and a companion of ostriches.<sup>30</sup>My skin turns black and falls from me, and my bones burn with heat.<sup>31</sup>My lyre is turned to mourning, and my pipe to the voice of those who weep.
30.overview: But now Job is laughed at by young outcasts, men whose fathers he would not have set with his dogs, driven from society to live in gullies and eat roots (vv. 1-8). He has become their song and byword; they spit at him; because God has loosed his cord they break through against him, and his honour and prosperity are gone (vv. 9-15). His soul is poured out, pain gnaws his bones, God has thrown him into the mire; he cries and God does not answer; God has turned cruel and will bring him to death (vv. 16-23). He wept for others, but when he hoped for good evil came; he is a brother of jackals, his skin blackened, his lyre turned to mourning (vv. 24-31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — But Now They Laugh at Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But now they laugh at me, men who are younger than I, whose fathers I would have disdained to set with the dogs of my flock (v. 1). They are broken men, gnawing roots in the desert, driven out of every town, braying among the bushes, a senseless, a nameless brood (vv. 2-8).
verseByVerse.theology: The man before whom princes fell silent is mocked by outcasts. And the bitterness of it shows in how he speaks of them.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now they laugh at me, men who are younger than I, whose fathers I would have disdained to set with the dogs of my flock. What could I gain from the strength of their hands, men whose vigor is gone?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now they laugh at me, men who are younger than I, whose fathers I would have disdained to set with the dogs of my flock. What could I gain from the strength of their hands, men whose vigor is gone?

Chapter 29 was then. This chapter answers it three times: but now (v. 1), and now (v. 9), and now (v. 16). The man who once sat at the city gate while princes fell silent is laughed at by young men of the lowest kind, men whose fathers he would not have trusted to guard his sheepdogs.

Something has to be said honestly here. These are harsh words, and they do not sit well beside the Job of chapter 29, a father to the needy (29:16), or the Job who described the homeless poor with such compassion (24:5-8). Suffering has done what suffering often does: it has brought pride to the surface. The mockers are cruel, and Job is right that they are. But the contempt in his reply is not the best of him. The one who was mocked by the lowest of men and answered differently is Christ: When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Pet 2:23). Job is a real man, not a plaster saint, and the book lets us see it.

verseByVerse.quote: Through want and hard hunger they gnaw the dry ground by night in waste and desolation; they pick saltwort and the leaves of bushes, and the roots of the broom tree for their food. They are driven out from human company; they shout after them as after a thief. In the gullies of the torrents they must dwell, in holes of the earth and of the rocks. Among the bushes they bray; under the nettles they huddle together. A senseless, a nameless brood, they have been whipped out of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through want and hard hunger they gnaw the dry ground by night in waste and desolation; they pick saltwort and the leaves of bushes, and the roots of the broom tree for their food. They are driven out from human company; they shout after them as after a thief. In the gullies of the torrents they must dwell, in holes of the earth and of the rocks. Among the bushes they bray; under the nettles they huddle together. A senseless, a nameless brood, they have been whipped out of the land.

These are outcasts: men driven out of the towns, living in dry wadis and caves, eating salty desert plants and bitter roots, chased off like thieves, huddling in the scrub like animals. They have nothing and no name. And even they look down on Job now. He has fallen below the bottom of society.

Compare the picture with 24:5. There Job described the homeless poor as wild donkeys in the desert, scavenging for their children, and he wrote with tenderness. Here the same kind of men bray among the bushes, and he writes with scorn. The picture is the same; the heart has changed, because now they are mocking him. Every reader should hold that mirror up to himself: how we speak of the poor can change the moment they turn on us.

It is the depth of social disgrace, and the Son of God went there too. The men who spat on him, the passers-by who shook their heads at the cross, the criminal who mocked him as he hung there: he was despised by the despised. He came down further than Job, and he came down on purpose.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — I Have Become Their Song
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And now I have become their song; I am a byword to them; they spit at the sight of him (vv. 9-10). Because God has loosed his cord, they throw off restraint, break up his path and pour through the breach (vv. 11-14); terrors chase him and his prosperity is gone like a cloud (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: He is a joke and a song among the lowest of men, as the sufferer of Psalm 69 was, and as Christ was.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now I have become their song; I am a byword to them. They abhor me; they keep aloof from me; they do not hesitate to spit at the sight of me. Because God has loosed my cord and humbled me, they have cast off restraint in my presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now I have become their song; I am a byword to them. They abhor me; they keep aloof from me; they do not hesitate to spit at the sight of me.

They make up songs about him. The psalm of innocent suffering the New Testament applies to Christ says the same: I am the talk of those who sit in the gate, and the drunkards make songs about me (Ps 69:12). A byword, a joke, a face spat on (17:6). The spitting will come again at the trial of Jesus.

Because God has loosed my cord and humbled me, they have cast off restraint in my presence. God has cut his tent-rope, or unstrung his bow; either way, his strength and standing are gone, and people who once feared him feel free to do as they like. Job traces even their insolence back to God's hand. He is right that God's hand is in it (2:3), and still does not know why.

verseByVerse.quote: On my right hand the rabble rise; they push away my feet; they cast up against me their ways of destruction. They break up my path; they promote my calamity; they need no one to help them. As through a wide breach they come; amid the crash they roll on. Terrors are turned upon me; my honor is pursued as by the wind, and my prosperity has passed away like a cloud.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On my right hand the rabble rise; they push away my feet; they cast up against me their ways of destruction. They break up my path; they promote my calamity; they need no one to help them. As through a wide breach they come; amid the crash they roll on.

The siege of 19:12 again, but now it is a mob, not an army: rabble pushing him off the path, pouring through the breach in his defences. Terrors are turned upon me; my honor is pursued as by the wind, and my prosperity has passed away like a cloud. His honour blown away, his wealth gone like a cloud that crosses the sky and is not there any more.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–23 — I Cry to You and You Do Not Answer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And now my soul is poured out within me (v. 16); pain gnaws his bones by night (vv. 17-18); God has thrown him into the mire, and I have become like dust and ashes (v. 19). I cry to you for help and you do not answer me (v. 20). God has turned cruel, tosses him in the storm, and will bring him to death (vv. 21-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The words of Psalm 22, and of the cross. God did not answer yet. He would.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now my soul is poured out within me; days of affliction have taken hold of me. The night racks my bones, and the pain that gnaws me takes no rest. With great force my garment is disfigured; it binds me about like the collar of my tunic. God has cast me into the mire, and I have become like dust and ashes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now my soul is poured out within me; days of affliction have taken hold of me. The night racks my bones, and the pain that gnaws me takes no rest.

The third now, and the deepest. His life drains out of him like water from a jar. At night the pain is in his bones, gnawing, never resting. It is the language of Psalm 22, the psalm of the cross: I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint (Ps 22:14).

With great force my garment is disfigured; it binds me about like the collar of my tunic. God has cast me into the mire, and I have become like dust and ashes. His clothes cling to his sores; he is thrown in the mud. Dust and ashes: Abraham used the words of himself before God, I who am but dust and ashes (Gen 18:27), and Job will use them once more, at the very end, when he has seen God: I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes (42:6). Here they are the words of humiliation. There they will be the words of worship.

verseByVerse.quote: I cry to you for help and you do not answer me; I stand, and you only look at me. You have turned cruel to me; with the might of your hand you persecute me. You lift me up on the wind; you make me ride on it, and you toss me about in the roar of the storm. For I know that you will bring me to death and to the house appointed for all living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I cry to you for help and you do not answer me; I stand, and you only look at me.

One of the loneliest lines in Job's prayers. He cries, and there is no answer. He stands up, and God just looks at him. Many believers have prayed into that silence. The psalm of the cross prays it: O my God, I cry by day, but you do not answer (Ps 22:2). And on the cross Jesus cried My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matt 27:46). The Son of God entered the silence Job describes, so that for those who belong to him it would never be the last word.

You only look at me. Job feels God's gaze as cold, a spectator watching him suffer. But he said himself, in a better hour, he knows the way that I take (23:10). God's eyes on Job were never the eyes of indifference. They were the eyes that had looked at him in the council and said, there is none like him on the earth (1:8).

You have turned cruel to me; with the might of your hand you persecute me. You lift me up on the wind; you make me ride on it, and you toss me about in the roar of the storm. For I know that you will bring me to death and to the house appointed for all living.

This is Job's hardest charge: God has become cruel. It is not true, and the reader must not take it as true; God will ask Job, Will you condemn me that you may be in the right? (40:8). But notice that Job says it to God, and God does not strike him for it. God can bear his children's worst words spoken to his face. And the storm Job says tosses him about is the storm God will speak from (38:1). The grave, the house appointed for all living, is coming for everyone (Heb 9:27). Job expects to go there unanswered. He will not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–31 — My Lyre Is Turned to Mourning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Does not a ruined man cry out? Job wept for others in their hard days (vv. 24-25); when I hoped for good, evil came (v. 26). He is in turmoil, blackened, crying in the assembly, a brother of jackals and a companion of ostriches (vv. 27-29); his skin falls, his bones burn, my lyre is turned to mourning (vv. 30-31).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's closing lament. The God who turns mourning into dancing (Ps 30:11) has not finished.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet does not one in a heap of ruins stretch out his hand, and in his disaster cry for help? Did not I weep for him whose day was hard? Was not my soul grieved for the needy? But when I hoped for good, evil came, and when I waited for light, darkness came.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet does not one in a heap of ruins stretch out his hand, and in his disaster cry for help? Did not I weep for him whose day was hard? Was not my soul grieved for the needy?

Surely a man buried in the rubble may reach out his hand and shout for help. And Job had always helped others who cried: he wept for people having a hard day, he grieved for the poor. Weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15). He did it for others. Why will no one do it for him?

But when I hoped for good, evil came, and when I waited for light, darkness came. The prophet confessed the same for a whole people: we hope for light, and behold, darkness (Isa 59:9). It is the experience of disappointed hope, and Scripture does not pretend it never happens to the faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: My inward parts are in turmoil and never still; days of affliction come to meet me. I go about darkened, but not by the sun; I stand up in the assembly and cry for help. I am a brother of jackals and a companion of ostriches. My skin turns black and falls from me, and my bones burn with heat. My lyre is turned to mourning, and my pipe to the voice of those who weep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My inward parts are in turmoil and never still; days of affliction come to meet me. I go about darkened, but not by the sun; I stand up in the assembly and cry for help. I am a brother of jackals and a companion of ostriches.

His skin is blackened, but not by sunburn; it is the disease. He stands up in public and cries for help and gets none. His only kin now are jackals and ostriches, the creatures of the ruined places whose wailing cries in the night were proverbial; Micah would say, I will make lamentation like the jackals, and mourning like the ostriches (Mic 1:8). And when God speaks, he will talk about the ostrich (39:13-18), with something like a smile. The creature Job named as his companion in misery, God describes as his own handiwork.

My skin turns black and falls from me, and my bones burn with heat. My lyre is turned to mourning, and my pipe to the voice of those who weep.

The last lines of his lament. Fever in his bones, skin peeling off. And his music has changed: the lyre and pipe that should play at feasts play funeral songs. The wicked still rejoice to the sound of the pipe (21:12). Job's pipe weeps.

But the book is not over, and neither is God. You have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness (Ps 30:11). Job has stitched sackcloth to his skin (16:15). God will loose it.

30.theology:
Job's lament uses the words of Psalms 22 and 69, the psalms of the cross: poured out, a song of drunkards, crying without answer (vv. 9, 16, 20; Matt 27:46). His charge that God is cruel (v. 21) is false and God will correct it (40:8), yet God receives it without striking him.

Suffering exposes pride even in the godly (vv. 1-8); Christ, reviled, did not revile (1 Pet 2:23). The dust and ashes of humiliation (v. 19) become the dust and ashes of repentance (42:6), and mourning will be turned to dancing (Ps 30:11).
30.examples:
But now ... and now ... and now.

The contempt in Job's reply is not the best of him.

The drunkards make songs about me (Ps 69:12).

Dust and ashes: here humiliation, at 42:6 worship.

I cry to you for help and you do not answer me.

The ostrich: Job's companion, God's creature.

The lyre turned to mourning, and the promise of dancing.

31.title: Here Is My Signature
31.text: <sup>1</sup>"I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin?<sup>2</sup>What would be my portion from God above and my heritage from the Almighty on high?<sup>3</sup>Is not calamity for the unrighteous, and disaster for the workers of iniquity?<sup>4</sup>Does not he see my ways and number all my steps?<sup>5</sup>"If I have walked with falsehood and my foot has hastened to deceit;<sup>6</sup>(Let me be weighed in a just balance, and let God know my integrity!)<sup>7</sup>if my step has turned aside from the way and my heart has gone after my eyes, and if any spot has stuck to my hands,<sup>8</sup>then let me sow, and another eat, and let what grows for me be rooted out.<sup>9</sup>"If my heart has been enticed toward a woman, and I have lain in wait at my neighbor's door,<sup>10</sup>then let my wife grind for another, and let others bow down on her.<sup>11</sup>For that would be a heinous crime; that would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges;<sup>12</sup>for that would be a fire that consumes as far as Abaddon, and it would burn to the root all my increase.<sup>13</sup>"If I have rejected the cause of my manservant or my maidservant, when they brought a complaint against me,<sup>14</sup>what then shall I do when God rises up? When he makes inquiry, what shall I answer him?<sup>15</sup>Did not he who made me in the womb make him? And did not one fashion us in the womb?<sup>16</sup>"If I have withheld anything that the poor desired, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail,<sup>17</sup>or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it<sup>18</sup>(for from my youth the fatherless grew up with me as with a father, and from my mother's womb I guided the widow),<sup>19</sup>if I have seen anyone perish for lack of clothing, or the needy without covering,<sup>20</sup>if his body has not blessed me, and if he was not warmed with the fleece of my sheep,<sup>21</sup>if I have raised my hand against the fatherless, because I saw my help in the gate,<sup>22</sup>then let my shoulder blade fall from my shoulder, and let my arm be broken from its socket.<sup>23</sup>For I was in terror of calamity from God, and I could not have faced his majesty.<sup>24</sup>"If I have made gold my trust or called fine gold my confidence,<sup>25</sup>if I have rejoiced because my wealth was abundant or because my hand had found much,<sup>26</sup>if I have looked at the sun when it shone, or the moon moving in splendor,<sup>27</sup>and my heart has been secretly enticed, and my mouth has kissed my hand,<sup>28</sup>this also would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges, for I would have been false to God above.<sup>29</sup>"If I have rejoiced at the ruin of him who hated me, or exulted when evil overtook him<sup>30</sup>(I have not let my mouth sin by asking for his life with a curse),<sup>31</sup>if the men of my tent have not said, 'Who is there that has not been filled with his meat?'<sup>32</sup>(the sojourner has not lodged in the street; I have opened my doors to the traveler),<sup>33</sup>if I have concealed my transgressions as others do by hiding my iniquity in my heart,<sup>34</sup>because I stood in great fear of the multitude, and the contempt of families terrified me, so that I kept silence, and did not go out of doors—<sup>35</sup>Oh, that I had one to hear me! (Here is my signature! Let the Almighty answer me!) Oh, that I had the indictment written by my adversary!<sup>36</sup>Surely I would carry it on my shoulder; I would bind it on me as a crown;<sup>37</sup>I would give him an account of all my steps; like a prince I would approach him.<sup>38</sup>"If my land has cried out against me and its furrows have wept together,<sup>39</sup>if I have eaten its yield without payment and made its owners breathe their last,<sup>40</sup>let thorns grow instead of wheat, and foul weeds instead of barley." The words of Job are ended.
31.overview: Job swears his innocence in a series of oaths. He made a covenant with his eyes; let him be weighed in a just balance; if he had deceived, or lusted after his neighbour's wife, let the curse fall (vv. 1-12). He heard his servants' complaints, for the same God made them in the womb; he fed the orphan, clothed the naked and never raised his hand against the helpless (vv. 13-23). He did not trust gold or worship the sun and moon, did not gloat over his enemy or curse him, opened his door to travellers, and did not hide his sins as others do (vv. 24-34). Here is his signature: let the Almighty answer, and let his accuser write the charge; he would wear it as a crown. If his land cries against him, let thorns grow. The words of Job are ended (vv. 35-40).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — A Covenant with My Eyes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin? God sees his every step (vv. 1-4). If he has walked in falsehood, let me be weighed in a just balance, and let another eat his harvest (vv. 5-8). If his heart has been enticed toward his neighbour's wife, let his own wife grind for another; adultery is a fire that burns to Abaddon (vv. 9-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's innocence begins where Jesus' teaching begins: not only with the deed, but with the look.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin? What would be my portion from God above and my heritage from the Almighty on high? Is not calamity for the unrighteous, and disaster for the workers of iniquity? Does not he see my ways and number all my steps?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin?

This is Job's last speech, and it takes a form every reader in the ancient world would have recognised: the oath of clearance. "If I have done this, then let that happen to me." A man who swore it was calling God's judgment down on himself if he lied. Job goes through the whole of life, sin by sin, and swears to each. It answers Eliphaz's invented charges (22:5-9) more thoroughly than any argument could.

And he starts with the eyes. Not with adultery but with the look that comes before it. He made a solemn agreement with his own eyes that they would not linger on a young woman with desire. Jesus would teach the same: everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt 5:28). Job's righteousness was not only a matter of what people saw him do. It went down to where he let his eyes go.

What would be my portion from God above and my heritage from the Almighty on high? Is not calamity for the unrighteous, and disaster for the workers of iniquity? Does not he see my ways and number all my steps? Job kept his covenant because he knew God was watching every step. That is not fear of being caught. It is the fear of the Lord, which is wisdom (28:28).

verseByVerse.quote: "If I have walked with falsehood and my foot has hastened to deceit; (Let me be weighed in a just balance, and let God know my integrity!) if my step has turned aside from the way and my heart has gone after my eyes, and if any spot has stuck to my hands, then let me sow, and another eat, and let what grows for me be rooted out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I have walked with falsehood and my foot has hastened to deceit; (Let me be weighed in a just balance, and let God know my integrity!) if my step has turned aside from the way and my heart has gone after my eyes, and if any spot has stuck to my hands, then let me sow, and another eat, and let what grows for me be rooted out.

Deceit in business, dishonest gain, the heart following wherever the eyes lead (Num 15:39), a stain on his hands. If so, let someone else eat his harvest. And in the middle, a cry: let me be weighed in a just balance. He asked the same at the start (6:2). A king of Babylon was once weighed by God and found wanting (Dan 5:27). Job asks to be weighed, because he believes the scales will show his integrity, the word God used of him (2:3).

verseByVerse.quote: "If my heart has been enticed toward a woman, and I have lain in wait at my neighbor's door, then let my wife grind for another, and let others bow down on her. For that would be a heinous crime; that would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges; for that would be a fire that consumes as far as Abaddon, and it would burn to the root all my increase.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If my heart has been enticed toward a woman, and I have lain in wait at my neighbor's door, then let my wife grind for another, and let others bow down on her. For that would be a heinous crime; that would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges; for that would be a fire that consumes as far as Abaddon, and it would burn to the root all my increase.

If he had waited at his neighbour's door for the husband to go out, then let his own wife become another man's servant and worse. It is one of the harshest curses in the chapter, and it measures how seriously he takes the sin. Adultery is a crime for the courts, and more: a fire that burns all the way down to destruction and takes everything a man has with it. Can a man carry fire next to his chest and his clothes not be burned? ... So is he who goes in to his neighbor's wife (Prov 6:27, 29). Job knew it, and did not touch the fire.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Did Not He Who Made Me Make Him?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If he has dismissed his servants' complaints, what will he answer God? Did not he who made me in the womb make him? (vv. 13-15). If he has withheld from the poor, eaten alone while the orphan went hungry, or let anyone go without clothing, let his arm be broken from its socket, for he feared God's majesty (vv. 16-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Master and servant were made by the same God in the same way. Job lived as if that were true.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I have rejected the cause of my manservant or my maidservant, when they brought a complaint against me, what then shall I do when God rises up? When he makes inquiry, what shall I answer him? Did not he who made me in the womb make him? And did not one fashion us in the womb?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I have rejected the cause of my manservant or my maidservant, when they brought a complaint against me, what then shall I do when God rises up? When he makes inquiry, what shall I answer him?

In Job's world a servant had no rights against his master. Job listened to his servants' complaints anyway, because he knew he had a Master too, who would one day ask him how he had treated them.

Did not he who made me in the womb make him? And did not one fashion us in the womb? Here is the reason, and it is one of the great sentences of the Old Testament. The same God made master and slave, in the same way, in their mothers' wombs. Neither is more human than the other. Has not one God created us? asks Malachi (Mal 2:10). Paul tells Christian masters to treat their servants well, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him (Eph 6:9). The dignity of every human being rests here: not on what he can do, or what he owns, but on the fact that God made him.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I have withheld anything that the poor desired, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail, or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it (for from my youth the fatherless grew up with me as with a father, and from my mother's womb I guided the widow), if I have seen anyone perish for lack of clothing, or the needy without covering, if his body has not blessed me, and if he was not warmed with the fleece of my sheep,
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I have withheld anything that the poor desired, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail, or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it (for from my youth the fatherless grew up with me as with a father, and from my mother's womb I guided the widow), if I have seen anyone perish for lack of clothing, or the needy without covering, if his body has not blessed me, and if he was not warmed with the fleece of my sheep.

Eliphaz said Job had withheld bread from the hungry, stripped the naked and sent widows away (22:6-9). Job answers every item on oath. He never ate alone while an orphan went without; orphans grew up in his house as if he were their father; he never let a poor man freeze while his own sheep had wool. The poor man's body blessed him, warm under Job's fleece.

It is the religion James describes: Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction (James 1:27). And it is the religion of the sheep in Jesus' judgment, who fed the hungry and clothed the naked (Matt 25:35-36). Eliphaz charged Job with the sins of the goats. Job's life was the life of the sheep.

verseByVerse.quote: if I have raised my hand against the fatherless, because I saw my help in the gate, then let my shoulder blade fall from my shoulder, and let my arm be broken from its socket. For I was in terror of calamity from God, and I could not have faced his majesty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I have raised my hand against the fatherless, because I saw my help in the gate, then let my shoulder blade fall from my shoulder, and let my arm be broken from its socket. For I was in terror of calamity from God, and I could not have faced his majesty.

It would have been easy. An orphan had no one to speak for him at the city gate, where the elders were Job's friends and Job himself sat as judge (29:7). Job could have raised his hand against the helpless and won. If he had, let that arm be torn off. He did not, because he feared God more than he feared any man, and loved justice more than advantage. Power over the defenceless is the real test of a man, and Job passed it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–34 — If I Have Made Gold My Trust
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If he trusted gold, or kissed his hand to the sun and moon, he would have been false to God (vv. 24-28). He did not gloat over his enemy or curse him (vv. 29-30); no traveller slept in the street (vv. 31-32). He did not hide his sin as others do for fear of what people would say (vv. 33-34).
verseByVerse.theology: The inward sins, greed, idolatry, spite, secrecy, are the ones a man could hide. Job swears he did not hide them.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I have made gold my trust or called fine gold my confidence, if I have rejoiced because my wealth was abundant or because my hand had found much, if I have looked at the sun when it shone, or the moon moving in splendor, and my heart has been secretly enticed, and my mouth has kissed my hand, this also would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges, for I would have been false to God above.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I have made gold my trust or called fine gold my confidence, if I have rejoiced because my wealth was abundant or because my hand had found much, if I have looked at the sun when it shone, or the moon moving in splendor, and my heart has been secretly enticed, and my mouth has kissed my hand, this also would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges, for I would have been false to God above.

Now the sins no one could see. Trusting in money: Job was the richest man in the east, and he swears his confidence was never in his gold. That is why he could lose it and still bless God (1:21). Paul calls greed what it is, covetousness, which is idolatry (Col 3:5), and tells the rich not to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God (1 Tim 6:17).

And the worship of the sun and moon, the religion of most of the ancient world, which Moses warned Israel against (Deut 4:19). To kiss the hand was to blow a kiss of worship toward the sky. Job never did it, even secretly. Either sin, trusting in gold or bowing to the heavens, would have been false to God above. Idolatry is unfaithfulness to the one true God, and Job was faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I have rejoiced at the ruin of him who hated me, or exulted when evil overtook him (I have not let my mouth sin by asking for his life with a curse), if the men of my tent have not said, 'Who is there that has not been filled with his meat?' (the sojourner has not lodged in the street; I have opened my doors to the traveler),
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I have rejoiced at the ruin of him who hated me, or exulted when evil overtook him (I have not let my mouth sin by asking for his life with a curse).

He did not gloat when an enemy fell, and he never cursed an enemy's life. Do not rejoice when your enemy falls (Prov 24:17). Jesus went further: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matt 5:44). This is a higher standard than Job kept in his worst moment, when he said of his accusers, Let my enemy be as the wicked (27:7). That was an appeal for justice against false witnesses, not a curse on a man's life; but here, in his better self, Job holds to more.

If the men of my tent have not said, Who is there that has not been filled with his meat? (the sojourner has not lodged in the street; I have opened my doors to the traveler). His servants could say there was no one who had not eaten at his table. No traveller ever had to sleep in the square. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers (Heb 13:2). Job's door was always open.

verseByVerse.quote: if I have concealed my transgressions as others do by hiding my iniquity in my heart, because I stood in great fear of the multitude, and the contempt of families terrified me, so that I kept silence, and did not go out of doors—
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I have concealed my transgressions as others do by hiding my iniquity in my heart, because I stood in great fear of the multitude, and the contempt of families terrified me, so that I kept silence, and did not go out of doors.

Job has never claimed to be sinless. What he swears here is that he did not hide the sins he had. As others do can also be read, as the ESV's note says, as Adam did. The first man, when he sinned, hid himself (Gen 3:10). Job did not hide. He did not keep quiet about his faults out of fear of what the neighbours would think.

That is the way of the gospel. Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy (Prov 28:13). If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9). The fear of people is what makes us hide, and the fear of man lays a snare (Prov 29:25). Job feared God, and so he did not need to hide from anyone.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oh, that I had one to hear me! (Here is my signature! Let the Almighty answer me!) Oh, that I had the indictment written by my adversary! He would wear it on his shoulder like a crown and approach God like a prince (vv. 35-37). If his land has cried out against him, let thorns grow instead of wheat (vv. 38-40). The words of Job are ended.
verseByVerse.theology: Job signs his defence and rests his case. The next voice he hears will be God's.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, that I had one to hear me! (Here is my signature! Let the Almighty answer me!) Oh, that I had the indictment written by my adversary! Surely I would carry it on my shoulder; I would bind it on me as a crown; I would give him an account of all my steps; like a prince I would approach him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh, that I had one to hear me! (Here is my signature! Let the Almighty answer me!) Oh, that I had the indictment written by my adversary!

Job ends his defence like a man in court signing his statement. Here is my signature is, in Hebrew, "here is my mark": the word is the name of the last letter of the alphabet, which in the old script was written as a simple cross-mark and could serve as a signature. He has said everything. He puts his mark to it. Now let God answer.

And he asks for the charge sheet: let my accuser write out the case against me. Surely I would carry it on my shoulder; I would bind it on me as a crown; I would give him an account of all my steps; like a prince I would approach him. He would wear the indictment proudly, like a crown, because he knows it would prove nothing, and he would walk into God's presence with his head up.

Read those words beside the cross. Christ was crowned, with thorns, and over his head they put the charge against him, which read, This is Jesus, the King of the Jews (Matt 27:37). He carried a written charge that was no crime, and he carried ours, which were real: the record of debt that stood against us, which God set aside, nailing it to the cross (Col 2:14). Job wanted to wear his indictment as a crown because he was innocent. Christ wore ours because we were not. And because he did, we can do what Job longed to do, and approach God with confidence (Heb 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: "If my land has cried out against me and its furrows have wept together, if I have eaten its yield without payment and made its owners breathe their last, let thorns grow instead of wheat, and foul weeds instead of barley." The words of Job are ended.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If my land has cried out against me and its furrows have wept together, if I have eaten its yield without payment and made its owners breathe their last, let thorns grow instead of wheat, and foul weeds instead of barley. The words of Job are ended.

A last oath, about the land itself. If he had got his fields by fraud or worked his labourers to death without paying them, the soil would cry out against him, as Abel's blood cried from the ground (Gen 4:10) and as the unpaid wages of the harvesters are crying out against you (James 5:4). If so, let the curse of Eden fall on his fields: thorns and thistles instead of grain (Gen 3:18).

The words of Job are ended. He has nothing more to say to the friends, and he has made his last appeal to God. The next time Job opens his mouth it will be to God, and it will be short: Behold, I am of small account; what shall I answer you? I lay my hand on my mouth (40:4). Between here and there, a young man will speak, and then the LORD himself.

31.theology:
Job's oath answers Eliphaz's invented charges (22:5-9) and describes righteousness from the heart outward: the eye (Matt 5:28), the servant made by the same God (Mal 2:10; Eph 6:9), the orphan and widow (James 1:27), the heart that does not trust in gold (Col 3:5), the enemy not cursed (Matt 5:44), sin confessed and not hidden (Prov 28:13).

Job would wear his indictment as a crown because he was innocent (vv. 35-36). Christ wore a crown and the written charge because we were guilty, and the record against us was nailed to the cross (Matt 27:37; Col 2:14).
31.examples:
A covenant with my eyes.

Did not he who made me in the womb make him?

The poor man warmed by the fleece of Job's sheep.

As others do, or as Adam did: he did not hide.

Here is my signature: Job's mark, and the charge over the cross.

The words of Job are ended.

32.title: I Am Young in Years
32.text: <sup>1</sup>So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes.<sup>2</sup>Then Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, burned with anger. He burned with anger at Job because he justified himself rather than God.<sup>3</sup>He burned with anger also at Job's three friends because they had found no answer, although they had declared Job to be in the wrong.<sup>4</sup>Now Elihu had waited to speak to Job because they were older than he.<sup>5</sup>And when Elihu saw that there was no answer in the mouth of these three men, he burned with anger.<sup>6</sup>And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said: "I am young in years, and you are aged; therefore I was timid and afraid to declare my opinion to you.<sup>7</sup>I said, 'Let days speak, and many years teach wisdom.'<sup>8</sup>But it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand.<sup>9</sup>It is not the old who are wise, nor the aged who understand what is right.<sup>10</sup>Therefore I say, 'Listen to me; let me also declare my opinion.'<sup>11</sup>"Behold, I waited for your words, I listened for your wise sayings, while you searched out what to say.<sup>12</sup>I gave you my attention, and, behold, there was none among you who refuted Job or who answered his words.<sup>13</sup>Beware lest you say, 'We have found wisdom; God may vanquish him, not a man.'<sup>14</sup>He has not directed his words against me, and I will not answer him with your speeches.<sup>15</sup>"They are dismayed; they answer no more; they have not a word to say.<sup>16</sup>And shall I wait, because they do not speak, because they stand there, and answer no more?<sup>17</sup>I also will answer with my share; I also will declare my opinion.<sup>18</sup>For I am full of words; the spirit within me constrains me.<sup>19</sup>Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins ready to burst.<sup>20</sup>I must speak, that I may find relief; I must open my lips and answer.<sup>21</sup>I will not show partiality to any man or use flattery toward any person.<sup>22</sup>For I do not know how to flatter, else my Maker would soon take me away.
32.overview: The three friends stop answering Job because he is righteous in his own eyes. Elihu the Buzite, who had waited because he was younger, burns with anger at Job for justifying himself rather than God, and at the friends for condemning Job without an answer (vv. 1-5). He says that wisdom comes not from age but from the Spirit of the Almighty; none of the friends refuted Job; he is full of words like new wineskins ready to burst, and will show no partiality or flattery (vv. 6-22).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The three friends stop answering, because Job is righteous in his own eyes (v. 1). Elihu, son of Barachel the Buzite, burns with anger at Job because he justified himself rather than God (v. 2), and at the friends because they had found no answer, although they had declared Job to be in the wrong (v. 3). He had waited because they were older (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: A new voice, angry at both sides. The narrator does not tell us whether he is right; the end of the book will, by what it does not say.

verseByVerse.quote: So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes.

The debate is over. The friends have no more to say, and the narrator tells us why, from their point of view: Job was righteous in his own eyes. They could not move him. The reader knows that Job was righteous in God's eyes too (1:8). But the phrase is a warning as well. There is a way of holding on to one's innocence that begins to look like self-righteousness, and the next speaker will say so.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, burned with anger. He burned with anger at Job because he justified himself rather than God. He burned with anger also at Job's three friends because they had found no answer, although they had declared Job to be in the wrong. Now Elihu had waited to speak to Job because they were older than he. And when Elihu saw that there was no answer in the mouth of these three men, he burned with anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, burned with anger. He burned with anger at Job because he justified himself rather than God.

A new voice, and one the reader has not been told was there. Elihu is the only speaker in the book given a family tree. His name means "He is my God". His father's name, Barachel, contains the word for bless, the word that ran through the first two chapters. Buz was the brother of Uz in the family of Abraham's brother Nahor (Gen 22:21), so Elihu's clan and Job's homeland carry the names of two brothers.

And he is angry. The narrator says it four times in four verses. He is angry at Job because he justified himself rather than God. That is a real charge, and it is not the friends' charge. The friends said Job had sinned before his suffering. Elihu says Job is going wrong in how he speaks now: defending himself at God's expense. God himself will put the same question to Job: Will you condemn me that you may be in the right? (40:8).

He burned with anger also at Job's three friends because they had found no answer, although they had declared Job to be in the wrong. Now Elihu had waited to speak to Job because they were older than he. And when Elihu saw that there was no answer in the mouth of these three men, he burned with anger. The friends condemned Job and could not prove it. Elihu sees that too.

Hold the phrase burned with anger in mind. At the end of the book the LORD will say to Eliphaz, My anger burns against you and against your two friends (42:7), the same expression. Elihu's anger burns against Job and the friends. God's burns against the friends alone. Elihu is half right.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–22 — I Am Young in Years
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I am young in years, and you are aged; he waited for age to speak, but it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand (vv. 6-10). None of them refuted Job; let them not say only God can (vv. 11-14). They are silent; he is full of words, like new wineskins ready to burst, and will flatter no one (vv. 15-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu is right that wisdom is God's gift and not the property of the old. Whether he has it is what the next five chapters will show.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said: "I am young in years, and you are aged; therefore I was timid and afraid to declare my opinion to you. I said, 'Let days speak, and many years teach wisdom.' But it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand. It is not the old who are wise, nor the aged who understand what is right. Therefore I say, 'Listen to me; let me also declare my opinion.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said: I am young in years, and you are aged; therefore I was timid and afraid to declare my opinion to you. I said, Let days speak, and many years teach wisdom.

He has kept quiet out of respect, as a young man should. He expected the old men to show their wisdom. They did not.

But it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand. It is not the old who are wise, nor the aged who understand what is right. Therefore I say, Listen to me; let me also declare my opinion. Understanding is not a matter of grey hair. It comes from God's Spirit, the breath God breathed into man at the beginning. Job had quoted the friends' proverb, Wisdom is with the aged (12:12), and answered it: With God are wisdom and might. Elihu agrees.

That is a true word for the church. Paul told a young pastor, Let no one despise you for your youth (1 Tim 4:12), and he taught that God's things are known not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit (1 Cor 2:13). Age deserves respect. It does not guarantee wisdom, and youth does not rule it out.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I waited for your words, I listened for your wise sayings, while you searched out what to say. I gave you my attention, and, behold, there was none among you who refuted Job or who answered his words. Beware lest you say, 'We have found wisdom; God may vanquish him, not a man.' He has not directed his words against me, and I will not answer him with your speeches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I waited for your words, I listened for your wise sayings, while you searched out what to say. I gave you my attention, and, behold, there was none among you who refuted Job or who answered his words.

Searched out: the friends' favourite verb once more (5:27; 8:8). They searched and searched for what to say, and none of them actually answered Job. Elihu has been listening carefully, and he has noticed what the friends never admitted: they lost the argument.

Beware lest you say, We have found wisdom; God may vanquish him, not a man. He has not directed his words against me, and I will not answer him with your speeches. Do not retreat into saying "only God can deal with him". Elihu promises a fresh approach: he will not recycle their arguments. How far he keeps that promise is the question of the next chapters. At times he says new and true things. At times he sounds exactly like them.

verseByVerse.quote: "They are dismayed; they answer no more; they have not a word to say. And shall I wait, because they do not speak, because they stand there, and answer no more? I also will answer with my share; I also will declare my opinion. For I am full of words; the spirit within me constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins ready to burst. I must speak, that I may find relief; I must open my lips and answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They are dismayed; they answer no more; they have not a word to say. And shall I wait, because they do not speak, because they stand there, and answer no more? I also will answer with my share; I also will declare my opinion.

For I am full of words; the spirit within me constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins ready to burst. I must speak, that I may find relief; I must open my lips and answer.

He is bursting to speak, like new wine fermenting in a sealed skin. Jesus used the picture: new wine is put into fresh wineskins (Matt 9:17). A prophet described the same compulsion: there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones (Jer 20:9).

Readers have heard this preface two ways. Some hear a true messenger, pressed by God's Spirit to speak, preparing for the voice from the whirlwind. Others hear a young man in love with his own words: seventeen verses about how much he has to say before he says any of it. Both readings have something in the text to stand on. What settles it is the end of the book: when the LORD speaks, he rebukes the three friends by name and commends Job, and he says nothing about Elihu at all, neither thanks nor rebuke (42:7-9). Elihu says many true things. He is not the last word. God is.

verseByVerse.quote: I will not show partiality to any man or use flattery toward any person. For I do not know how to flatter, else my Maker would soon take me away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will not show partiality to any man or use flattery toward any person. For I do not know how to flatter, else my Maker would soon take me away.

He will not take sides for anyone's sake, and he will not flatter. That is the right spirit for anyone who speaks about God: God shows no partiality (Acts 10:34), and his servants should not either. Job had accused the friends of showing partiality to God, lying in his defence (13:8). Elihu promises to tell the truth to everyone, Job and friends alike. It is a fair promise. The best test of it will be whether he can tell the difference between Job's words, which were sometimes wrong, and Job's life, which was not.

32.theology:
Elihu is right that understanding is the Spirit's gift and not the property of the old (vv. 8-9; 1 Cor 2:12-13), and right that Job has begun to justify himself at God's expense (v. 2; 40:8). God neither rebukes nor commends him at the end (42:7-9): he says true things and is not the last word.

Elihu's anger burns against Job and the friends; God's burns against the friends alone (42:7).
32.examples:
The only speaker with a family tree.

Burned with anger, four times.

He justified himself rather than God: a charge God will press.

It is not the old who are wise.

New wineskins ready to burst.

God says nothing about Elihu at the end.

33.title: I Have Found a Ransom
33.text: <sup>1</sup>"But now, hear my speech, O Job, and listen to all my words.<sup>2</sup>Behold, I open my mouth; the tongue in my mouth speaks.<sup>3</sup>My words declare the uprightness of my heart, and what my lips know they speak sincerely.<sup>4</sup>The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.<sup>5</sup>Answer me, if you can; set your words in order before me; take your stand.<sup>6</sup>Behold, I am toward God as you are; I too was pinched off from a piece of clay.<sup>7</sup>Behold, no fear of me need terrify you; my pressure will not be heavy upon you.<sup>8</sup>"Surely you have spoken in my ears, and I have heard the sound of your words.<sup>9</sup>You say, 'I am pure, without transgression; I am clean, and there is no iniquity in me.<sup>10</sup>Behold, he finds occasions against me, he counts me as his enemy,<sup>11</sup>he puts my feet in the stocks and watches all my paths.'<sup>12</sup>"Behold, in this you are not right. I will answer you, for God is greater than man.<sup>13</sup>Why do you contend against him, saying, 'He will answer none of man's words'?<sup>14</sup>For God speaks in one way, and in two, though man does not perceive it.<sup>15</sup>In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falls on men, while they slumber on their beds,<sup>16</sup>then he opens the ears of men and terrifies them with warnings,<sup>17</sup>that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man;<sup>18</sup>he keeps back his soul from the pit, his life from perishing by the sword.<sup>19</sup>"Man is also rebuked with pain on his bed and with continual strife in his bones,<sup>20</sup>so that his life loathes bread, and his appetite the choicest food.<sup>21</sup>His flesh is so wasted away that it cannot be seen, and his bones that were not seen stick out.<sup>22</sup>His soul draws near the pit, and his life to those who bring death.<sup>23</sup>If there be for him an angel, a mediator, one of the thousand, to declare to man what is right for him,<sup>24</sup>and he is merciful to him, and says, 'Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom;<sup>25</sup>let his flesh become fresh with youth; let him return to the days of his youthful vigor';<sup>26</sup>then man prays to God, and he accepts him; he sees his face with a shout of joy, and he restores to man his righteousness.<sup>27</sup>He sings before men and says: 'I sinned and perverted what was right, and it was not repaid to me.<sup>28</sup>He has redeemed my soul from going down into the pit, and my life shall look upon the light.'<sup>29</sup>"Behold, God does all these things, twice, three times, with a man,<sup>30</sup>to bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be lighted with the light of life.<sup>31</sup>Pay attention, O Job, listen to me; be silent, and I will speak.<sup>32</sup>If you have any words, answer me; speak, for I desire to justify you.<sup>33</sup>If not, listen to me; be silent, and I will teach you wisdom."
33.overview: Elihu addresses Job: he speaks sincerely, made by God's Spirit, and he is clay like Job, so Job need not fear him (vv. 1-7). Job has claimed to be pure and said God counts him an enemy; he is wrong, for God is greater than man and does answer (vv. 8-13). God speaks in one way and in two: in warning dreams that turn a man from pride and the pit, and in pain that wastes him until he nears death (vv. 14-22). If a mediator is there to say, Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom, the man is restored, prays and is accepted, sees God's face with joy and confesses his sin; God does this again and again to bring him to the light of life. Elihu wants to justify Job (vv. 23-33).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — I Too Was Pinched Off from Clay
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hear my speech, O Job; Elihu speaks sincerely, made by the Spirit of God (vv. 1-4). Let Job answer him: I am toward God as you are; I too was pinched off from a piece of clay. Behold, no fear of me need terrify you (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu offers to meet Job as an equal. It is a kinder start than the friends', and a faint picture of the Mediator Job wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now, hear my speech, O Job, and listen to all my words. Behold, I open my mouth; the tongue in my mouth speaks. My words declare the uprightness of my heart, and what my lips know they speak sincerely. The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now, hear my speech, O Job, and listen to all my words. Behold, I open my mouth; the tongue in my mouth speaks. My words declare the uprightness of my heart, and what my lips know they speak sincerely. The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.

Elihu turns to Job and addresses him by name, O Job, which the three friends never once did in all their speeches. He promises honesty, and grounds it where he grounded his right to speak: the Spirit of God made him, the breath of the Almighty keeps him alive (32:8; Gen 2:7). Whatever else is true of Elihu, he knows where his life comes from.

verseByVerse.quote: Answer me, if you can; set your words in order before me; take your stand. Behold, I am toward God as you are; I too was pinched off from a piece of clay. Behold, no fear of me need terrify you; my pressure will not be heavy upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Answer me, if you can; set your words in order before me; take your stand. Behold, I am toward God as you are; I too was pinched off from a piece of clay. Behold, no fear of me need terrify you; my pressure will not be heavy upon you.

Job had asked God, let not dread of you terrify me (13:21), and longed for an arbiter who was a man, as I am (9:32). Elihu steps forward almost as if to be that: I am clay too, pinched off the same lump as you; you need not be afraid of me. It is gracious, and it is a kinder beginning than the friends made.

But Elihu cannot be what Job needs, because he is only clay. The arbiter Job longed for had to be able to lay his hand on God as well as on man (9:33). Only one person has ever been both. Elihu's gentleness is a faint outline; Christ is the portrait.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — In This You Are Not Right
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job has said, I am pure, without transgression, and that God counts him an enemy and watches his paths (vv. 8-11). Behold, in this you are not right. I will answer you, for God is greater than man. Why does Job complain that God does not answer (vv. 12-13)?
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu has listened to Job, and he quotes him fairly for the most part. His point: God has not been silent; Job has not been hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Surely you have spoken in my ears, and I have heard the sound of your words. You say, 'I am pure, without transgression; I am clean, and there is no iniquity in me. Behold, he finds occasions against me, he counts me as his enemy, he puts my feet in the stocks and watches all my paths.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Surely you have spoken in my ears, and I have heard the sound of your words. You say, I am pure, without transgression; I am clean, and there is no iniquity in me. Behold, he finds occasions against me, he counts me as his enemy, he puts my feet in the stocks and watches all my paths.

Elihu has been listening, and most of this is Job's own words: count me as your enemy (13:24), you put my feet in the stocks and watch all my paths (13:27). He quotes Job fairly there. The first line overstates him. Job never claimed to be without any sin; he asked God to pardon his transgression (7:21) and spoke of the iniquities of his youth (13:26). What Job denied was sin that could explain this suffering. Elihu, like the friends, has flattened that distinction a little. But he has heard far more than they did.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, in this you are not right. I will answer you, for God is greater than man. Why do you contend against him, saying, 'He will answer none of man's words'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, in this you are not right. I will answer you, for God is greater than man. Why do you contend against him, saying, He will answer none of man's words?

Here is Elihu's charge. Not that Job sinned before his trouble, but that he is wrong now in how he speaks of God: as if God owed him an answer and had refused to give it. Job had said, I cry to you for help and you do not answer me (30:20). Elihu replies: God is greater than man; he is not bound to answer on our terms. And God has not been silent. You have not been hearing him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — God Speaks in One Way, and in Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For God speaks in one way, and in two, though man does not perceive it (v. 14): in dreams that warn a man and turn him from pride and from the pit (vv. 15-18), and in pain on his bed, when he cannot eat, his flesh wastes away, and he draws near to death (vv. 19-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu's real contribution: suffering can be God's speech, meant to rescue, not to repay. It is true, and it was not the reason for Job's suffering.

verseByVerse.quote: For God speaks in one way, and in two, though man does not perceive it. In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falls on men, while they slumber on their beds, then he opens the ears of men and terrifies them with warnings, that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man; he keeps back his soul from the pit, his life from perishing by the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God speaks in one way, and in two, though man does not perceive it. In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falls on men, while they slumber on their beds, then he opens the ears of men and terrifies them with warnings, that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man; he keeps back his soul from the pit, his life from perishing by the sword.

This is the heart of what Elihu adds. God speaks, and more than one way. First, at night: dreams that frighten a man away from what he was about to do, that cut his pride short before it ruins him, that keep him from the grave. Eliphaz's night vision gave him a doctrine to use against Job (4:13). Elihu's night warnings are rescues.

Hebrews begins with the same thought and brings it to its end: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Heb 1:1-2). God speaks in one way and in two, says Elihu. In the end he spoke in a Son, and everything he has to say to us is in him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Man is also rebuked with pain on his bed and with continual strife in his bones, so that his life loathes bread, and his appetite the choicest food. His flesh is so wasted away that it cannot be seen, and his bones that were not seen stick out. His soul draws near the pit, and his life to those who bring death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Man is also rebuked with pain on his bed and with continual strife in his bones, so that his life loathes bread, and his appetite the choicest food. His flesh is so wasted away that it cannot be seen, and his bones that were not seen stick out. His soul draws near the pit, and his life to those who bring death.

The second way God speaks is pain. Illness on the bed, aching bones, no appetite, flesh wasting until the bones show, death coming near. Elihu is describing Job, and he says: this too can be God speaking.

That is a real step beyond the friends. They asked what Job had done to deserve it. Elihu asks what God might be saying through it. Suffering, he says, can be God's warning and his discipline, meant to rescue a man, not to repay him. Scripture agrees: Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word (Ps 119:67). It is good for me that I was afflicted, that I might learn your statutes (Ps 119:71). God disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness (Heb 12:10). A believer in pain may ask God what he is teaching, and should.

But hold the limit. This is not why Job suffered; the prologue said his suffering was without reason in him (2:3). Elihu has found a true word about suffering. He is still applying it to a man whose case it does not fit. Pain can be discipline. Not all pain is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–33 — I Have Found a Ransom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If there be for him an angel, a mediator, one of the thousand, who is gracious to him and says, Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom (vv. 23-24), his flesh will be renewed, he will pray and see God's face with joy, and confess, I sinned ... and it was not repaid to me (vv. 25-28). God does this again and again, that he may be lighted with the light of life (vv. 29-30). Let Job listen, or answer; Elihu wants to justify him (vv. 31-33).
verseByVerse.theology: The clearest picture in the book of a mediator who pays a ransom. The New Testament names him: one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Tim 2:5-6).

verseByVerse.quote: If there be for him an angel, a mediator, one of the thousand, to declare to man what is right for him, and he is merciful to him, and says, 'Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom;
verseByVerse.commentary:
If there be for him an angel, a mediator, one of the thousand, to declare to man what is right for him, and he is merciful to him, and says, Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom.

This is the high point of Elihu's speeches, and one of the clearest pictures of the gospel in the Old Testament. A man is dying, near the pit. Then, if there is a messenger from God, a mediator, one in a thousand, who speaks up for him and shows him the right way; who is gracious to him and says, Let him go; do not send him down to the grave; I have found a ransom.

Two words here carry the whole Bible's hope. Mediator is the word Job used when he said his friends were his mockers when they should have been his spokesmen (16:20): one who stands between and speaks for another. Ransom is the price paid to set a condemned life free. The psalmist knew that no human being can pay it: Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life, for the ransom of their life is costly (Ps 49:7-8).

Elihu speaks of a heavenly messenger who finds a ransom. The New Testament speaks of a Mediator who is the ransom. For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Tim 2:5-6). Both of Elihu's words, in one sentence. The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). The price that no man could pay, God paid.

verseByVerse.quote: let his flesh become fresh with youth; let him return to the days of his youthful vigor'; then man prays to God, and he accepts him; he sees his face with a shout of joy, and he restores to man his righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let his flesh become fresh with youth; let him return to the days of his youthful vigor; then man prays to God, and he accepts him; he sees his face with a shout of joy, and he restores to man his righteousness.

The dying man is restored: his skin fresh as a child's, as Naaman's was when his skin disease was cleansed in the Jordan: his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean (2 Kgs 5:14). He prays, God accepts him, he sees God's face and shouts for joy, and God gives him back his righteousness. Every part of this will happen to Job: the LORD will accept his prayer (42:9), he will see God (42:5), and he will be restored. It happens to every believer in Christ, whose ransom has been paid: accepted, righteous, and one day raised with a body that will never wear out.

verseByVerse.quote: He sings before men and says: 'I sinned and perverted what was right, and it was not repaid to me. He has redeemed my soul from going down into the pit, and my life shall look upon the light.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He sings before men and says: I sinned and perverted what was right, and it was not repaid to me. He has redeemed my soul from going down into the pit, and my life shall look upon the light.

The rescued man sings, and his song is a confession. I sinned; I twisted what was right; and I did not get what I deserved. That is the song of grace. I acknowledged my sin to you ... and you forgave the iniquity of my sin (Ps 32:5). It is the prodigal's Father, I have sinned (Luke 15:21), met by a father running down the road. He has redeemed my soul: God redeems your life from the pit (Ps 103:4).

Notice that the restored man confesses sin. Elihu's gospel is not "you were innocent all along" but "you were not, and you were ransomed." That is closer to the truth about every human being than anything the friends said, and it is the truth Job will come to when he sees God (42:6).

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, God does all these things, twice, three times, with a man, to bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be lighted with the light of life. Pay attention, O Job, listen to me; be silent, and I will speak. If you have any words, answer me; speak, for I desire to justify you. If not, listen to me; be silent, and I will teach you wisdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, God does all these things, twice, three times, with a man, to bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be lighted with the light of life.

God does not give up after one warning. Again and again he works to bring a man back from the edge. And the goal is the light of life, the very phrase Jesus used of himself: I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life (John 8:12). The man brought back from the pit lives in the light of Christ.

Pay attention, O Job, listen to me; be silent, and I will speak. If you have any words, answer me; speak, for I desire to justify you. If not, listen to me; be silent, and I will teach you wisdom. I desire to justify you: Elihu, unlike the friends, wants Job to come out in the right. His manner is lecturing, and he will go on for four more chapters. But his heart, at least here, is for Job.

33.theology:
Suffering can be God's speech, a warning and discipline meant to rescue (vv. 14-22; Ps 119:71; Heb 12:10-11): Elihu's real advance on the friends, though not the reason for Job's suffering (2:3).

The mediator who finds a ransom (vv. 23-24) is fulfilled in one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Tim 2:5-6). No man can ransom another (Ps 49:7-8); God did.
33.examples:
Elihu offers to meet Job as clay to clay.

He quotes Job fairly, mostly.

God speaks in one way, and in two: and at last by his Son.

Pain as God's speech, with the limit stated.

A mediator ... I have found a ransom: 1 Timothy 2:5-6.

Flesh fresh as a child's: Naaman.

The light of life: John 8:12.

34.title: Far Be It from God to Do Wickedness
34.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Elihu answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Hear my words, you wise men, and give ear to me, you who know;<sup>3</sup>for the ear tests words as the palate tastes food.<sup>4</sup>Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good.<sup>5</sup>For Job has said, 'I am in the right, and God has taken away my right;<sup>6</sup>in spite of my right I am counted a liar; my wound is incurable, though I am without transgression.'<sup>7</sup>What man is like Job, who drinks up scoffing like water,<sup>8</sup>who travels in company with evildoers and walks with wicked men?<sup>9</sup>For he has said, 'It profits a man nothing that he should take delight in God.'<sup>10</sup>"Therefore, hear me, you men of understanding: far be it from God that he should do wickedness, and from the Almighty that he should do wrong.<sup>11</sup>For according to the work of a man he will repay him, and according to his ways he will make it befall him.<sup>12</sup>Of a truth, God will not do wickedly, and the Almighty will not pervert justice.<sup>13</sup>Who gave him charge over the earth, and who laid on him the whole world?<sup>14</sup>If he should set his heart to it and gather to himself his spirit and his breath,<sup>15</sup>all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust.<sup>16</sup>"If you have understanding, hear this; listen to what I say.<sup>17</sup>Shall one who hates justice govern? Will you condemn him who is righteous and mighty,<sup>18</sup>who says to a king, 'Worthless one,' and to nobles, 'Wicked man,'<sup>19</sup>who shows no partiality to princes, nor regards the rich more than the poor, for they are all the work of his hands?<sup>20</sup>In a moment they die; at midnight the people are shaken and pass away, and the mighty are taken away by no human hand.<sup>21</sup>"For his eyes are on the ways of a man, and he sees all his steps.<sup>22</sup>There is no gloom or deep darkness where evildoers may hide themselves.<sup>23</sup>For God has no need to consider a man further, that he should go before God in judgment.<sup>24</sup>He shatters the mighty without investigation and sets others in their place.<sup>25</sup>Thus, knowing their works, he overturns them in the night, and they are crushed.<sup>26</sup>He strikes them for their wickedness in a place for all to see,<sup>27</sup>because they turned aside from following him and had no regard for any of his ways,<sup>28</sup>so that they caused the cry of the poor to come to him, and he heard the cry of the afflicted—<sup>29</sup>When he is quiet, who can condemn? When he hides his face, who can behold him, whether it be a nation or a man?—<sup>30</sup>that a godless man should not reign, that he should not ensnare the people.<sup>31</sup>"For has anyone said to God, 'I have borne punishment; I will not offend any more;<sup>32</sup>teach me what I do not see; if I have done iniquity, I will do it no more'?<sup>33</sup>Will he then make repayment to suit you, because you reject it? For you must choose, and not I; therefore declare what you know.<sup>34</sup>Men of understanding will say to me, and the wise man who hears me will say:<sup>35</sup>'Job speaks without knowledge; his words are without insight.'<sup>36</sup>Would that Job were tried to the end, because he answers like wicked men.<sup>37</sup>For he adds rebellion to his sin; he claps his hands among us and multiplies his words against God."
34.overview: Elihu appeals to the wise. Job has said he is in the right and God has taken away his right; Job drinks scoffing like water and says there is no profit in delighting in God (vv. 1-9). But God cannot do wickedness or pervert justice; he answers to no one, and if he withdrew his breath all flesh would perish; he shows no partiality, for all are the work of his hands (vv. 10-20). His eyes see every step; he needs no trial to judge the mighty; he hears the cry of the poor; when he is silent, who can condemn him? Job speaks without knowledge and adds rebellion to his sin (vv. 21-37).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — What Man Is Like Job?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu appeals to the wise, for the ear tests words as the palate tastes food (vv. 1-4). Job has said he is in the right and God has taken away his right (vv. 5-6). What man is like Job, who drinks up scoffing like water, keeping company with evildoers, saying there is no profit in delighting in God (vv. 7-9)?
verseByVerse.theology: Here Elihu starts to sound like the friends: their language, and their trick of putting the wicked's words in Job's mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Elihu answered and said: "Hear my words, you wise men, and give ear to me, you who know; for the ear tests words as the palate tastes food.
