Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good. For Job has said, 'I am in the right, and God has taken away my right; in spite of my right I am counted a liar; my wound is incurable, though I am without transgression.' What man is like Job, who drinks up scoffing like water, who travels in company with evildoers and walks with wicked men? For he has said, 'It profits a man nothing that he should take delight in God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elihu's second speech. His introduction (ch 32) and his real contribution, that God speaks through pain and provides a ransom (ch 33), have been set out. Much of this chapter restates what the friends and Elihu have already said about God's justice. What is new needs watching closely, because Elihu begins to slide.

Hear my words, you wise men ... for the ear tests words as the palate tastes food. That is Job's own line (12:11), almost word for word. For Job has said, I am in the right, and God has taken away my right; that is fair, Job said it (27:2). And let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good is a sound instinct: test the arguments and keep what is true, as Paul says, test everything; hold fast what is good (1 Thess 5:21). The trouble is what Elihu does next.

What man is like Job, who drinks up scoffing like water, who travels in company with evildoers and walks with wicked men? For he has said, It profits a man nothing that he should take delight in God. Now listen to the voice. Drinks ... like water is Eliphaz's picture of a man who drinks injustice like water (15:16). In company with evildoers is the friends' charge. And the last sentence is not Job's at all. Job described the wicked saying, what profit do we get if we pray to him? (21:15), and said their counsel was far from him. Elihu has put the wicked's words into Job's mouth, exactly as Eliphaz did (22:13, 17). The young man who promised not to answer Job with your speeches (32:14) is doing it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–20 — Far Be It from God to Do Wickedness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Far be it from God that he should do wickedness; he repays each man by his ways and does not pervert justice (vv. 10-12). No one appointed him over the earth; if he withdrew his breath all flesh would die (vv. 13-15). Can one who hates justice govern? He shows no partiality to kings or rich, for they are all the work of his hands, and the mighty die in a moment (vv. 16-20).
verseByVerse.theology: True, and needed: Job had said things that put God in the wrong. God is just, and the one who gives every breath owes no one an explanation.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, hear me, you men of understanding: far be it from God that he should do wickedness, and from the Almighty that he should do wrong. For according to the work of a man he will repay him, and according to his ways he will make it befall him. Of a truth, God will not do wickedly, and the Almighty will not pervert justice. Who gave him charge over the earth, and who laid on him the whole world? If he should set his heart to it and gather to himself his spirit and his breath, all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, hear me, you men of understanding: far be it from God that he should do wickedness, and from the Almighty that he should do wrong ... Of a truth, God will not do wickedly, and the Almighty will not pervert justice.

Bildad said it (8:3), and it is true. Paul says it: Is there injustice on God's part? By no means! (Rom 9:14). And Job needed to hear it, because he had said God put me in the wrong (19:6) and turned cruel to me (30:21). God is not unjust, however things look from the ash heap.

Who gave him charge over the earth ...? If he should set his heart to it and gather to himself his spirit and his breath, all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust. God answers to no one; no one handed him the world to run. Every breath in every creature is his, lent moment by moment. When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust. When you send forth your Spirit, they are created (Ps 104:29-30). A God like that is not a debtor to anyone.

Notice too according to the work of a man he will repay him (v. 11). That is true, and the New Testament says it as plainly: He will render to each one according to his works (Rom 2:6); we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Cor 5:10). The question has never been whether God repays. It is when. The friends, and Elihu here, expected the repayment to be visible now, in each man's health and wealth. Scripture places the full reckoning at the last day. Put the truth at the wrong time and it becomes a lie about the sufferer in front of you.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you have understanding, hear this; listen to what I say. Shall one who hates justice govern? Will you condemn him who is righteous and mighty, who says to a king, 'Worthless one,' and to nobles, 'Wicked man,' who shows no partiality to princes, nor regards the rich more than the poor, for they are all the work of his hands? In a moment they die; at midnight the people are shaken and pass away, and the mighty are taken away by no human hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shall one who hates justice govern? Will you condemn him who is righteous and mighty, who says to a king, Worthless one, and to nobles, Wicked man, who shows no partiality to princes, nor regards the rich more than the poor, for they are all the work of his hands?

Could a God who hated justice rule the world? He tells kings to their face what they are; he treats rich and poor alike, for they are all the work of his hands. That was Job's own argument about his servants: Did not he who made me in the womb make him? (31:15). Elihu turns it on Job: if God is impartial with kings, will he be unjust to you? In a moment they die ... and the mighty are taken away by no human hand. The great fall overnight at his word.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's eyes see every step; there is no darkness to hide in (vv. 21-22). He needs no trial to judge the mighty; he hears the cry of the poor (vv. 23-28); when he is silent, who can condemn him (vv. 29-30)? Has anyone asked God to teach him (vv. 31-33)? Job speaks without knowledge; let him be tried to the end, for he adds rebellion to his sin (vv. 34-37).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu is right that Job has spoken without knowledge; God will say the same (38:2). He is wrong that Job has added rebellion to sin; God will say Job spoke rightly (42:7).

verseByVerse.quote: "For his eyes are on the ways of a man, and he sees all his steps. There is no gloom or deep darkness where evildoers may hide themselves. For God has no need to consider a man further, that he should go before God in judgment. He shatters the mighty without investigation and sets others in their place. Thus, knowing their works, he overturns them in the night, and they are crushed. He strikes them for their wickedness in a place for all to see, because they turned aside from following him and had no regard for any of his ways, so that they caused the cry of the poor to come to him, and he heard the cry of the afflicted— When he is quiet, who can condemn? When he hides his face, who can behold him, whether it be a nation or a man?— that a godless man should not reign, that he should not ensnare the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For his eyes are on the ways of a man, and he sees all his steps. There is no gloom or deep darkness where evildoers may hide themselves. God sees everything; the deep darkness of 3:5 hides no one.

For God has no need to consider a man further, that he should go before God in judgment. Here is a new point, aimed straight at Job's great demand. Job has wanted a hearing, a day in court (13:18; 23:4; 31:35). Elihu says: God does not need one. He knows everything already; he does not have to hold an inquiry. That is true. And yet in a few chapters God will grant Job the audience he asked for (38:1). He did not owe it. He gave it. That is grace.

He shatters the mighty without investigation ... because they turned aside from following him ... so that they caused the cry of the poor to come to him, and he heard the cry of the afflicted. God hears the poor; that answers Job's complaint that the dying groan and God does nothing (24:12). When he is quiet, who can condemn? When he hides his face, who can behold him? God's silence is not injustice. Job took God's silence as proof that God was against him (30:20). Elihu is right that silence proves nothing of the kind.

And the mighty whom God shatters, he replaces: sets others in their place (v. 24). Daniel praised the same God: he removes kings and sets up kings (Dan 2:21). History is not a machine running on its own. Every throne is held at his pleasure, and he takes it back when he chooses, often suddenly, in the night (v. 25).

verseByVerse.quote: "For has anyone said to God, 'I have borne punishment; I will not offend any more; teach me what I do not see; if I have done iniquity, I will do it no more'? Will he then make repayment to suit you, because you reject it? For you must choose, and not I; therefore declare what you know. Men of understanding will say to me, and the wise man who hears me will say: 'Job speaks without knowledge; his words are without insight.' Would that Job were tried to the end, because he answers like wicked men. For he adds rebellion to his sin; he claps his hands among us and multiplies his words against God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For has anyone said to God, I have borne punishment; I will not offend any more; teach me what I do not see; if I have done iniquity, I will do it no more? Elihu wants Job to say this. Job had said something very like it long ago: Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand how I have gone astray (6:24).

Will he then make repayment to suit you, because you reject it? God does not adjust his justice to our preferences. That is a fair word to Job, who had wanted God's ways to fit his expectations. It is a fair word to the friends too, who wanted them to fit theirs.

Men of understanding will say to me ... Job speaks without knowledge; his words are without insight. Here Elihu is right, and God will say the same thing in almost the same words: Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge? (38:2). Job had spoken about things he did not understand.

Would that Job were tried to the end, because he answers like wicked men. For he adds rebellion to his sin; he claps his hands among us and multiplies his words against God. And here Elihu is wrong. He wishes Job more suffering, calls his answers those of the wicked, and assumes a sin to which Job has added rebellion. That is the friends' verdict, and God will overturn it: you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has (42:7). In two verses Elihu is right about Job's words and wrong about Job's heart. It is a warning to every critic, however sound his doctrine: it is possible to be right about what a sufferer said and wrong about who he is.

34.theology:
God cannot do wrong (vv. 10-12; Rom 9:14), every breath is his (vv. 14-15; Ps 104:29-30), and his silence is not injustice (v. 29). God owes no one a hearing (v. 23), and grants Job one as grace (38:1).

Elihu slides into the friends' voice (vv. 7-9) and is half right: Job spoke without knowledge (v. 35; 38:2), but did not add rebellion to sin (v. 37; 42:7).
34.examples:
Job's own words (12:11) quoted back.

The wicked's creed put in Job's mouth, as Eliphaz did.

Far be it from God that he should do wickedness.

God needs no trial, and gives Job one anyway.

Job speaks without knowledge: God agrees. He adds rebellion to his sin: God does not.

35.title: Songs in the Night
35.text: <sup>1</sup>And Elihu answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Do you think this to be just? Do you say, 'It is my right before God,'<sup>3</sup>that you ask, 'What advantage have I? How am I better off than if I had sinned?'<sup>4</sup>I will answer you and your friends with you.<sup>5</sup>Look at the heavens, and see; and behold the clouds, which are higher than you.<sup>6</sup>If you have sinned, what do you accomplish against him? And if your transgressions are multiplied, what do you do to him?<sup>7</sup>If you are righteous, what do you give to him? Or what does he receive from your hand?<sup>8</sup>Your wickedness concerns a man like yourself, and your righteousness a son of man.<sup>9</sup>"Because of the multitude of oppressions people cry out; they call for help because of the arm of the mighty.<sup>10</sup>But none says, 'Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night,<sup>11</sup>who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and makes us wiser than the birds of the heavens?'<sup>12</sup>There they cry out, but he does not answer, because of the pride of evil men.<sup>13</sup>Surely God does not hear an empty cry, nor does the Almighty regard it.<sup>14</sup>How much less when you say that you do not see him, that the case is before him, and you are waiting for him!<sup>15</sup>And now, because his anger does not punish, and he does not take much note of transgression,<sup>16</sup>Job opens his mouth in empty talk; he multiplies words without knowledge."
35.overview: Elihu asks whether it is just for Job to claim his right and ask what he gains by not sinning. Let him look at the heavens: his sin does not harm God and his righteousness gives God nothing; they affect only men (vv. 1-8). People cry out under oppression but none asks, Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night? God does not hear the empty cry of the proud, much less Job's claim that he is waiting; Job multiplies words without knowledge (vv. 9-16).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Is it just for Job to say he is in the right, and ask what he gains by not sinning (vv. 1-3)? Elihu will answer him and the friends (v. 4). Look at the sky: your sin does nothing to God, your righteousness gives him nothing; both affect only men like you (vv. 5-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu repeats Eliphaz (22:2-3). God is not harmed by us and needs nothing from us; that does not mean he does not care.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elihu answered and said: "Do you think this to be just? Do you say, 'It is my right before God,' that you ask, 'What advantage have I? How am I better off than if I had sinned?' I will answer you and your friends with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Elihu answered and said: Do you think this to be just? Do you say, It is my right before God, that you ask, What advantage have I? How am I better off than if I had sinned?

Elihu's third and shortest speech. He puts a question in Job's mouth: what good has my righteousness done me? Job never said it in those words. He said God destroys both the blameless and the wicked (9:22), and he quoted the wicked asking what profit do we get if we pray to him? (21:15). But the question deserves an answer, and it is the book's question turned round. Satan said Job served God for profit (1:9). If Job now asked what profit his goodness had brought him, Satan would have won. The whole point of Job's faith is that it is not a bargain.

I will answer you and your friends with you. Elihu will correct all four of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Look at the heavens, and see; and behold the clouds, which are higher than you. If you have sinned, what do you accomplish against him? And if your transgressions are multiplied, what do you do to him? If you are righteous, what do you give to him? Or what does he receive from your hand? Your wickedness concerns a man like yourself, and your righteousness a son of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look at the heavens, and see; and behold the clouds, which are higher than you. If you have sinned, what do you accomplish against him? ... If you are righteous, what do you give to him? ... Your wickedness concerns a man like yourself, and your righteousness a son of man.

Look up. The clouds are higher than you, and God is higher than the clouds. Your sin cannot reach up and damage him; your goodness cannot add anything to him. What you do affects other people. Eliphaz said the same (22:2-3), and what was said there stands: half of it is true. God needs nothing and cannot be harmed. But he is not indifferent. He can be grieved by his people's sin, do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God (Eph 4:30), and he delights in his servants, Have you considered my servant Job? (1:8). A God who could not be harmed and did not care would not be the God of this book.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: People cry out under oppression, but none says, Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night, who makes us wiser than the beasts (vv. 9-11)? God does not answer the proud and empty cry (vv. 12-13), much less Job's complaint that he is waiting for God (v. 14). Job opens his mouth in empty talk; he multiplies words without knowledge (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The best line in the chapter: there is a difference between crying out for relief and seeking God himself. Job, for all his faults, has been seeking God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Because of the multitude of oppressions people cry out; they call for help because of the arm of the mighty. But none says, 'Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night, who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and makes us wiser than the birds of the heavens?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of the multitude of oppressions people cry out; they call for help because of the arm of the mighty. But none says, Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night, who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and makes us wiser than the birds of the heavens?

This is the one new thing in the chapter, and it is beautiful. People who are crushed cry out. Of course they do. But crying out for relief is not the same as seeking God. How many call for help, and never ask, Where is God my Maker? They want the pain gone. They do not want him.

Who gives songs in the night: the God who, in the dark, gives his people something to sing. At night his song is with me, a prayer to the God of my life (Ps 42:8). Let me remember my song in the night (Ps 77:6). In a Philippian prison, about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God (Acts 16:25). A person who seeks God himself in suffering, not only rescue, may find a song in the night before he finds the morning.

Elihu means this as a rebuke to Job, and it does not fit him. Job has not only cried out for relief. He has cried for God: Oh, that I knew where I might find him (23:3). But the sentence is true, and every sufferer should ask it of himself: am I seeking relief, or am I seeking him?

verseByVerse.quote: There they cry out, but he does not answer, because of the pride of evil men. Surely God does not hear an empty cry, nor does the Almighty regard it. How much less when you say that you do not see him, that the case is before him, and you are waiting for him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
There they cry out, but he does not answer, because of the pride of evil men. Surely God does not hear an empty cry, nor does the Almighty regard it. God does not answer the proud, who want his gifts without him. You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly (James 4:3).

How much less when you say that you do not see him, that the case is before him, and you are waiting for him! Elihu faults Job for saying he cannot see God and is waiting for his case to be heard. But waiting for God is not sin; it is faith. Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the LORD! (Ps 27:14). And Job's case was before God, and God was about to answer it (38:1). Here Elihu is simply wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, because his anger does not punish, and he does not take much note of transgression, Job opens his mouth in empty talk; he multiplies words without knowledge."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, because his anger does not punish, and he does not take much note of transgression, Job opens his mouth in empty talk; he multiplies words without knowledge.

Because God has not struck Job down for his words, Elihu says, Job has taken advantage of God's patience and piled up empty talk, hevel, vapour. And words without knowledge is exactly the phrase God will use: Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge? (38:2). On that, Elihu and God agree. Job had said much he did not understand. What Elihu missed, God will not: that the man who said it was still his servant, and had spoken to him, and of him, rightly (42:7).

35.theology:
God cannot be harmed by our sin nor enriched by our goodness (vv. 6-7), yet he is grieved and delighted by his people (Eph 4:30; 1:8). Crying out for relief is not the same as seeking God, who gives songs in the night (v. 10; Ps 42:8).

Elihu faults Job for waiting on God (v. 14), but waiting on God is faith (Ps 27:14), and God will answer (38:1). Words without knowledge (v. 16) is the charge God himself will make (38:2).
35.examples:
What advantage have I?: Satan's question turned round.

Your sin does not harm God; it does grieve him.

God my Maker, who gives songs in the night.

Relief or God himself?

Waiting for God is faith, not sin.

36.title: He Delivers the Afflicted by Their Affliction
36.text: <sup>1</sup>And Elihu continued, and said:<sup>2</sup>"Bear with me a little, and I will show you, for I have yet something to say on God's behalf.<sup>3</sup>I will get my knowledge from afar and ascribe righteousness to my Maker.<sup>4</sup>For truly my words are not false; one who is perfect in knowledge is with you.<sup>5</sup>"Behold, God is mighty, and does not despise any; he is mighty in strength of understanding.<sup>6</sup>He does not keep the wicked alive, but gives the afflicted their right.<sup>7</sup>He does not withdraw his eyes from the righteous, but with kings on the throne he sets them forever, and they are exalted.<sup>8</sup>And if they are bound in chains and caught in the cords of affliction,<sup>9</sup>then he declares to them their work and their transgressions, that they are behaving arrogantly.<sup>10</sup>He opens their ears to instruction and commands that they return from iniquity.<sup>11</sup>If they listen and serve him, they complete their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasantness.<sup>12</sup>But if they do not listen, they perish by the sword and die without knowledge.<sup>13</sup>"The godless in heart cherish anger; they do not cry for help when he binds them.<sup>14</sup>They die in youth, and their life ends among the cult prostitutes.<sup>15</sup>He delivers the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ear by adversity.<sup>16</sup>He also allured you out of distress into a broad place where there was no cramping, and what was set on your table was full of fatness.<sup>17</sup>"But you are full of the judgment on the wicked; judgment and justice seize you.<sup>18</sup>Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing, and let not the greatness of the ransom turn you aside.<sup>19</sup>Will your cry for help avail to keep you from distress, or all the force of your strength?<sup>20</sup>Do not long for the night, when peoples vanish in their place.<sup>21</sup>Take care; do not turn to iniquity, for this you have chosen rather than affliction.<sup>22</sup>Behold, God is exalted in his power; who is a teacher like him?<sup>23</sup>Who has prescribed for him his way, or who can say, 'You have done wrong'?<sup>24</sup>"Remember to extol his work, of which men have sung.<sup>25</sup>All mankind has looked on it; man beholds it from afar.<sup>26</sup>Behold, God is great, and we know him not; the number of his years is unsearchable.<sup>27</sup>For he draws up the drops of water; they distill his mist in rain,<sup>28</sup>which the skies pour down and drop on mankind abundantly.<sup>29</sup>Can anyone understand the spreading of the clouds, the thunderings of his pavilion?<sup>30</sup>Behold, he scatters his lightning about him and covers the roots of the sea.<sup>31</sup>For by these he judges peoples; he gives food in abundance.<sup>32</sup>He covers his hands with the lightning and commands it to strike the mark.<sup>33</sup>Its crashing declares his presence; the cattle also declare that he rises.
36.overview: Elihu has more to say for God, and claims to be perfect in knowledge. God is mighty and despises no one; he gives the afflicted their right, and when his people are bound in affliction he shows them their sin and calls them back; those who listen prosper and those who do not perish (vv. 1-14). He delivers the afflicted by their affliction; let Job not be turned aside by anger, long for death, or choose iniquity over affliction (vv. 15-21). God is exalted and no one teaches him; let Job extol his work; God is great beyond knowing; he draws up the rain, thunders and throws the lightning, judging and feeding the peoples, and the crash of the storm declares his presence (vv. 22-33).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — God Is Mighty, and Does Not Despise Any
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu has more to say for God: one who is perfect in knowledge is with you (vv. 1-4). God is mighty, and does not despise any; he gives the afflicted their right and keeps his eyes on the righteous (vv. 5-7). When they are bound in affliction he shows them their sin and calls them back; those who listen prosper, those who do not perish (vv. 8-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu restates his teaching of chapter 33: affliction as God's instruction. And he claims for himself a title he will soon give to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elihu continued, and said: "Bear with me a little, and I will show you, for I have yet something to say on God's behalf. I will get my knowledge from afar and ascribe righteousness to my Maker. For truly my words are not false; one who is perfect in knowledge is with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Elihu continued, and said: Bear with me a little, and I will show you, for I have yet something to say on God's behalf. I will get my knowledge from afar and ascribe righteousness to my Maker. For truly my words are not false; one who is perfect in knowledge is with you.

Elihu's last speech, two chapters long. He will defend God, ascribe righteousness to my Maker, and that is a good aim. But listen to the last line: one who is perfect in knowledge is with you. He means himself. In the next chapter he will use exactly this phrase of God: the wondrous works of him who is perfect in knowledge (37:16). Elihu has claimed for himself, without noticing, the title that belongs to God alone. Every preacher who speaks on God's behalf should feel the warning.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, God is mighty, and does not despise any; he is mighty in strength of understanding. He does not keep the wicked alive, but gives the afflicted their right. He does not withdraw his eyes from the righteous, but with kings on the throne he sets them forever, and they are exalted. And if they are bound in chains and caught in the cords of affliction, then he declares to them their work and their transgressions, that they are behaving arrogantly. He opens their ears to instruction and commands that they return from iniquity. If they listen and serve him, they complete their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasantness. But if they do not listen, they perish by the sword and die without knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, God is mighty, and does not despise any; he is mighty in strength of understanding. A lovely line. The mighty God despises no one, however small. A bruised reed he will not break (Isa 42:3), said of the Servant who is Christ.

He does not keep the wicked alive, but gives the afflicted their right. He does not withdraw his eyes from the righteous ... And if they are bound in chains and caught in the cords of affliction, then he declares to them their work and their transgressions ... He opens their ears to instruction and commands that they return from iniquity. If they listen and serve him, they complete their days in prosperity ... But if they do not listen, they perish by the sword and die without knowledge.

This is Elihu's teaching of chapter 33 again: affliction as God's instruction, opening the ear, calling a man back from pride (33:14-30). What was said there stands, including its limit. It is true of how God often deals with his people, and it is not the explanation of Job's suffering (2:3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — He Delivers the Afflicted by Their Affliction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The godless will not cry for help when bound, and die young (vv. 13-14). He delivers the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ear by adversity (v. 15). God would lead Job out into a broad place (v. 16), but Job is full of the judgment on the wicked; let him not be turned aside by anger or the size of the ransom, nor long for the night, nor choose iniquity over affliction (vv. 17-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu's best sentence: God rescues his people not only from affliction but through it.

verseByVerse.quote: "The godless in heart cherish anger; they do not cry for help when he binds them. They die in youth, and their life ends among the cult prostitutes. He delivers the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ear by adversity. He also allured you out of distress into a broad place where there was no cramping, and what was set on your table was full of fatness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The godless in heart cherish anger; they do not cry for help when he binds them. They die in youth, and their life ends among the cult prostitutes. The godless nurse their resentment and never turn to God, even in chains.

He delivers the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ear by adversity.

This is the one truly new thought in Elihu's last speeches, and it is one of the most important sentences in the book. God does not only rescue his people from affliction. He rescues them by it. The suffering itself becomes the means of their deliverance: it opens their ears, loosens their grip on the world, drives them to God. In Hebrew the words for afflicted and affliction are almost the same, as if to say: the thing that crushes is the thing that saves.

Paul knew it: suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope (Rom 5:3-4); this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory (2 Cor 4:17). And it is the pattern of Christ himself: Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered (Heb 5:8). God delivered the world by the affliction of his Son. The believer may trust that his own affliction is not wasted.

He also allured you out of distress into a broad place where there was no cramping, and what was set on your table was full of fatness. God wants to bring Job out into open country, with a full table. He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me (Ps 18:19). Elihu does not know how true that last phrase is of Job (1:8).

verseByVerse.quote: "But you are full of the judgment on the wicked; judgment and justice seize you. Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing, and let not the greatness of the ransom turn you aside. Will your cry for help avail to keep you from distress, or all the force of your strength? Do not long for the night, when peoples vanish in their place. Take care; do not turn to iniquity, for this you have chosen rather than affliction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you are full of the judgment on the wicked; judgment and justice seize you. Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing, and let not the greatness of the ransom turn you aside.

Elihu warns Job: you are so taken up with the judgment you think the wicked deserve, and with your own case, that you may be tempted to scoff at God. The greatness of the ransom is the same word as 33:24's ransom: perhaps, do not let the price of your suffering turn you away from God; perhaps, do not think a great payment could buy you out. Either way, the one ransom that could was still to come.

Will your cry for help avail to keep you from distress ...? Do not long for the night, when peoples vanish in their place. Take care; do not turn to iniquity, for this you have chosen rather than affliction. Do not long for death, the night that swallows whole nations; Job had longed for it since chapter 3 (7:15). And do not choose sin as a way out of suffering. That is a real temptation for every sufferer, and Elihu is right to name it, though he is wrong to say Job had chosen it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–33 — God Is Great, and We Know Him Not
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behold, God is exalted in his power; who is a teacher like him? (vv. 22-23). Let Job extol his work; God is great, and we know him not; the number of his years is unsearchable (vv. 24-26). He draws up the water and pours it down as rain; his thunder rolls, his lightning strikes; by these he judges and feeds the peoples; its crashing declares his presence (vv. 27-33).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu turns from arguing to praising, and as he does, a storm begins to gather. God will speak from it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, God is exalted in his power; who is a teacher like him? Who has prescribed for him his way, or who can say, 'You have done wrong'? "Remember to extol his work, of which men have sung. All mankind has looked on it; man beholds it from afar. Behold, God is great, and we know him not; the number of his years is unsearchable.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, God is exalted in his power; who is a teacher like him? Who has prescribed for him his way, or who can say, You have done wrong?

Now Elihu turns from argument to praise, and his voice changes. God is the great Teacher, and no one teaches him: what man shows him his counsel? (Isa 40:13). No one can tell God he has done wrong. That is the answer to Job's worst charges (19:6; 30:21), and God will make it himself (40:8).

Remember to extol his work, of which men have sung. All mankind has looked on it; man beholds it from afar. Behold, God is great, and we know him not; the number of his years is unsearchable. The right response to God is not argument but praise. Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! (Rev 15:3). We know him not: he is greater than all our understanding. And his years are unsearchable, the word Eliphaz used at the start (5:9) and the psalmist sings: his greatness is unsearchable (Ps 145:3). The friends claimed to have searched God out. The book keeps saying that no one can.

verseByVerse.quote: For he draws up the drops of water; they distill his mist in rain, which the skies pour down and drop on mankind abundantly. Can anyone understand the spreading of the clouds, the thunderings of his pavilion? Behold, he scatters his lightning about him and covers the roots of the sea. For by these he judges peoples; he gives food in abundance. He covers his hands with the lightning and commands it to strike the mark. Its crashing declares his presence; the cattle also declare that he rises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he draws up the drops of water; they distill his mist in rain, which the skies pour down and drop on mankind abundantly. The water cycle: God draws the water up into the clouds and sends it down as rain. All streams run to the sea, but the sea is not full (Eccl 1:7). Ordinary weather is God at work.

Can anyone understand the spreading of the clouds, the thunderings of his pavilion? Behold, he scatters his lightning about him and covers the roots of the sea. For by these he judges peoples; he gives food in abundance. He covers his hands with the lightning and commands it to strike the mark. Its crashing declares his presence; the cattle also declare that he rises.

Clouds spreading like a tent over the sky, thunder, lightning thrown like a spear at its target. The same rain can destroy a nation's harvest or fill its barns; God did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons (Acts 14:17). And its crashing declares his presence: the thunder announces that God is near.

Many readers have noticed that Elihu seems to be describing a storm that is actually coming up as he speaks. The cattle sense it; the thunder rolls. Keep watching the sky. In a few verses the storm will break, and the LORD will speak out of it (38:1).

36.theology:
God delivers the afflicted by their affliction (v. 15): suffering can be the means of rescue (Rom 5:3-5; 2 Cor 4:17), as Christ learned obedience through what he suffered (Heb 5:8). God is great beyond our knowing, and his years are unsearchable (v. 26).

Elihu claims for himself the title perfect in knowledge (v. 4) that he gives to God (37:16), a warning to all who speak for God. His praise leads into the storm from which God speaks.
36.examples:
Perfect in knowledge: Elihu's claim, God's title.

God is mighty, and does not despise any.

He delivers the afflicted by their affliction.

God is great, and we know him not.

A storm gathering as Elihu speaks.

37.title: The Almighty: We Cannot Find Him
37.text: <sup>1</sup>"At this also my heart trembles and leaps out of its place.<sup>2</sup>Keep listening to the thunder of his voice and the rumbling that comes from his mouth.<sup>3</sup>Under the whole heaven he lets it go, and his lightning to the corners of the earth.<sup>4</sup>After it his voice roars; he thunders with his majestic voice, and he does not restrain the lightnings when his voice is heard.<sup>5</sup>God thunders wondrously with his voice; he does great things that we cannot comprehend.<sup>6</sup>For to the snow he says, 'Fall on the earth,' likewise to the downpour, his mighty downpour.<sup>7</sup>He seals up the hand of every man, that all men whom he made may know it.<sup>8</sup>Then the beasts go into their lairs, and remain in their dens.<sup>9</sup>From its chamber comes the whirlwind, and cold from the scattering winds.<sup>10</sup>By the breath of God ice is given, and the broad waters are frozen fast.<sup>11</sup>He loads the thick cloud with moisture; the clouds scatter his lightning.<sup>12</sup>They turn around and around by his guidance, to accomplish all that he commands them on the face of the habitable world.<sup>13</sup>Whether for correction or for his land or for love, he causes it to happen.<sup>14</sup>"Hear this, O Job; stop and consider the wondrous works of God.<sup>15</sup>Do you know how God lays his command upon them and causes the lightning of his cloud to shine?<sup>16</sup>Do you know the balancings of the clouds, the wondrous works of him who is perfect in knowledge,<sup>17</sup>you whose garments are hot when the earth is still because of the south wind?<sup>18</sup>Can you, like him, spread out the skies, hard as a cast metal mirror?<sup>19</sup>Teach us what we shall say to him; we cannot draw up our case because of darkness.<sup>20</sup>Shall it be told him that I would speak? Did a man ever wish that he would be swallowed up?<sup>21</sup>"And now no one looks on the light when it is bright in the skies, when the wind has passed and cleared them.<sup>22</sup>Out of the north comes golden splendor; God is clothed with awesome majesty.<sup>23</sup>The Almighty—we cannot find him; he is great in power; justice and abundant righteousness he will not violate.<sup>24</sup>Therefore men fear him; he does not regard any who are wise in their own conceit."
37.overview: Elihu trembles at the thunder of God's voice and his lightning. God commands snow and rain, stops men's work, sends whirlwind, cold and ice, and turns the clouds by his guidance, whether for correction, for his land, or for love (vv. 1-13). Let Job stop and consider God's works: does he know how the lightning shines or the clouds balance, or can he spread out the sky? No one can argue a case with God (vv. 14-20). The sky clears and golden splendour comes from the north; God is clothed with awesome majesty. The Almighty we cannot find; he is just, and men fear him; he does not regard the wise in their own conceit (vv. 21-24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Thunder of His Voice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elihu's heart trembles at the thunder of God's voice and his lightning (vv. 1-5). God commands the snow and the downpour, stops men's work and drives the beasts into their dens; the whirlwind, cold, ice and cloud do his bidding (vv. 6-12), whether for correction or for his land or for love (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu sees the storm as God's voice, and says the wisest thing in his speeches: God sends it for different reasons, and one of them is love.

verseByVerse.quote: "At this also my heart trembles and leaps out of its place. Keep listening to the thunder of his voice and the rumbling that comes from his mouth. Under the whole heaven he lets it go, and his lightning to the corners of the earth. After it his voice roars; he thunders with his majestic voice, and he does not restrain the lightnings when his voice is heard. God thunders wondrously with his voice; he does great things that we cannot comprehend.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At this also my heart trembles and leaps out of its place. Keep listening to the thunder of his voice and the rumbling that comes from his mouth. Under the whole heaven he lets it go, and his lightning to the corners of the earth.

The storm that began to gather at the end of chapter 36 is breaking, and Elihu's heart is pounding. He hears the thunder as God's voice, rolling across the sky; the lightning flashes to the ends of the earth. God thunders wondrously with his voice; he does great things that we cannot comprehend.

Scripture often hears God in the thunder: The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders (Ps 29:3). And once, when the Father spoke from heaven about his Son, the crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered (John 12:29). God's voice is too great for human ears to take in. Elihu is right to tremble. In a few moments God will speak from this storm in words.

verseByVerse.quote: For to the snow he says, 'Fall on the earth,' likewise to the downpour, his mighty downpour. He seals up the hand of every man, that all men whom he made may know it. Then the beasts go into their lairs, and remain in their dens. From its chamber comes the whirlwind, and cold from the scattering winds. By the breath of God ice is given, and the broad waters are frozen fast. He loads the thick cloud with moisture; the clouds scatter his lightning. They turn around and around by his guidance, to accomplish all that he commands them on the face of the habitable world. Whether for correction or for his land or for love, he causes it to happen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For to the snow he says, Fall on the earth, likewise to the downpour, his mighty downpour. He seals up the hand of every man, that all men whom he made may know it. Then the beasts go into their lairs, and remain in their dens.

Snow and heavy rain come at his word. When they do, work in the fields stops; every man's hand is sealed up, forced to rest, so that people may see who is really in charge. The animals take shelter. From its chamber comes the whirlwind, and cold from the scattering winds. By the breath of God ice is given, and the broad waters are frozen fast. Winter itself is his breath.

He loads the thick cloud with moisture; the clouds scatter his lightning. They turn around and around by his guidance, to accomplish all that he commands them ... Whether for correction or for his land or for love, he causes it to happen.

Here is the wisest thing Elihu says. God sends the storm for different reasons. Sometimes for correction: judgment on sin. Sometimes for his land: the earth needs rain. Sometimes for love: the word is chesed, God's covenant love, the word Job used of God's care for him (10:12). The friends knew only the first reason, and read every storm as punishment. Elihu, at his best, knows better. The same weather that judges one man waters another's field and is a gift of love to a third. A believer caught in a storm cannot tell from the storm itself which it is. He can know the God who sends it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–24 — God Is Clothed with Awesome Majesty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hear this, O Job; stop and consider the wondrous works of God (v. 14). Does Job know how God commands the lightning and balances the clouds, or can he spread out the sky (vv. 15-18)? No one can argue a case with God (vv. 19-20). Out of the north comes golden splendor; God is clothed with awesome majesty. The Almighty — we cannot find him; therefore men fear him (vv. 21-24).
verseByVerse.theology: Elihu ends by saying no one can find God. In the next verse, God finds Job.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear this, O Job; stop and consider the wondrous works of God. Do you know how God lays his command upon them and causes the lightning of his cloud to shine? Do you know the balancings of the clouds, the wondrous works of him who is perfect in knowledge, you whose garments are hot when the earth is still because of the south wind? Can you, like him, spread out the skies, hard as a cast metal mirror? Teach us what we shall say to him; we cannot draw up our case because of darkness. Shall it be told him that I would speak? Did a man ever wish that he would be swallowed up?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear this, O Job; stop and consider the wondrous works of God. Stop talking; look. Be still, and know that I am God (Ps 46:10). It is the right advice, and God is about to give Job the fullest possible opportunity to take it.

Do you know how God lays his command upon them and causes the lightning of his cloud to shine? Do you know the balancings of the clouds, the wondrous works of him who is perfect in knowledge, you whose garments are hot when the earth is still because of the south wind? Can you, like him, spread out the skies, hard as a cast metal mirror?

Elihu starts to ask Job questions: do you know how clouds float, how lightning is made? It is a foretaste of how God will speak in the next chapter, question after question. And him who is perfect in knowledge is now said of God, where Elihu had said it of himself (36:4). He has found its right owner.

Teach us what we shall say to him; we cannot draw up our case because of darkness. Shall it be told him that I would speak? Did a man ever wish that he would be swallowed up? No one can draw up a legal case against God; we are in the dark. Who would ask to be summoned before him, when it would be like being swallowed alive? Job had asked exactly that (31:35). He is about to get it, and he will not be swallowed up.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now no one looks on the light when it is bright in the skies, when the wind has passed and cleared them. Out of the north comes golden splendor; God is clothed with awesome majesty. The Almighty—we cannot find him; he is great in power; justice and abundant righteousness he will not violate. Therefore men fear him; he does not regard any who are wise in their own conceit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now no one looks on the light when it is bright in the skies, when the wind has passed and cleared them. Out of the north comes golden splendor; God is clothed with awesome majesty.

The wind sweeps the clouds away and the sky blazes, too bright to look at, and from the north comes a golden glory. God is dressed in terrifying majesty. Ezekiel saw God come the same way: behold, a stormy wind came out of the north, and a great cloud, with brightness around it, and fire flashing forth continually (Ezek 1:4). Elihu is describing the approach of God himself.

The Almighty — we cannot find him; he is great in power; justice and abundant righteousness he will not violate. Therefore men fear him; he does not regard any who are wise in their own conceit.

These are Elihu's last words. We cannot find him: it is what Job said, Oh, that I knew where I might find him (23:3). Elihu is right. No one can find God by searching. And the very next line of the book is, Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind (38:1). Job could not find God, so God came and found Job. That is the whole shape of the gospel: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10).

And the last line is a warning to everyone in the book: God does not regard any who are wise in their own conceit. Not the friends, sure they had searched him out; not Elihu, who called himself perfect in knowledge; not Job, who demanded that God answer him. Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD, and turn away from evil (Prov 3:7), the two things that were said of Job on the first page (1:1) and called wisdom in the poem (28:28). Now God speaks.

37.theology:
God sends storms, and sufferings, for different ends: for correction or for his land or for love (v. 13). No one can read God's purpose off the weather, and the friends' single explanation fails. Thunder is his voice (Ps 29:3), and his coming is glory (v. 22; Ezek 1:4).

The Almighty — we cannot find him (v. 23): and at once the LORD answers Job (38:1). Man cannot find God; God comes to man (Luke 19:10).
37.examples:
The thunder of his voice.

For correction or for his land or for love.

Elihu asks Job questions, as God will.

Perfect in knowledge: given to God at last.

Golden splendour out of the north.

We cannot find him, and God comes.

38.title: The LORD Answers from the Whirlwind: Where Were You?
38.text: Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said: 'Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge? Dress for action like a man; I will question you, and you make it known to me. Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding.' (Job 38:1–4)
38.overview: Chapter 38 is one of the great chapters of the Bible — the beginning of God's answer to Job from the whirlwind. And the answer is not what anyone expected. God does not explain why Job has suffered. He does not vindicate Job explicitly (that comes in 42:7). He does not condemn him. He asks questions — seventy questions across chapters 38–41 — about the cosmos: creation's foundations, the sea, light and darkness, the storehouses of snow and hail, lightning and rain, the Pleiades and Orion, the lion and the raven and the mountain goat. The questions are not rhetorical attacks; they are an invitation to wonder and reorientation. Job is not being bullied; he is being expanded. The God who answers from the whirlwind is bigger, stranger, more beautiful, and more trustworthy than any of the speakers — including Job — had imagined.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — God Speaks: The Foundation of the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The divine self-disclosure begins — not with explanation but with the most fundamental question: where were you at creation?
verseByVerse.theology: God's first question — 'Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?' (v. 4) — is not designed to humiliate Job but to reorient him. The question establishes the ontological difference between the Creator (present at creation, sovereign over it) and the creature (absent, dependent, derived). This is not the difference between worthy and unworthy; it is the difference between Creator and creature. Job is not being condemned for being a creature; he is being invited to occupy his actual creaturely position with appropriate wonder rather than inappropriate certainty.
verseByVerse.examples: The building metaphor of vv. 4–6 (foundations, measurements, cornerstone, morning stars singing) presents creation as a cosmic building project — an image that connects to Proverbs 8:27–31 (wisdom present at creation) and to the NT description of Christ as the one through whom all things were created (Col. 1:16; John 1:3). The creator of the cosmos is the Redeemer whom Job confessed in 19:25.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said: 'Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge? Dress for action like a man; I will question you, and you make it known to me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The opening words of the divine speech are startling in their form. God does not begin with comfort, explanation, condemnation, or vindication. He begins with a question: 'Who is this?' — and the question is not unkind; it is an invitation to self-examination. Job's words, for all their genuine integrity, have 'darkened counsel' — they have made the situation seem less comprehensible than it is, because they have treated the mystery of God's ways as though it could be fully grasped by human argument.

'Dress for action like a man' — the Hebrew is literally 'gird up your loins' — the posture of readiness for serious engagement. God is not dismissing Job; he is calling him to a more demanding form of attention. The questions that follow require more than argument; they require wonder, presence, and the willingness to be overwhelmed by what is real.

Timothy Keller: 'God's opening line to Job is not an insult but an invitation. "Who is this?" is the question that every encounter with the divine must ask: who are you, and where are you standing in relation to the God who speaks? Job has been standing in the position of the prosecutor; God invites him to the position of the creature who wonders. These are different postures, and the movement from one to the other is the most important thing that happens in chapters 38–41.'

verseByVerse.quote: Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is perhaps the most famous question in the book — and its purpose must be carefully understood. It is not a taunt ('you weren't there so shut up'). It is an ontological reminder: Job is a creature, not the Creator; a derived being, not the source; a participant in the cosmic order, not its architect. The question is not designed to produce shame but to produce accurate self-knowledge, which is the beginning of wisdom (cf. Prov. 1:7; Job 28:28).

The NT perspective on this question: the one who was 'there when I laid the foundation of the earth' is the pre-existent Word, through whom 'all things were made' (John 1:3; Col. 1:16; Prov. 8:27–31). The Redeemer whom Job confessed in 19:25 was present at creation. Job's cry for a Redeemer who lives has a cosmological grounding: his Redeemer is the one who laid the earth's foundations. The God who questions Job is the same God Job's faith has been reaching for throughout the book.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–18 — The Sea, Light, and the Gates of Death
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The divine questions expand — the boundaries of the sea, the morning that limits darkness, the gates of death.
verseByVerse.theology: The sea imagery of vv. 8–11 ('who shut in the sea with doors when it burst out from the womb?') draws on the ancient Near Eastern creation tradition in which the primordial sea (chaos) is restrained by the creator God. The sea is not an independent power; it is a creature under divine authority, bounded and governed. This has direct relevance to Job's suffering: the chaos-forces that have overwhelmed him (the Adversary, the disasters of chapters 1–2) are not free agents; they are under the same divine authority that bounds the sea.
verseByVerse.examples: The morning that 'takes hold of the skirts of the earth and shakes the wicked out of it' (v. 12–13) is a beautiful image of daily divine moral action: each dawn is a new assertion of divine authority over darkness. The wicked who operate at night (cf. 24:13–17) are shaken out by the morning light. Moral order is not an achieved state but a daily divine act.

verseByVerse.quote: Or who shut in the sea with doors when it burst out from the womb, when I made clouds its garment and thick darkness its swaddling band, and prescribed limits for it and set bars and doors, and said, 'Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sea imagery is one of the most powerful in the divine speeches. The primordial sea — which in ancient Near Eastern mythology represented chaos and the anti-creation force that the creator-god had to overcome — is here presented not as a conquered enemy but as a newborn wrapped in clouds and swaddling darkness, bounded by divine decree. The sea is not free; it is bounded. 'Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed' (v. 11).

The pastoral application is immense: the forces of chaos and suffering that have overwhelmed Job's life — the disasters, the disease, the abandonment — are all bounded. The Adversary operates within limits that God himself set (1:12; 2:6). The suffering has not exceeded its divine boundary. And the one who says to the sea 'thus far and no farther' is the same one who says to the storm of Job's life that it will end — that restoration is coming — because Job has been held within limits that God himself has set.

This verse is echoed in Mark 4:39, where Jesus rebukes the storm on the Sea of Galilee and it ceases: 'Peace! Be still!' The disciples ask 'Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?' The answer is the one who set the sea's limits in creation — the same Redeemer Job confessed in 19:25.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–38 — Light, Darkness, Weather, and the Cosmos
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The cosmic survey continues — light and darkness, snow and hail, rain and lightning, the constellations.
verseByVerse.theology: The questions of vv. 19–38 cover the full range of meteorological and astronomical phenomena: where is light's dwelling? (v. 19), the storehouses of snow and hail (v. 22), the way to where light is distributed (v. 24), the path of the thunderstorm (v. 25), rain for the uninhabited land (v. 26), the Pleiades and Orion (v. 31), the ordinances of the heavens (v. 33). Each question makes the same point: God's governance of the cosmos is comprehensive, purposive, and far beyond human comprehension.
verseByVerse.examples: The 'rain for the uninhabited desert' (vv. 26–27) is one of the most theologically significant details in the chapter: God sends rain where no human being benefits from it. Divine providence is not anthropocentric — God cares for the creation in its entirety, not merely for the parts that are useful to humans. This reorients Job's suffering: it is not the center of the universe, but it is within the governance of a God whose care is wider than Job's comprehension.

verseByVerse.quote: Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loose the belt of Orion?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The astronomical questions of vv. 31–33 are among the most beautiful in the chapter. The Pleiades (כִּימָה, Kimah) and Orion (כְּסִיל, Kesil) were the most recognizable constellations of the ancient Near East. To 'bind the chains of the Pleiades' is to prevent the spring rains that their rising announced; to 'loose the belt of Orion' is to release the winter storms that his constellation heralded. God governs the seasons through the constellations — and Job cannot.

The question is humbling not as an insult but as an invitation to appropriate creatureliness: you are a creature, not the Creator. The stars obey orders you cannot give. The seasons proceed according to a governance you cannot override. This is not a diminishment of Job's dignity — it is an invitation to the appropriate posture of a creature before the Creator: wonder, reverence, trust.

38.theology:
The divine speeches as answer that is not an answer. God's speeches do not answer Job's specific question ('why am I suffering?'). They answer a deeper question: 'who is God, and can he be trusted?' The answer to the first question (why suffering?) is never given within the book. The answer to the second (who is God?) is given comprehensively and overwhelmingly. This is, in the end, the most adequate answer available: not an explanation but an encounter with the God who is sovereign over the cosmos, who governs what he has made, and who can be trusted precisely because he is so comprehensively and purposively in control.

Creation as theological argument. The divine speeches use creation — the sea, the stars, the weather, the wild animals — as the primary theological argument. This is not a distraction from Job's question; it is the answer. The God who governs the cosmos is the same God who governs Job's suffering. The sovereignty that provides rain for the uninhabited desert is the same sovereignty that permitted the Adversary's test. To see one is to begin to trust the other.
38.examples:
Then: The divine speeches draw on ancient Near Eastern cosmological traditions — the binding of the sea, the storehouses of weather, the divine governance of constellations — and transform them: what is mythology elsewhere becomes theology here. These are not stories about competing gods but descriptions of the one sovereign God's governance of his creation. The cultural accessibility of the imagery makes the theological point land with greater force.

Now: Job 38 is a text for those who have demanded explanation from God and received questions instead. The questions are not evasions; they are the answer. To stand before the magnitude of God's governance of the cosmos — even to begin to comprehend its complexity and beauty — is to begin to find the ground on which trust can stand, even without explanation. Keller: 'God's answer to Job is not "here is why you suffered" but "here is who I am." And it is enough. Not because it eliminates the pain, but because the one who governs the constellations can be trusted with the suffering of a man on an ash heap.'

39.title: The LORD Continues: Have You Considered the Wild Creatures?
39.text: Do you know when the mountain goats give birth? Do you observe the calving of the does? Can you number the months that they fulfill, and do you know the time when they give birth... Is it by your understanding that the hawk soars and spreads his wings toward the south? (Job 39:1–2, 26)
39.overview: Chapter 39 continues God's speech from the whirlwind with a remarkable series of portraits of wild animals: the mountain goat and doe (vv. 1–4), the wild donkey (vv. 5–8), the wild ox (vv. 9–12), the ostrich (vv. 13–18), the war horse (vv. 19–25), the hawk and eagle (vv. 26–30). The animals are chosen not for their usefulness to humans but for their wildness, freedom, and the specificity of God's care for them. The cumulative effect is to demonstrate that God's governance extends to every corner of the creation — including the parts that human beings cannot control or comprehend.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Mountain Goat, Doe, Wild Donkey, and Wild Ox
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tends wild creatures that humans cannot domesticate or govern — a demonstration of comprehensive care.
verseByVerse.theology: The choice of wild animals in chapter 39 is theologically deliberate: God describes his care for creatures that humans cannot control — the wild donkey ('free from the driver's load... scorns the tumult of the city,' vv. 5–7), the wild ox ('will the wild ox consent to serve you? Will he spend the night at your manger?' vv. 9–10). These are not useful animals; they are free animals under God's direct governance, outside the sphere of human utility. Divine care extends beyond the domesticated sphere of human interest to the wild margins of creation.
verseByVerse.examples: The wild donkey's freedom ('free from the driver's load,' v. 5) and the wild ox's refusal to be harnessed (v. 9) illustrate that God's creation is not designed entirely for human use. Creation has its own integrity and freedom under God's governance — a theological point that anticipates modern ecological theology while grounding it in divine sovereignty rather than inherent nature-value.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you know when the mountain goats give birth? Do you observe the calving of the does? Can you number the months that they fulfill, and do you know the time when they give birth, when they crouch, bring forth their offspring, and are delivered of their young?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's first animal question concerns the mountain goat — one of the most inaccessible creatures of the ancient world, giving birth on rocky cliffs beyond human observation. God knows when they give birth; he counts the months of their pregnancy; he is present at their calving. Job does not know and cannot observe. The point is not to humiliate Job but to expand his conception of divine care: God is attentive to mountain goat births in places Job has never visited and cannot reach.

This has enormous pastoral import: the God who knows the moment of a mountain goat's labor knows the moment of Job's greatest suffering. The comprehensive divine attentiveness that Job has experienced as surveillance and prosecution is, in reality, the same attentiveness that God shows to the most remote and inaccessible creatures of his creation. The care is real; it is comprehensive; it extends to places Job cannot go.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–18 — The Ostrich: God's Strange Sense of Humor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ostrich — the most surprising animal portrait in the divine speeches — reveals something of God's creative delight.
verseByVerse.theology: The ostrich portrait (vv. 13–18) is the most surprising and, in a sense, the funniest in the chapter. God describes the ostrich as simultaneously foolish (she leaves her eggs in the sand, forgets they might be crushed, treats them harshly as if they were not hers, v. 16) and astonishingly fast ('when she rouses herself to flee, she laughs at the horse and his rider,' v. 18). God made the ostrich the way she is; God delights in the ostrich; the ostrich's apparent foolishness is not a failure of divine design but part of its specific and surprising character.
verseByVerse.examples: The ostrich's laughter at the horse and rider (v. 18) is one of the most unexpected images in the divine speeches — and it introduces an element of divine playfulness into what could otherwise feel like a relentless lecture. God made a creature that cannot fly, apparently abandons its eggs, and then outruns the fastest horse. This is not an accident; it is a design choice. And it says something about the God who made it: he delights in the surprising, the unexpected, the creature that defies easy categorization.

verseByVerse.quote: because God has made her forget wisdom and given her no share in understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The extraordinary statement that God 'made the ostrich forget wisdom and gave her no share in understanding' is one of the most theologically striking in chapter 39. God made an animal that is, by conventional standards, foolish — and he delights in it. This is a profound challenge to any theology that equates divine blessing with human conceptions of wisdom and goodness.

Tremper Longman: 'Job 39:17 is the most surprising theological statement in the animal portraits: God deliberately made a foolish creature. This should completely demolish any assumption that divine goodness looks like human prudence. God's creational freedom extends to the wild, the strange, and the apparently unwise. The ostrich is not a mistake; she is a feature. And she laughs at the horse and rider.'

The pastoral application: if God can delight in an apparently foolish creature that he deliberately made without conventional wisdom, perhaps God's ways in human suffering are also stranger and more deliberately designed than conventional theology suggests. The categories of wisdom and foolishness that human beings apply to divine action may be inadequate to the actual God who made ostriches.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The war horse — the most magnificent animal portrait in the chapter.
verseByVerse.theology: The war horse portrait (vv. 19–25) is the most magnificent animal description in the OT — a sustained celebration of creaturely power, beauty, and courage. 'He paws in the valley and exults in his strength; he goes out to meet the weapons... He smells the battle from afar, the thunder of the captains, and the shouting' (vv. 21, 25). The war horse is not useful in the way domestic animals are useful; it is majestic, powerful, and oriented toward combat in a way that cannot be tamed or reduced to utility.
verseByVerse.examples: The war horse does not fear the sword (v. 22), cannot be made to stand still in its excitement for battle (v. 24). It is an embodiment of creaturely power and courage that exceeds what humans can fully harness or control. God made this creature; God delights in this creature; God is asking Job whether he could have made or described such a thing.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you give the horse his might? Do you clothe his neck with a mane? Do you make him leap like the locust? His majestic snorting is terrifying.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The war horse questions are among the most beautiful in the divine speeches: 'Do you give the horse his might? Do you clothe his neck with a mane?' The expected answer is No — Job did not create the horse's power, design his mane, or instill in him the impulse to charge into battle. These are divine gifts, divine design choices, expressions of the creative freedom and delight of the God who makes things.

The mane as clothing ('do you clothe his neck with a mane?') is a detail that reveals the creator's attention to aesthetics — not just function but beauty. The war horse's mane serves no military function; it is a purely aesthetic addition that makes the creature magnificent. This is the God who made Job — and who made Job's suffering in a way that will ultimately reveal God's own character and Job's integrity.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–30 — The Hawk and the Eagle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes with the birds of prey — free, southward-migrating, nesting on cliffs, seeing from afar.
verseByVerse.theology: The hawk and eagle that close chapter 39 (vv. 26–30) represent the upper reaches of the creation — the heights of air and cliff that are as far beyond Job's governance as the depths of the sea or the remoteness of mountain goat territory. The eagle nests where Job cannot climb; she sees prey from a distance Job cannot fathom; her young 'lap up blood' (v. 30). God made and governs this creature too.
verseByVerse.examples: The eagle's far-seeing eye (v. 29, 'from there she spies out the prey; her eyes behold it from far away') is an image of comprehensive divine perception that reaches beyond human sight — a fitting close to the animal portraits and a transition to the Leviathan and Behemoth speeches of chapters 40–41.

verseByVerse.quote: Is it at your command that the eagle mounts up and makes his nest on high?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The final question of the animal sequence is among the simplest and most powerful: 'Is it at your command that the eagle mounts up?' No. The eagle does not await human instruction; it soars by divine design and divine enabling. Job cannot give that command; he cannot make the eagle rise or cause her to descend. The freedom and power of the eagle are entirely outside human governance.

And yet God governs it — 'from there she spies out the prey; her eyes behold it from far away' (v. 29). The eagle's apparently autonomous freedom is within the comprehensive governance of the God who created her. The same principle applies to every force that has appeared in Job's story: the Adversary, the disasters, the disease — none of them are free from the divine governance that allows them their scope and sets their limits. The eagle's freedom is bounded freedom; so is everything that has been unleashed against Job.

39.theology:
God's care extends to the wild margins. Chapter 39's animal portraits are theologically designed to expand Job's conception of divine governance beyond the domesticated sphere of human interest. God cares for mountain goats, wild donkeys, ostriches, war horses, and eagles — creatures that serve no human purpose, live outside human control, and inhabit the wild margins of creation. If divine care is this comprehensive in the animal world, it is at least as comprehensive in Job's world.

Divine delight in the surprising. The ostrich portrait in particular reveals something about God's character that no theodicy manual contains: God delights in the strange, the apparently foolish, the creature that defies easy categorization. This divine delight in diversity and surprise challenges every neat and tidy theology of how God must work. The God who made the ostrich can be trusted to work in ways that seem foolish to conventional wisdom (cf. 1 Cor. 1:25).
39.examples:
Then: The animals of chapter 39 include creatures from the full range of the ancient Near Eastern landscape: mountain goats and does from the rocky highlands, wild donkeys from the steppes, wild oxen from the wilderness, ostriches from the desert, war horses from the city, hawks and eagles from the heights. God's governance is as geographically comprehensive as it is taxonomically comprehensive.

Now: The animal portraits of chapter 39 have a direct contemporary pastoral application: in a world increasingly shaped by human technology and control, the wildness of God's creation is a reminder that human beings are not the center of the universe and that divine governance extends beyond the sphere of human utility. The experience of the natural world — the storm, the wild animal, the eagle in flight — can be a form of encounter with the God who governs it all. Job 38–39 commend attention to the natural world as a form of theological education.

40.title: Job's First Response and the Behemoth
40.text: Then Job answered the LORD and said: 'Behold, I am of small account; what shall I answer you? I lay my hand on my mouth. I have spoken once, and I will not answer; twice, but I will proceed no further.' (Job 40:3–5)
40.overview: Chapter 40 marks a crucial turning point — Job's first response to the divine speeches (vv. 3–5) and God's second address (vv. 6–14), followed by the introduction of Behemoth (vv. 15–24). Job's response is not yet the full transformation of 42:1–6; it is a first step — the recognition of his smallness ('I am of small account') and the silencing of his mouth. God then challenges Job directly with the question of whether he can govern moral evil (vv. 8–14), before introducing Behemoth as the first of two cosmic creatures that only God can master.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Job's First Response: Smallness and Silence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job's initial response to the divine speeches — not the full transformation but a first recognition of his smallness.
verseByVerse.theology: Job's 'I am of small account' (v. 4) is not self-condemnation — it is accurate self-assessment in the light of the divine speeches. He is not saying 'I was wrong to protest'; he is saying 'I see myself differently now.' The 'hand on the mouth' (v. 4) is the gesture of silent reverence before the overwhelming (cf. 21:5; 29:9), not the gesture of a man who has been crushed into submission. It is the beginning of the reorientation that will be completed in 42:1–6.
verseByVerse.examples: The silencing of Job's mouth (v. 4) is not the silencing that the friends demanded throughout the debate — it is a different kind of silence. The friends demanded silence as an admission of guilt; God's presence produces silence as an experience of transcendence. The difference between these two silences is the difference between condemnation and encounter.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am of small account; what shall I answer you? I lay my hand on my mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Job's response to the first divine speech is, in its brevity, one of the most theologically precise responses in the book. He does not apologize, retract his speeches, or confess sins he hasn't committed. He does not perform a dramatic spiritual transformation. He simply recognizes his smallness in the presence of the speaking God: 'I am of small account.' The encounter with the divine speeches has begun to reorient him — not by answering his questions but by changing the questioner's self-understanding.

The hand on the mouth is the gesture Job himself prescribed for others in 21:5 ('look at me and be appalled, and lay your hand over your mouth'). Now he is performing the gesture himself — not for Job's suffering but for God's speech. The astonishment he wished others would feel at his suffering, he now feels at God's self-disclosure. Something is shifting in him.

Christopher Ash: 'Job's "I am of small account" is the first movement of the transformation that chapter 42 will complete. He has not yet seen God with his eye (42:5); he has heard him. And hearing is already beginning to change him. This is the trajectory of the divine speeches: not to crush but to reorient, not to silence but to redirect the speech of a man who will, in the end, be told to pray for his friends (42:8).'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — God's Second Address: Can You Govern Moral Evil?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's most direct challenge: if Job can govern pride and wickedness, God will concede the argument.
verseByVerse.theology: God's challenge in vv. 8–14 is the most direct in the divine speeches: 'Will you even put me in the wrong? Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?' (v. 8). The challenge is honest: Job's complaint has, at times, implied divine injustice in order to defend his own innocence. God now asks: if you want to be in the right and I in the wrong, can you govern the moral universe? Can you tread down the wicked and bring them to the dust?
verseByVerse.examples: The specific challenge — 'Can you save yourself by your own right hand?' (v. 14) — is the most soteriologically significant question in the divine speeches. The expected answer is No: Job cannot save himself; only God can. This is the ground on which the gospel rests: human beings cannot achieve their own salvation; they need the God who alone has the power and right to save (cf. Ps. 44:3; Isa. 59:16; John 15:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Will you even put me in the wrong? Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's direct challenge in v. 8 is the most personally confrontational moment in the divine speeches. He has seen what Job's protest has been reaching toward: a position in which God is the defendant and Job is the plaintiff. 'Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?' — the question is devastating in its precision. Job's desire to be vindicated has sometimes edged toward an implicit desire to convict God of injustice. God names this dynamic directly.

But the naming is not condemnation. It is honesty. And God's own answer in 42:7 — 'you have spoken of me what is right' — means that even Job's most extreme speeches, for all their edge of accusation, were fundamentally oriented toward God in a way the friends' comfortable orthodoxy was not. The implicit accusation in Job's protest is judged and corrected by this question; the fundamental orientation of Job's protest is later vindicated. Both are true simultaneously.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — Behemoth: The First Chaos Creature
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behemoth — the greatest of land creatures, made by God, mastered only by God.
verseByVerse.theology: Behemoth (vv. 15–24) is typically identified with the hippopotamus — the most powerful land animal of the ancient world — though some scholars see it as a mythological chaos creature (like Leviathan) or as a combination of both.
